Recognition is deliberately conservative (axis-aligned rect/ellipse only; a tilted grid is not recognised). VERIFY. Pure classifier + grid spacing + the PDF grid-divider commit/undo/redo are unit-tested (TestShapeRecognition, TestGridDivider); gestures need the real app (no key-injection tool here) — user checklist handed over.

column2: Non-uniform lasso resize (side handles)
column5: Non-uniform lasso resize — SIDE handles. The selection box grew from 4 corner handles to 8: the four CORNERS still scale uniformly (aspect preserved, unchanged), the four SIDE midpoints (T/R/B/L) stretch ONE axis so the aspect ratio can change. Works on strokes/shapes AND images alike — a stroke/shape is points, an image is a rect, both transform by the same per-axis (fx,fy) about a fixed anchor. A side handle anchors on the OPPOSITE edge (drag the right edge, the left stays put); a corner anchors on the opposite corner as before. SHARED, one policy for both canvases (the 'one table' rule): module helpers lasso_handle_points (the 8 handle centres, used by BOTH the hit-test and the painter so a handle is grabbed exactly where it is drawn), lasso_handle_anchor (handle -> mode 'uniform'/'x'/'y' + anchor point), lasso_scale_factors (start/cur/anchor -> clamped (fx,fy)), lasso_handle_cursor. The old single _lasso_scale_factor became _lasso_scale_fx/_fy + _lasso_scale_mode on both PDFCanvas and TextPageView. The undo op 'lasso_scale' now carries (fx,fy,ax,ay) instead of (f,ax,ay) — in-memory only, no serialization change; undo/redo divide/multiply per axis. STROKE WIDTH scales by the geometric mean sqrt(fx*fy): a uniform corner keeps the old width*f exactly (so existing tests/behaviour hold), a pure one-axis stretch barely thickens the line (a defensible single scalar — width can't be per-axis). On the sheet the resize re-anchors via the existing _reanchor_selected with a per-axis transform + width_factor=sqrt(fx*fy); image w/h fall out of transform((x+w,y+h))-transform((x,y)) for free. KNOWN LIMIT (flagged, not silently dropped): a non-uniform stretch of an already-ROTATED image stretches along PAGE axes, not the image's own axes (the rect model can't skew — same reason rotation is stored as an angle and applied at render, row 118). Un-rotated images and all strokes/shapes stretch exactly. VERIFY: TestLassoSelect.test_side_handle_stretches_one_axis / test_bottom_handle_stretches_y_only (PDF, with undo/redo) + the text-sheet resize test updated to the per-axis factors; full suite green (643). Gesture feel (dragging the actual handles) still needs an in-app pass — no key/pointer-injection tool here.

column2: Merge import: drop many documents -> one, a chapter each
column5: Merge import — several documents dropped at once become ONE document with a CHAPTER per file. Two entry points, one pipeline (merge_documents): dropping files on the PAGE THUMBNAILS inserts them as chapters at the drop gap; dropping them on the WINDOW asks 'Open All' vs 'Merge...' and merges into a NEW file. The ask on the window is also how the feature is DISCOVERED (before, a multi-file drop silently opened only the first file). A single dropped file is unchanged in both places (a .pptx aside, which needs conversion). WHAT COMES ALONG: the '<name>-notes.md' sidecar's per-page notes and the '<name>-ink.json' sidecar's pasted images, both re-keyed by the chapter's page offset; ink needs NO merging code because strokes ARE native PDF ink annotations, which insert_pdf copies and load() reads back as editable strokes; anchors/callouts/text boxes ride inside the note text as '<!-- anchor:x:y -->' comments, so they follow the notes for free. A .pptx is converted (LibreOffice, off the main thread) and its SPEAKER NOTES become that chapter's notes. ORDER: natural sort by filename is the default and is the whole point of the sort key — plain sorted() gives 1, 10, 101, 2, 99 for the way lectures are actually named. 'As dropped' is offered as the alternative because the drop hands us an ORDERED file list; it is not the default because most Linux file managers fill that list in their VIEW's display order, not the order you clicked (macOS Finder is the one usually claimed to preserve click order) — so it is offered honestly labelled, not assumed. No drag-reorder inside the import dialog: chapters reorder in the outline sidebar afterwards (the dialog says so), which is one mechanism instead of two. CHAPTER REORDER: dragging a level-1 outline row moves the whole page RANGE it owns (chapter_spans: a chapter runs to the next level-1 entry). move_page_range does it in ONE select() + ONE re-key — page-by-page would re-key every model and re-render the page once per page, which a 40-page chapter feels. The destination is computed from PAGES, not from a count of chapters, so pages belonging to no chapter (a title page before the first outline entry) stay put. The payload is a string ('sidemark-chapter:N'), NOT the int the thumbnails use: both lists live in one window and an int would let a chapter be dropped on a page. TRAPS, each verified against the installed PyMuPDF rather than assumed, each now guarded by a test that was CHECKED to fail when the trap is reintroduced: (1) insert_pdf does NOT carry the source outline (only the destination's survives), so the merged TOC is ours to build — which is what we want anyway. (2) set_toc() REJECTS a tree that starts deeper than level 1 or skips a level ('bad hierarchy level in row N'), and outlines in the wild do both — normalize_toc repairs every source outline before it is hung under its chapter, or one bad source would fail the whole merge. (3) THE BIG ONE: a source's pasted-image LAYER must be stripped out of the copy BEFORE insert_pdf. insert_pdf copies the placements and their /OC marks but not the catalog's OCProperties, so in the merged file get_ocgs() finds nothing, _image_ocg() returns None, and the layer can never be stripped again — every image would render TWICE, once baked into the page and once as its object from the merged sidecar, with the object's ghost appearing the moment you move it (row 118's doubled-render symptom, one level up). take_source_images() therefore takes the images as OBJECTS (from the source's own -ink.json, the truth, which is the only place a rotation or crop survives; else adopted from the layer geometry so a lost sidecar does not lose the pictures) and strips the layer. (4) document.select() DOES renumber the pages an outline entry points at, but does NOT reorder the ENTRIES — a moved chapter stays listed first while sitting at page 30. resort_toc() re-sorts blocks by page after every reorder; this PRE-DATES chapters (single-page reorder has always left the outline out of sequence), it was just invisible with no outlines around. Deleting a page leaves its entry pointing at page -1 (PyMuPDF's 'no destination'), now clamped in the sidebar so a click cannot jump off the front. (5) NotesModel.load()'s marker-less fallback ('the whole file is page 0') is invisible to a merge and would dump a hand-written note onto one page of a chapter — the parse moved to parse_note_sections(), which RETURNS whether there were page markers. DESTINATION: a new merged document asks for its filename UP FRONT. Its notes and image sidecars are derived from the PDF's path (notes_path_for / _ink_path_for) and autosave keys off it too, so an untitled merge would have nowhere to put them; the sidecars are written inside merge_documents, before anything opens the file, so the new tab never sees a document whose notes are missing. Merging into an OPEN document instead switches sidecar writing off and folds the returned notes/images into the live models at the insertion point (write_sidecars=False), since the open document already has sidecars of its own to protect. REPORTING: files that cannot be imported get a DIALOG, not a toast (a toast truncates and vanishes) — and it is the one place the naming rule is taught: a notes file is picked up automatically when it is named after its document (slides.pdf -> slides-notes.md, the name Sidemark itself writes). A '-notes.md' whose PDF is in the same drop is silent; any other loose .md is reported, because which document it belongs to genuinely cannot be guessed. REFACTORS this pulled in, all 'one table, not two': the image-ownership helpers (image_ocg_xref / our_placements / strip_image_layer / layer_images_as_sidecar) moved to module level and take a doc, because the merge works on documents no canvas has opened — PDFCanvas now delegates, and _adopt_image_layer became three lines on the shared reader; images_from_sidecar() is shared by load_images() and the merge; _reorder_pages() is shared by the single-page and range moves. NOT done: the merge does not de-duplicate identical images across sources (PyMuPDF's own dedup is the row 118 hazard, so uniquify_png stays), and cross-document links between two merged files still break (insert_pdf keeps links only within the copied range) — both are cosmetic next to the doubling bug. FOLLOW-UP PASS (same session, user feedback): the order dropdown DEFAULTS to 'as dropped' (the file manager's own order — it is what you were looking at when you dragged; the label says 'file manager', not 'selection', because click order is not what most Linux file managers send) and sub-chapters default OFF. Every sidebar drop opens the import dialog, including a SINGLE file — one file is still a chapter with a name, and one path is one thing to learn instead of two (the old plain-page-insert confirm is gone). The OUTLINE view had no file target at all, so dropping documents on it did nothing; the target now sits on the _toc_list itself, which covers the outline, the empty space below the thumbnails, and (via per-thumbnail targets deeper in the tree) the pages themselves. In the outline the rows are CHAPTERS, so the drop gap comes from the entry's page (top half = before this chapter, bottom half = where the next one starts), not from a row index. Its accept filter asks 'are there FILES?', never 'is there a string?': a file manager offers text/plain beside the uris, so a string test would have rejected every real drop. And the PARITY MISS worth remembering: dropping documents on a TEXT-FIRST page did nothing, because a GtkTextView installs its own GtkDropTarget for gchararray and matched the text/plain the file manager also offered — swallowing the drop before the window's target ever ran. Same reachability trap as the scroll handlers, in DND form. attach_file_drop() REPLACES the built-in target (two targets on one widget are tried in the order they were added, and the built-in was first) on MarkdownNotesView, which is both the notes panel and the text-first sheet — one call, both surfaces. Ceiling: dropping selected TEXT into the editor goes with it. The general rule this cost: consider BOTH modes for every feature, not just the one the request names.

column2: Page previews as the default sidebar view
column5: Page previews are the DEFAULT sidebar view, even for a document that has an outline. Before, an outline (when the PDF had one) took precedence and thumbnails were only the fallback; now the Outline/Pages switcher still appears for a document with a TOC, but it opens on Pages. Reason: you recognise the slide you want by LOOKING at it faster than by reading a chapter title, which is the lecture-notes workflow the app is for. Purely a default — one set_active() on the segmented switcher at build time; _populate_toc already derives the view from that toggle, and the user's pick still sticks per tab for the session. The old 'toc takes precedence over thumbnails' test became 'page previews open by default with or without a toc'.

column2: Lasso selection keeps its loop; a chip toggles to the resize box
column5:
The lasso selection KEEPS the loop you drew instead of replacing it with a bounding box the instant you lift. The loop stays as marching ants, you grab anywhere INSIDE it to move, and a small chip at its top-left switches to the 8-handle resize box (and back). GoodNotes' model, and it is the right one: the loop is the thing you just aimed with, so it is what your eye expects to see selected — a box that jumps out to the extents of a diagonal stroke reads as "it picked up more than I circled", even when it did not. The box is still the only way to scale/rotate, hence the chip rather than a replacement.

WHAT WAS ALREADY THERE: grab-anywhere-inside already worked (selection_grab_at -> _point_in_selection), so this is mostly a presentation change plus swapping the grab region from the bbox to the polygon. _finish_lasso previously DISCARDED _lasso_path; now the loop survives in _selection_loop, in DOCUMENT coords (the pen-width lesson, row 116: never store what the zoom happened to be).

WHEN THERE IS NO LOOP the selection falls back to box mode, because there genuinely is no outline to show: a CLICK-select (_lasso_was_click), a paste, a duplicate, and Shift-additive selection. ceiling: additive drops the loop rather than unioning two polygons — a polygon union is real work for a case where the box is a perfectly good answer; if it ever matters, keep a LIST of loops and draw/hit-test each.

TRANSFORMS: a move/scale/rotate commit applies the same transform to the loop (and the live drag preview transforms it alongside the strokes), or the outline drifts off the ink it belongs to. Undo/redo is free: both canvases already clear_lasso_selection() on undo (PDFCanvas.undo_last, TextPageView.undo_ink), so a stale loop after an undone move cannot happen — do NOT remove that call thinking it is unrelated.

WHY THIS ONE FIRST of the GoodNotes lasso/shape cluster: the persistent loop IS the visual half of circle-to-lasso (row 126) — "your circle turns into a dotted line" is literally this outline — so building it first makes row 126 mostly wiring instead of a second selection presentation.

column2: Circle to lasso: press-and-hold the stroke you just drew
column5:
Draw a loop around some ink with the PEN, lift, then press-and-hold on that stroke: it becomes the lasso path and selects what it encloses. GoodNotes' "circle to select". The point is that you NEVER LEAVE THE PEN — the same reason the dwell shape-snap (row 121) is a dwell and not a shape tool.

THE KEY INSIGHT, and it is not obvious: this does NOT collide with the loop->ellipse dwell snap, because the two are separated by the PEN LIFT, not by the shape. Hold at the end of a stroke WITHOUT lifting = snap to a clean shape. Lift, then press and hold ON the finished stroke = turn it into a lasso. Same gesture shape, two phases, and the mental model is honest enough to be learnable. An earlier reading of this feature concluded the gesture space was already claimed by the ellipse snap and that we therefore could not have it; that was wrong, and the lift is the whole answer.

TARGET (widened from GoodNotes on purpose): the press counts if it lands ON the last stroke OR anywhere INSIDE it when that stroke is a closed loop. GoodNotes wants the stroke itself ("long press with your pen on the circle stroke you have made"); having to hit a hand-drawn line exactly is needless precision when the interior is the region you are pointing at anyway. The cost is that a hold inside your last closed shape converts it — bounded by the last-stroke rule and one Ctrl+Z away. "Closed" comes from polyline_is_closed(), extracted from recognize_shape so the shape snap and this share ONE definition of what a loop is; an OPEN stroke has no meaningful interior (a squiggle would claim the whole area its ends happen to span), so it converts only by being touched.

MECHANICS: the press starts an ordinary stroke and arms a hold timer with a movement slop — move past the slop and it is just a stroke (timer cancelled); the timer firing with the pen still put converts. Only the MOST RECENT stroke qualifies to be converted: holding over arbitrary old ink would mean any rest of the hand mid-page silently eats a stroke into a selection. Conversion reuses everything downstream — the stroke's points become the lasso path and the existing containment test picks the objects — and removing the stroke plus selecting is ONE undo entry, so a mis-fire is one Ctrl+Z. The canvas long-press is unclaimed; the two existing Gtk.GestureLongPress uses are both on TOOLBAR buttons (the select-style and highlighter-style variant menus).

Do NOT gate this on the shape_snap setting: that setting governs the dwell, and circle-to-lasso is an independent mechanism that must keep working at shape_snap=off. A stroke available for conversion was by construction never snapped (a snap requires not lifting), so the two can never fight over the same stroke.

OPEN, deliberately not designed yet: on a touchscreen press-and-hold is also what a resting hand does. The last-stroke restriction plus one-Ctrl+Z recovery is the whole mitigation for now — the user's call was to ship it and find out whether it is a problem in practice rather than pre-engineer palm rejection.

AFTER THE FIRE, THE REST OF THE DRAG MEANS NOTHING — and this bit was a real bug, not a hypothetical. The pen is still down when the hold fires, and on the text sheet _on_ink_update's final ELSE means "no stroke in flight, so this is an erase drag": emptying current_stroke to drop the nascent stroke therefore turned every further motion into an ERASER, rubbing out everything the pen passed over. The sheet now carries _ink_ignoring (the PDF canvas' _ignoring by another name), set when the conversion fires, checked at the top of _on_ink_update and cleared in _on_ink_end. Both canvases have a regression test that drags on after a conversion and asserts nothing was drawn and nothing erased.

A PRESS THAT IS NOT A GRAB FINISHES THE SELECTION (both canvases). Ink left glowing while you draw somewhere else reads as stuck, not as selected. The LASSO tool is excluded because its own press router owns the rule there (Shift ADDS, a fresh loop replaces). On the PDF canvas the dismissal sits BEHIND the selection_grab_at test in _on_drag_begin, plus the right-drag erase and Ctrl+Shift highlighter branches; on the sheet it goes in _on_chord_lasso_begin's deny path, which is the only handler that sees EVERY press — with the caret in hand the ink overlay is not targetable, so _on_ink_begin never fires.

THE DISMISSING TAP LEAVES NO DOT. A tap that only ended a selection meant "done with this", not "draw here" — but the PDF canvas commits tiny strokes as DOTS on purpose, so it left one behind every time you tapped away. _dismissed_selection is set when a press clears a selection and checked at commit: a stroke that never moved beyond the click slop is dropped. Only the dot is swallowed — a press that goes on to DRAG still draws, from where it landed. The slop is LASSO_CLICK_SLOP_PX divided by the scale, because current_stroke is in PDF units and the slop is screen px. The text sheet needs none of this: _commit_stroke returns for len(pts) < 2, so a tap there cannot make a dot in the first place — this is a genuine substrate difference, not a parity gap.

column2: Polygon shape recognition and vertex editing
column5:
Extend the dwell snap (row 121) from line/rect/ellipse to irregular POLYGONS, and make a recognised shape's corners draggable afterwards — dragging a vertex moves the two edges meeting there. GoodNotes' model; the workflow, not the look, is what is being copied.

CLASSIFIER: extract corners (simplify the polyline, then keep points whose turn angle exceeds a threshold), then choose polygon vs ellipse by the same smallest-mean-residual method recognize_shape already uses for rect vs ellipse. Two constraints that are load-bearing: RECT stays its own kind detected first, because rect_bbox_of re-derives rectangles geometrically and the grid dividers depend on it; and the LINE stays the fallback, so shape_snap="lines"/"off" cannot regress. Output is still a plain polyline, so no new object kind — lasso, erase and sidecar round-trip come free, exactly as in row 121.

VERTEX HANDLES: re-derive the corners geometrically at SELECTION time (the rect_bbox_of pattern) rather than storing a vertex list, so nothing is tagged and a reload keeps working. The real design question is the collision with the 8-handle resize box, since both want to own the same selection; resolve it by object count the way GoodNotes does — ONE recognised shape selected shows vertex handles, anything else shows the box — and let row 125's chip be the escape hatch when you want to scale a polygon instead of nudging one corner. One undo entry per vertex drag.

SMALLER PIECES worth doing with it, in rough value order: (1) SELECT THE SHAPE RIGHT AFTER IT SNAPS, so it is adjustable with the pen still in hand — the precedent is already ours ("a paste comes back selected"), it is nearly free, and nothing else here is reachable without it; it also defuses row 121's un-snap wart, because if the shape is immediately adjustable then "undo the snap" stops being the reflex. (2) CLOSE-ON-RETURN as a LIVE mechanism: our `closed` test judges the loop retroactively, but what makes it feel magnetic is feedback DURING the stroke — the start point lighting up as the pen comes back to it (draw_snap_label is the place to hang the hint). (3) TRUE CIRCLE when |rx - ry| is inside a tolerance: a hand-drawn circle currently lands as a faintly oval ellipse, which reads as sloppy recognition even though it is faithful. (4) ENDPOINT SNAPPING between strokes, which is what makes axes and diagrams feel precise.

WON'T DO (both deliberate): MULTI-STROKE shapes, i.e. a triangle drawn as three strokes recognised as one — it needs a grouping concept the flat stroke model does not have, and endpoint snapping delivers most of the practical value; and CURVE FITTING (parabolas, line of best fit), which is real classifier growth for a narrow maths-notes payoff.

IP: copied behaviour is not a copyright problem — copyright covers expression, not function (SAS v World Programming in the EU; the functional/interface side treated as fair use in Google v Oracle). The actual copyright line is their icons, artwork, UI strings and help text, none of which we take. Microsoft's "Lasso select" patents (US 7,890,890 / 8,037,417) are the classic hits here and EXPIRED in 2022 (filed May 2002). Goodnotes' own portfolio was not audited; for a personal FOSS app the exposure is negligible, and shape recognition has decades of prior art (Rubine 1991, the sketch-recognition literature). Revisit only if Sidemark is ever commercialised, and then with a proper FTO check rather than by dropping features.

SHIPPED SO FAR — the classifier half. recognize_shape now returns "polygon" as well: polygon_corners() runs Ramer-Douglas-Peucker (simplify_polyline) at a tolerance that is a FRACTION of the loop's diagonal, so a big sloppy shape and a small neat one are judged alike, and the survivors are the corners. The loop is closed BEFORE simplifying, because RDP pins both ends and a freehand loop usually starts and ends mid-edge — without that there is a phantom vertex at the join. Corner count is bounded by POLYGON_MAX_CORNERS = 8: above that a wobbly circle "simplifies" into a many-sided nothing that beats the ellipse on residual while being obviously wrong to a human.

RECT vs POLYGON was the trap. A hand-drawn box is also a good 4-corner polygon — and a slightly TILTED quad through its real corners fits BETTER than the axis-aligned bbox does, so on residual alone the polygon wins and quietly takes the grid-divider snap away (rect_bbox_of re-derives rectangles geometrically). The distinction therefore has to be made on ANGLE, not on fit: four corners running square to the page (quad_is_axis_aligned, 12 degrees) mean rectangle, anything else is a polygon. 18 degrees was too generous — a box tilted 17 degrees still read as square.

Also landed: TRUE CIRCLE. When |rx - ry| is within CIRCLE_TOLERANCE (12%) of the larger radius, both radii become their mean. A hand-drawn circle used to land as a faintly oval ellipse, which reads as sloppy recognition even though it is perfectly faithful. Note when testing this that the ellipse is SAMPLED, so its spans match to within one sample step, not exactly. SNAP_LABELS became one module-level table for both canvases: a missing entry is a KeyError mid-gesture.

STILL OPEN: vertex handles (drag a corner, both adjacent edges follow) and endpoint snapping between strokes.

DROPPED, and deliberately — "select the shape right after it snaps". It was going to be step one, on the precedent that a paste comes back selected. That precedent does not transfer: a paste has nowhere else to go, whereas a snapped shape is mid-flow, and a live selection OWNS ITS INTERIOR as the grab region. Auto-selecting a freshly snapped rectangle would mean the next press inside it MOVES the box instead of drawing in it — and drawing inside a box you just drew is the common case in a diagram. GoodNotes agrees: it wants a deliberate tap to select. So vertex editing will hang off an ordinary lasso selection instead.

OPEN PATHS ("a path of lines"). recognize_shape now also returns "path": an OPEN stroke drawn as a run of straight segments is straightened segment by segment and left OPEN. Closing is decided by exactly the test the closed shapes already use — polyline_is_closed — so "only if it comes back near the start does it snap together" needs no new rule. open_path_corners() reuses simplify_polyline, and the single straight LINE stays the fallback: the path has to beat it by a margin (gain=2.5) or every slightly bowed stroke turns into a two-segment path and the classic straight snap is gone. Two old tests changed meaning here and were rewritten rather than patched: [(0,0),(5,3),(8,1),(12,9)] was called "a squiggle stays a line", but with paths in the vocabulary it IS three line segments — the honest line case is a bowed, near-straight stroke, and that is what those tests assert now.

A SNAPPED SHAPE COMES BACK SELECTED, IN BOX MODE, so it can be adjusted with the pen still in hand — the user asked for this directly after it had been dropped (see above), and the objection that killed it is answered rather than ignored: an AUTO selection (_selection_auto) shows the box and claims its HANDLES, but never its INTERIOR. So the resize/rotate handles are right there, and a press in the middle still draws — which is the diagram case that made auto-selection look unworkable. Grabbing a handle clears the flag and it becomes an ordinary selection, interior and all. A press elsewhere dismisses it and, unlike a selection you actually made, does NOT get eaten: you never asked for it, so it must not swallow your dot.

CONTROL POINTS shipped, and they close the row. A single selected shape in BOX mode grows round control points at its vertices; dragging one moves the two edges meeting there (which needs no code — moving the shared point IS both edges). shape_vertices() re-derives them from the geometry every time, nothing stored and no tag on the stroke (the rect_bbox_of pattern), so they survive a reload and a sidecar round-trip for free.

WHICH STROKES GET THEM: corner polylines only — a line (2 points), a path, a polygon, a rectangle. A sampled curve does not: an ellipse is 24+ points, and twenty-five handles on one wobble is not editing, it is a hedgehog. The bound is POLYGON_MAX_CORNERS + 1 core points. ONE shape only, images excluded: with two selected there is no single geometry to edit and the box is the right tool for a group. A closed ring drops its repeated last point, and moving vertex 0 moves BOTH ends or the ring tears open (move_shape_vertex).

PRECEDENCE: a control point sits INSIDE the selection box, on top of the corner resize handles, and must WIN there — it is the finer verb. Both press routers test it before the handles, and selection_grab_at includes it so a control point is grabbable with any tool. On the sheet that reachability comes from the capture-phase chord gesture (the same one that makes a pasted image movable with the caret), NOT from _on_ink_begin — a test that calls _on_ink_begin directly with the pen will see nothing happen, which is the row 118 reachability trap wearing a new hat.

UNDO: one ("reshape", ...) entry per drag on both sides — new on the PDF canvas (undo and redo), already there on the sheet. On the sheet the moved points go back through _overlay_to_stroke_pts, the exact inverse of _stroke_overlay_pts and the FLOAT converter, because these offsets are STORED: the int helpers are what made a rotated stroke go lumpy.

ONE TEST CHANGED MEANING: test_move_translates_points_with_undo_redo grabbed a 2-point stroke at its own endpoint, which is now a control point. Its grab moved to the middle of the box; the endpoint press is correct new behaviour, not a regression.

STILL OPEN, deliberately: endpoint snapping between strokes (draw a line and have its end snap to a nearby stroke's end). Independent of everything here.

CONTROL POINTS, SECOND PASS (all three asked for after the first version was in use):

1. THE PEN KEEPS THE LAST CONTROL POINT after the dwell fires. A recognised path or polygon is no longer frozen: continued motion drags the vertex the pen was on, exactly as a snapped LINE always let you drag its endpoint. For a closed polygon that is index 0, the shared first/last point, so the ring cannot tear. Rect/ellipse/divider stay frozen — their geometry is not a vertex the pen is holding.

2. MAGNETIC SNAP, then WELD. While a control point is dragged, the nearest other control point within reach captures it VISUALLY (the point sits on the target, ringed) while the pen is still down, and pulling past the reach lets go again — so the snap is previewed, never committed early. On release the two simply share a coordinate. From then on welded_vertices() picks up EVERY control point at that coordinate when one is grabbed, so a merged pair drags as the single point it has become. No stored join, nothing to persist: the same derive-don't-store principle as shape_vertices. ceiling: two points that coincide by ACCIDENT also move together and cannot be prised apart except by dragging one away; storing real breakable joins needs per-stroke ids — see row 131. The reach is a fraction of the VIEWPORT (vertex_snap_radius, clamped 10..44 px), not of the document, because it is a reach on screen and must not shrink when you zoom in on a detail.

3. EVERY SELECTED SHAPE shows its control points, not just a single one — merging two drawings means seeing both sets at once and dragging one onto the other. The old "exactly one shape" rule is gone. The hedgehog argument survives as a CAP (MAX_VISIBLE_VERTICES = 40): thirty selected strokes are as unusable as a 25-point ellipse.

EDGE SNAP WITHOUT BINDING, and LIVE MAGNETS WHILE DRAWING (the third pass):

4. A dragged control point now also snaps onto a LINE between two other points — snap_point() tries the nearest control point first and falls back to the nearest point on an edge. The vertex MUST win: landing next to the corner you were aiming at is the whole failure that ordering prevents. Segments touching a held vertex are skipped, or the point would snap to its own two edges and never move. This is POSITIONAL ONLY, which is the user's own call after row 131's analysis: the point lands on the line and is then an ordinary vertex, and if that line later moves it stays where it was. That keeps the derive-don't-store model intact — the false-positive problem in row 131 is entirely about PERSISTING an accidental adjacency, and nothing is persisted here.

5. LIVE MAGNETS. When the dwell recognises a line/path/polygon, the pen keeps its last control point AND every corner polyline on the page becomes a snap target for it, so a fresh shape joins what is already drawn without lifting the pen. Targets are gathered from the whole PAGE, not from a selection: the shape being drawn is not committed yet, so there is nothing selected to aim at. They are frozen at dwell time so the set cannot change mid-drag, and cleared on release. Only the magnets WITHIN REACH of the pen are painted — every control point on the page at once is noise, and what you need to see is what you can actually hit. A rect/ellipse/divider arms nothing, because the dwell settled it and the pen is not holding one of its vertices. This is row 127's old "endpoint snapping between strokes" item, arrived at from the other direction.

6. THE LIVE SHAPE SNAPS TO ITSELF TOO. Its own vertices and edges are targets alongside the page's — that is how you close a path onto its own start, or bring an end back to an earlier corner, without lifting the pen. Two exclusions make it work rather than lock: the HELD point is excluded (it would always be its own nearest target), and nearest_edge_point already drops the segments touching it (the held point lies ON its own two edges by definition, so it would pin itself in place and never move). Everything else of the live shape is fair game, including edges that are not adjacent to the held point.

7. SNAPPING ONTO FREEHAND INK, which turned out to be cheap: freehand ink is a polyline like any other, so nearest_edge_point already did the geometry — what was missing was only the targets, since shape_vertices deliberately returns nothing for it. snap_point() therefore takes a second list, `curves`: freehand strokes offer their two ENDPOINTS as vertex targets (the ends of a pen line are real, aimable points) and their whole polyline as edges. Their INTERIOR points are deliberately NOT vertex targets — a freehand stroke has hundreds, they are sampling artefacts rather than anything a person drew, and treating them as corners would make the snap grab a different pixel every time.

The only real cost is performance, and it is handled twice over: the candidate set is FROZEN at the start of the gesture (press for a vertex drag, dwell for a live shape) rather than rebuilt per motion event — neither the page nor the view moves mid-drag, so converting every freehand point to screen coords on each event was pure waste — and curve_snap_shapes() bbox-filters what survives. Without both, a page of lecture handwriting is tens of thousands of segments evaluated on every motion event.

GHOST LINE BUG (reported in the app, fixed): while a point was snapping, a line appeared from the "path" snap label to the cursor, visible only while drawing. Cause: draw_snap_label ends with show_text(), which leaves cairo's CURRENT POINT at the end of the text, and ctx.restore() does NOT clear the path — the path is not part of the saved graphics state. draw_vertex_snap_ring then called arc() with that current point live, and cairo joins an arc to an existing current point with a straight line. Fixed in both places: the label ends with new_path() so it cannot poison the next painter (the real fix — it protects every future caller), and the ring does new_sub_path() before its arc, which is what draw_shape_vertices already did correctly. Worth remembering generally: ctx.save()/restore() does not save or restore the PATH.

column2: BUG: switching to the text tool and clicking selects to the end of the document and scrolls there
column5:
FIXED (2026-07-30). Root cause: MarkdownNotesView._buf_replace_line — the live-Markdown renderer replaces a whole line by DELETE + INSERT, and both the insert and the selection_bound mark sit inside that deleted range whenever the caret is on the line. The delete collapses them onto the line start and the re-insert then drags them to the line END on their right gravity. The user's read was exactly right: the bound is stale and the click only supplies the other end.

The trigger is the un-render. Clicking onto a rendered line makes it the cursor line, and _rehighlight -> _restore_line puts the markdown source back (α -> \alpha), which is a _buf_replace_line on the line you just clicked. So the caret jumps to the line end. It becomes a SELECTION because a pen press always jitters: GTK follows the press with a drag-update, and gtk_text_view_drag_gesture_update -> move_mark_to_pointer_and_scroll("insert") moves the insert mark ALONE back to the pointer, leaving the bound where the re-render parked it. Then it walks: every further motion changes the cursor line, each rehighlight re-substitutes the line the caret LEFT, and if the bound is on such a line it is carried to that line's end too — which is how a line-end bound reads as "the end of the document", and why the view scrolls after it.

It is not the tool switch. The tool switch only makes it VISIBLE: it is what puts you back on the caret with a pen in your hand, so the first click after it is a jittery pen press onto a line that has been rendered while you were drawing. The same defect was always there in the notes panel (same class), just far rarer with a mouse, where a clean click leaves insert == bound and you only see the caret jump to the line end. That is the "it has happened before".

FIX: _buf_replace_line carries both marks across the replace by hand. _remap_column maps a column through the edit on the common prefix/suffix — a rendering only ever swaps one span for another, so a column in the prefix keeps its number, one in the suffix keeps its distance from the line end, and only a column inside the changed span is clamped. Both marks are re-placed with select_range, so a live selection keeps BOTH ends (a bound on a non-cursor line that renders is the same bug and is fixed by the same code).

HOW IT WAS FOUND, worth keeping: reading the code could not settle it, because every candidate (set_tool, the capture-phase chord gestures, event reachability via pick()) tested clean headless. What cracked it was a mark-set logger on the buffer in the real app: the log showed the bound moving from 354 to 375 with NO mark-set signal in between while the buffer grew by exactly 5 characters — a mark that moves without a signal is a mark riding a buffer EDIT, and +5 is \alpha minus α. GTK does not emit mark-set for marks displaced by a delete/insert, so this class of bug is invisible to the obvious instrumentation.

TRAP for the future: any code that rewrites a line under the caret must carry the marks. get_iter_at_* returns iters that are invalidated by the edit, so save COLUMNS (ints) before and re-derive iters after.

SECOND ROOT CAUSE, and the one the user spotted ("the window moves to some other position"): the SHEET SCROLLS OUT FROM UNDER THE PRESS. TextPageView puts the text view in a Box so it grows to its full content height (endless paper) — that makes it a NON-SCROLLABLE child, so GtkScrolledWindow wraps it in a GtkViewport, and a viewport scrolls to its focus widget by default (GtkViewport:scroll-to-focus, TRUE). The sheet's only focusable child is that full-height view, which is never fully visible, so "reveal the focus widget" can only mean "jump to the top of the paper".

That is why the TOOL SWITCH is in the repro and why nobody could find anything wrong in the tool code: scroll-to-focus needs a focus CHANGE, and picking a tool from the toolbar is what parks focus on a button. The first thing gtk_text_view_click_gesture_pressed does is grab_focus() on the view — so the sheet jumped to the top mid-press, and GTK then resolved the pointer against the moved view (get_iter_from_gesture -> gtk_text_layout_get_iter_at_pixel). The caret landed pages from the click and the following drag-update dragged a selection out to it. "Often to the top" is the viewport's scroll target showing through. Fix: viewport.set_scroll_to_focus(False) in TextPageView.__init__. Confirmed by hand in the app.

The two faults stacked, which is why the first fix changed the symptom instead of removing it: the mark bug decided WHERE the stale end sat, the viewport bug decided where the caret landed. Worth remembering as a method note — after a fix that changes a symptom without curing it, assume a second cause rather than re-doubting the first.

The notes PANEL is unaffected: its text view goes straight into the ScrolledWindow, is scrollable itself, and so gets no viewport.

GUARDING TEST, resolved 2026-07-30 (the loose end this row left): test_focusing_the_sheet_does_not_scroll_it passed alone and failed in every full run, at its precondition — the sheet was never taller than its viewport, so there was nothing to scroll. It is not a race and not a slow settle: by that point in a full suite Weston has taken the surface away (VK_ERROR_SURFACE_LOST_KHR), which stops the frame clock, and layout only happens in the clock's layout phase. Instrumenting the assertion showed a 206-line sheet allocating 534 px inside a 594 px viewport; forcing the height with set_size_request(-1, 3000) did not move the adjustment either, which is what proves it is allocation and not GtkTextView's incremental validation alone. The test now asserts the FIX (viewport.get_scroll_to_focus() is False) unconditionally — checked to fail when set_scroll_to_focus is put back to True — and skips only the scroll half when the sheet did not lay out. The scroll half was likewise checked to bite in isolation: with the fix reverted the sheet jumps 600 -> 30. Written up in CLAUDE.md under 'layout needs a live frame clock'.

column2: Link a page's notes to the previous page (notes that run over several PDF pages)
column5:
SHIPPED (2026-07-30). Two verbs, one boolean per page, exactly as scoped — "continue notes from previous page" is a CHECKBOX in the notes panel header (the user's UI call: no menu, no second row; the header line that said "Notes" now also carries the box and, on a run's first page, a dim "continues on page N"). A run of linked pages is consecutive trues.

THE MODEL STORES THE TEXT ONCE. NotesModel gains _links (pages that continue their predecessor) and run_start/run_pages/run_end. get(idx) resolves to own_text(run_start(idx)) and set(idx) writes to the run start, so a linked page holds NOTHING of its own — duplication is impossible rather than merely discouraged. That split is the whole trap of the feature: get() is for the human looking at one page, own_text() is for everything that walks all pages. Export (_export_pdf_with_notes), the share render (_render_share_page) and the page marks were moved to own_text, so A RUN PRINTS ONCE instead of the same paragraph on all five slides — the exact failure a resolving get() produces by accident, pinned by a test. Search already read the raw dict, so it reports the run's start page and needed no change.

SIDECAR: the existing marker grew a word — `<!-- page:13 continued -->` with an empty body, parsed by widening _PAGE_MARKER_RE. It is the one case where an empty page must still be written out. parse_note_sections/read_note_sections now return a NoteSections named tuple (sections, linked, had_markers): a named tuple precisely because `sections, had = ...` unpacking is spread through the merge import, and a silent third field would have rebound had_markers to a set. A hand-edited file that gives a continued page a body is normalised at load — the body is folded into the run rather than hidden behind it forever.

LINK APPENDS, UNLINK KEEPS. Linking a page that already had text appends it to the run's body (a link must never eat what someone wrote); unlinking leaves everything with the run's FIRST page and starts the freed page empty, deterministically, with a toast naming the page and an Undo that re-links. Guessing which half of a paragraph belonged to which slide is exactly the logic the scope ruled out.

RE-KEYING was the actual work — every path in row 123. Insert: the new pages are blank and unlinked, so the tail is cut loose too (discard idx+count) rather than letting text reach across the gap. Delete: THE TRAP — deleting a run's START hands the body to the next page in the run, which becomes the new start; the old code simply dropped the deleted page's note, which here would have vaporised the whole run's text. Reorder: a link survives only where the page's predecessor is still its predecessor, so a run moved as a block keeps its links and a torn run degrades to plain unlinked pages holding their text. Merge import carries a source's run into its chapter (contiguous insert, and a source's page 0 can never be linked, which is what stops one chapter reaching into the one before it). Dragging pages out re-derives the same way: a continued page torn from its start exports the text it was SHOWING, or it would come out blank.

The undo timelines needed no re-keying beyond what they had: ops go through set()/get(), which resolve, so an edit recorded on a continued page lands on the run's body.

TURNING THE PAGE INSIDE A RUN IS A NON-EVENT: _restore_note now returns early when the buffer already holds the text, so the caret stays put mid-sentence instead of being thrown to offset 0 by a pointless set_text.

BOTH MODES? NO — and this is the FIRST feature that is genuinely one-sided: a text-first page has no page-to-page structure to continue. _can_link_notes() says so in one place and the checkbox hides in text mode. Said loudly here per the parity rule.

Ceiling: a continued page prints NOTHING in the export, not even a "continued from page N" line; add one to the notes page if anyone misses it.

THE TICK CASCADES (2026-07-31, the user's call). The feature is ONE body across five slides and it was costing five clicks — which is the thing it exists to avoid. Ticking the box now runs `link_forward(idx, page_count)`: it links idx and carries on through every FOLLOWING page that has nothing of its own to say, stopping at the first page that already has notes (or the end of the document). Unticking runs `unlink_forward(idx)`, which breaks the run at idx AND at every page after it — what one tick joined, one untick parts. Pages BEFORE idx keep their run and the body never moves.

Why the stop condition is "a page with notes" and not "the end of the document": `link()` APPENDS a linked page's own text into the run, which is right for a deliberate single tick and wrong for a cascade — swallowing a slide's notes into the run above is the one outcome you cannot see coming from the checkbox you clicked. So the walk stops short of it.

A page ALREADY linked is not a stop sign either: its own_text is "" by construction, so the walk flows through it and the pages beyond join the same run rather than starting a second one. Both new methods return the pages they touched, which is what the toast names ("pages 2-4") and what the unlink toast's Undo re-links — `_relink_notes` takes a LIST now and re-links in order, because a later page can only continue one already back in the run.

Nothing downstream changed: `set` still routes to the run start, so undo, the merge import, the drag-export and the re-keying paths are untouched.

column2: Gestures between PDF mode and text-first mode (drag the notes panel full width, drag a blank page back in)
column5:
USER IDEA (2026-07-30). The two document modes are one app to the user, but there is no gesture BETWEEN them — you pick the mode when the document is created and that is that. Proposal: make the notes-panel divider the transition.

PDF -> TEXT: drag the notes panel wider until it covers the whole window, and you are in text-first mode (the notes become the sheet). Hitting the toggle-notes button at full width would be the keyboard/button-shaped equivalent. It reads naturally because a full-width notes panel already IS a text page in everything but name — TextPageView is a MarkdownNotesView styled as paper.

TEXT -> PDF: the mirror. Drag in from the LEFT edge of the window and a blank PDF page appears beside the text, i.e. the document gains a PDF the way the divider suggests. Same via the toggle button.

QUESTIONS TO SETTLE BEFORE BUILDING, none of them blocking but all of them cheap to get wrong:
- Is this a MODE change on one document or a conversion of the FILE? A text page's ink lives in <name>-ink.json while a PDF's strokes are native annotations, so a real conversion has to move ink between substrates. The cheaper first version is a VIEW state that only flips doc_mode when the document actually has both parts.
- Where does the blank PDF come from on the way back — a real one-page PDF written next to the .md (so the .md's ![[name.pdf]] embed line gains a target), or an in-memory page that is only persisted once you draw on it? The second avoids littering blank PDFs on an accidental drag.
- It must be UNDOABLE or at least trivially reversible, because it is an accidental-drag-shaped gesture. A drag that crosses the threshold and comes back should leave no trace.
- Chrome follows _MODE_CHROME (see CLAUDE.md), so the header should already do the right thing once doc_mode flips — that table is the reason this is Medium and not High effort.

Related: this is the same "one app, two modes" thread as the parity rule; if it lands, the mode a document was CREATED in stops being a permanent decision, which is the actual win. 2026-08-13: pulling the page back in now uses the width the DRAG ended at, not the divider position from before the sheet opened — that one describes a layout you left a while ago. It is remembered like any other divider position, and a programmatic leave (no drag) still restores the old one.

column2: Constrained control points: a vertex bound to a point ON another edge
column5:
NOT PLANNED — the user's call after the analysis below: the positional edge snap (row 127) gives the useful half without any of the cost, so a point that genuinely FOLLOWS its edge is not worth a constraint model. Kept as a record of why, so the question is not re-opened from scratch.

THE ONE PIECE THE CURRENT MODEL CANNOT DO. Snapping a control point onto a LINE BETWEEN two other points, such that moving either of those two later drags the bound point along with the edge.

WHY THE OTHERS FIT AND THIS DOES NOT. Vertex-to-vertex welding (row 127) needs no stored state at all: two control points that share a COORDINATE are one point, re-derived at every grab by welded_vertices(). That is the same principle as shape_vertices and rect_bbox_of — derive, never store — so a weld survives a reload, a sidecar round-trip and undo for free. A point on an EDGE has no such property to re-derive. "Lies within epsilon of that segment" is derivable, but it is not evidence of intent: a vertex sitting near a long line is common by accident, whereas two vertices at exactly the same coordinate essentially only happens because someone snapped them. Re-deriving would silently glue unrelated drawings together the moment one is nudged.

WHAT IT WOULD REALLY TAKE: a stored constraint — (stroke, vertex) bound to (other stroke, segment index, parameter t) — which needs STABLE PER-STROKE IDENTITY in both persistence paths. On the text sheet that is a field in the JSON sidecar, awkward but plain. On a PDF it is the hard one: strokes ARE native PDF ink annotations, so an id has to ride in annotation metadata and survive PyMuPDF, a merge import re-keying pages (row 123) and another editor touching the file. Segment indices also have to be rewritten whenever the host shape gains or loses a vertex, and a cycle (A bound to B bound to A) needs breaking.

VERDICT: worth doing only as a deliberate step into a constraint model, not as an extension of the derive-at-drag-time approach — and the moment there are stored per-stroke ids, other things want them too (grouping, real joins that can be broken, multi-stroke shapes from row 127's WON'T-DO list). Decide the identity question first; the geometry is the easy half.

column2: Rebindable button/chord assignments (no active tool; the toolbar binds)
column5:
SHIPPED (2026-07-31), confirmed by hand in the real app after the second pass below. Replaces the fixed chord grammar (row 115) with a rebindable table. THE MODEL CHANGE, and everything follows from it: there is NO ACTIVE TOOL any more. Every mouse button, alone or under modifiers, HAS a tool, and pressing it uses that tool — left draws, right erases, middle pans, all at the same time. The toolbar stops being a selector and becomes a BINDING SURFACE: click a tool with the mouse button you want it on and it goes there (plain left-click is still just "put this on the left button", which is why picking a tool feels unchanged).

DEFAULTS: left pen, right eraser, middle pan, THUMB UNBOUND — the user's call: most mice have no thumb button, and a tool nobody can reach is worse than an empty slot. Modifier chords keep their meanings (Ctrl pan, Ctrl+Shift highlighter, Ctrl+Shift+Alt lasso, Ctrl+Alt anchor, Shift and Alt+Shift zoom) MINUS the Alt flip, which had no job left once every button carries its own tool. Shift-alone is bindable: the user saw no reason for the old exception, so the "never load-bearing" rule is gone — the DEFAULT table still leaves the caret its Shift+click text selection, and an explicit binding overrides that.

Bindings is the table (settings.json `button_bindings`, unknown tools dropped on load rather than kept as a binding nothing can execute). ONE instance per window, shared by every canvas and every text sheet, so a rebinding is instantly true in every tab and both modes. `canvas.tool` survives as a DERIVED value — the tool of the button being pressed, else what LEFT would do — which is what the cursor should promise and what pen attrs, the snap timer and the ink handlers mean when they ask; assigning to it binds the left button, so older code and tests still mean what they meant. `highlighter` / `select_mode` are derived the same way, and the window must NOT set them (a `select_mode = False` while the caret is on left hands the button straight back to the pen — that bug cost a debugging round).

ROUTING IS THE POINT. chord_tool() only ever fed the highlight and the tooltips; the real routing was inline `if ctrl and shift and alt:` cascades in two canvases plus per-button controllers. Both are now ONE press router each, resolving button+modifiers through the table. The text page's five competing capture gestures (Alt-ink, temp-highlighter, chord-lasso, right-erase, pan) collapsed into one that either claims the press for its tool or DENIES so the caret keeps it — and with that, the borrow-and-restore dance around self.tool disappeared. The ink overlay is no longer made targetable per tool: the router is above it either way, so targeting only ever stole clicks from the TextView. THE THUMB IS A REAL BUTTON NOW: button 10 never reaches a GestureDrag, so its press is replayed through the same router with a _SyntheticDrag stand-in, which is what lets it hold ANY tool instead of a hardwired pan.

TWO EXCEPTIONS, both deliberate and both AT the router rather than forks of the table: with the lasso on the plain button Shift ADDS to the selection (Shift+lasso is still the lasso), and a live selection is grabbable with any tool in hand (row 125), which must be claimed on the sheet's capture gesture or a pasted image is unmovable.

UI: badges are the colour of each UNMODIFIED button a tool owns (left accent, right red, middle green, thumb amber) as a tinted edge; MODIFIED chords get none on purpose — otherwise every button wears a constellation — and live in a tooltip GENERATED from the table (`Lasso — left · Ctrl+Shift+Alt+left`), which retires the hand-written tooltip strings. Binding toasts what it displaced (`Ctrl+right → Lasso (was Eraser)`) with an Undo, because a chord maps to exactly one tool so binding always MOVES it. The pen popover grows a Buttons list: every binding with a ✕, plus Reset to defaults — it is the discovery surface (chord-clicking is fast but unguessable) and the only way to CLEAR a binding, since a chord-click can move one but never remove it.

Keyboard tool shortcuts became HOLD-TO-BORROW (the user's call): Ctrl+H lends the left button the highlighter for as long as it is held, letting go of either key gives it back. The keyboard twin of a modifier chord, and it cannot strand you in a mode you forgot you were in. Ctrl+M is the caret the same way.

CARET UNIFICATION (the user asked for it in the same breath): one I-beam button in both modes; _mode_select is gone and "select" is an alias of "text". TOOL_MODES drives the bar order, the _MODE_CHROME rows and the resolver, so a tool cannot be in the bar and missing from the grammar.

ALSO WORTH KNOWING: entering text mode no longer force-binds the caret to left. The table is shared with PDF pages, so rewriting it whenever a .md opens would undo the user's own binding — which means a text page now opens with the PEN on left. Typing is unaffected (keys go to the focused view); it is CLICKING to move the caret that wants the caret tool. The user chose to try this rather than special-case the mode.

STILL OPEN: real-hardware verification of every binding and every chord (gestures, so headless tests cannot see them), README lines, and CLAUDE.md's Input chords bullet rewritten as a DEFAULT table.

WAS OPEN AFTER THE FIRST PASS, all since resolved — kept because each entry names a trap. The user's verdict at the time: "it is still not 100% correct", WITHOUT a specific repro. So the first job of the next session is to get one: launch standalone, exercise each button and chord in both modes, and read the `[input]` log lines against what the mouse actually did. The log prints the resolved tool on every press (`[input] text right -> highlighter`) and the table + stripe mapping on every refresh (`[bar] table` / `[bar] stripes`), which is enough to tell a ROUTING bug from a PAINTING one — do not guess between them.

Known-open, roughly in order:
(a) THE STRIPE POSITION. Reported repeatedly, never reproduced with data. What is needed is the two `[bar]` lines next to what is coloured on screen, left to right — the table and the painter disagreeing is the whole bug class, and it is invisible without printing both.
(b) THE CARET ON A NON-LEFT BUTTON in text mode. `_on_press_begin` DENIES when the resolved tool is `text`, and GTK's TextView only places a caret for button 1 — so binding the caret to right/middle resolves correctly and then does nothing. Fix: claim the press and place the caret ourselves. `_reopen_context_menu` already does that exact dance (`_overlay_to_buffer` -> `get_iter_at_location` -> `place_cursor` -> `grab_focus`); extract a `_place_caret(x, y)` and call it from the router, plus drag-to-extend in `_on_press_update` for selection.
(c) THE THUMB WITH A NON-PAN TOOL on the sheet — unexplained. The `_SyntheticDrag` replay reaches the router, so check whether the `[input] text thumb -> ...` line appears at all and what tool it names; if it resolves and nothing happens the bug is downstream of `_on_ink_begin`, not in the replay.
(d) 17 STALE TESTS in TestTextFirstMode, all failing on a clean tree since the routing work and all ONE stale contract in two shapes: `assertEqual(tp.tool, "text")  # caret is the default` (a text page opens with the PEN on left now — see ALSO WORTH KNOWING above) and `tp.tool = "pen"` (the property lost its setter; they want `tp.set_tool`). No app bug behind any of them. The full suite has NOT been run since the routing work — do that before merging.
(e) README lines and CLAUDE.md's input bullet as a DEFAULT table (from STILL OPEN above).

FIXED IN THIS PASS, and each is a trap worth not re-introducing:
- The eight tool buttons are plain `Gtk.Button`, not `ToggleButton`. With no active tool there is no state for a checked button to show, and the `.tool-btn:checked { background: none }` CSS that neutralised the look left the button transparent against the window. Deleting the state beats styling it away: the radio group, the mirror `set_active` loop in `_set_tool_mode` and the `_syncing_mode` re-entrancy guard all went with it.
- RIGHT ALWAYS ERASED on the sheet however it was bound, while the log honestly said `-> highlighter`. `_on_ink_begin` branched on the raw button number (`elif self.tool == "eraser" or button == 3`) AFTER the router had already resolved the tool into `_press_tool`. `self.tool` IS the press's tool — consulting the button a second time is a second table, and it beat the first one.
- MIDDLE-CLICK PASTED THE PRIMARY SELECTION over the pan binding. A GtkTextView pastes primary from its own click gesture, which the capture-phase router cannot reliably out-claim, and there is no per-widget switch — so `gtk-enable-primary-paste` is turned off app-wide in `do_startup`. Right scope anyway: the middle button means the same thing on every surface.
- THE MODIFIER HIGHLIGHT lit the tool a chord USED to run: `_chord_highlight_tool` called `chord_tool()`, the default grammar, instead of the table. The grammar is only what the table was seeded with.
- CTRL+CLICK ON A TOOL BOUND IT TO PLAIN LEFT. `_attach_binding_click` read only `gesture.get_current_event_state()`; a press that arrives without the modifier mask falls into the plain-left path, which binds left — the one outcome the user did not ask for. It now merges the window's tracked held keys, the same rule `_chord_state` uses on both canvases.

THE SHIPPED DEFAULT TABLE (2026-07-31, the user's own list): left pen, middle lasso, right eraser; ctrl+left pan, ctrl+right text cursor, shift+left zoom to region. Nothing else. The THUMB is deliberately unbound — most mice have none, and a default nobody can press is a default nobody chose (it dropped out of the list on the second pass). Consequence worth knowing: middle=lasso means SHIFT+MIDDLE can never resolve to another tool, because Shift on the plain lasso button is the additive-selection exception at the router. The old grammar's chords (ctrl+shift highlighter, ctrl+shift+alt lasso, ctrl+alt anchor, shift+middle zoom) are gone from the defaults, so the tests that drove them now bind their chord explicitly first — a test asserting a MECHANISM must not ride on the default table.

=== SECOND PASS (2026-07-31): the modifiers move the STRIPES, and the tests stopped eating the user's settings ===

(d) above is DONE — the 18 stale tests in TestTextFirstMode/TestTextPageLasso now bind the chord each one drives instead of riding the default table, and the two that asserted `tp.ink.get_can_target()` were rewritten: `set_tool` deliberately never makes the overlay targetable any more (the capture router sees every press above it), so that assertion outlived its mechanism. Three others assigned `tp.tool = ...`, which is a read-only property on the sheet — a silent AttributeError inside the window body, reported as a bare test failure.

(1) THE SUITE WAS WRITING THE USER'S REAL settings.json. `Bindings.save()` persists on every rebind and `_settings_path()` reads XDG_CONFIG_HOME, which run_tests.sh never set — so a test that bound a chord rewrote the user's button table, and every window test after it resolved presses through whatever the last run left behind. The table found on disk was `left/ctrl+left/ctrl+right/shift+left` with NO middle, right or alt+left: a table nobody chose, on the machine reporting that the buttons were "still not 100% correct". Fixed in two places, both cheap: run_tests.sh points XDG_CONFIG_HOME at a throwaway dir under the test runtime, and an autouse conftest fixture deletes settings.json after every test so each one starts from the shipped defaults. The failure mode this removes is the nastiest kind — a test that passes alone, fails in a suite, and blames the wrong feature. THIS IS ALSO THE FIRST CREDIBLE EXPLANATION of (a) "the stripe position" and (c) "the thumb with a non-pan tool" above: both were read off a table that had been overwritten.

(2) ALT+LEFT IS THE TEXT CURSOR, by default. Alt is how you follow a PDF link, and following a link IS the cursor tool's click (`_open_link_at`, reached from `_text_selecting` on a release that did not move). With alt+left unbound, Alt lit the links up and then nothing opened them — the modifier promising what the table could not deliver.

(3) LINK HOVER READS THE TABLE, not Alt. `PDFCanvas.link_hover_active()` is "the left button's tool right now, under whatever is held, is `text`" — so links glow when the caret is picked in the bar AND when Alt is down, and stop glowing under Alt the moment you rebind alt+left away. One predicate for the glow and the click, which is the only way the promise and the behaviour stay the same thing. Falling off a link now restores the TOOL's cursor rather than none (with the caret on left the I-beam is what the page should wear), and `_refresh_tool_bindings` re-asks after any rebind — otherwise picking the cursor tool looks like it did nothing until you move the mouse.

(5) A MODIFIED CLICK ON A TOOL ALSO STOLE PLAIN LEFT. Ctrl+clicking a tool bound ctrl+left AND left. `_attach_binding_click` claims the press in the CAPTURE phase, which SHOULD cancel the Button's own click gesture — except `GtkButton`'s gesture is CAPTURE-phase too (probe it: `observe_controllers()` reports phase 1, button 1) and was added at construction, so it runs FIRST and the claim arrives too late. Same widget + same phase run in ADD order, the trap already written up for the notes-panel drop target. The fix cannot be a claim: the press sets `_binding_press` and `_pick_tool` (the new `clicked` handler) consumes it. Flagged only for BUTTON 1, because the Button's gesture is primary-only and flagging a right-click would eat the NEXT plain pick instead of this one.

(6) A CHECKOUT KEEPS ITS OWN settings.json (the user's call). `_application_id` already scoped the INSTANCE per copy of the source so a smoke test never forwards into the installed app — but both copies then wrote one settings.json, so a rebind while testing a checkout changed the button table of the app being used. Both are the same question, so there is now one answer: `_copy_key()` ("" installed, else a path hash; SIDEMARK_INSTANCE forces one) suffixes the app id AND the settings filename. Recent files stay SHARED — a copy is a different app, not a different person, and an Open-Recent list that empties itself when you smoke-test is a worse bug than the one being fixed.

(4) THE STRIPES FOLLOW THE MODIFIERS, and the glow is GONE. `_live_buttons_for(tool)` is the plain table with nothing held and the CHORD table under whatever is held, so holding Ctrl visibly moves the stripes to what Ctrl+button would run. A button whose chord is unbound shows nothing, because that is what pressing it would do — the table has no fallback to the plain binding and neither does the paint. The old `.tool-transient` background lit ONE tool and never said which BUTTON, so it said something different from the stripe beside it about the same table; two signals for one fact is how the bar comes to claim one thing while the mouse does another. It is deleted, along with the whole `on_gesture_tool`/`_fire_gesture_tool` plumbing that existed only to feed it — with the stripes live, a right-drag erase already shows red under the eraser without anyone announcing it.

column2: Ctrl+F on a text-first page
column5: SHIPPED (2026-07-31). (7) CTRL+F DID NOTHING ON A TEXT PAGE. Not the key path — `_on_key` fired and `_show_search()` ran. The search REVEALER was a child of the PDF column (`canvas_box` inside `_paned`), and text mode hides `_paned`, so the bar was revealed where nobody could see it. Moved above both modes: the session content is now vertical (search revealer, then a horizontal `_body` holding the outline, the paned and the sheet). The search itself needed no change and never did — a text page commits its sheet into the notes model on page 0, which is exactly what `_find_note_matches` reads, so hits, next/prev and the selection all worked the whole time. Only the placeholder lied ("Search PDF & notes…" on a page with no PDF); it now says "Search page…" in text mode. THE GENERAL LESSON, and it is the event-reachability trap in a new shape: when a feature is dead in exactly ONE mode, check which container its widget hangs in before reading its handler.

column2: Bookmarks (mark pages, jump to them, reopen where you left off)
column5:
SHIPPED (2026-07-31, user request). A bookmark button beside the search button: click adds, click again removes, long-press opens a popover with the add/remove verb and a scrollable list of every bookmark to jump to. Ctrl+B does the same from the keyboard.

NO, THERE IS NO PDF-NATIVE WAY, and that is worth writing down because it looks like there should be. The closest is the OUTLINE (/Outlines) — but that is the document's own table of contents, which Sidemark already shows in the sidebar and re-orders when you drag a chapter (resort_toc): user bookmarks there would be indistinguishable from chapters and a chapter drag would shuffle them. Named destinations have no viewer convention for "the user marked this", and /OpenAction would change how the file opens in every other reader. So the sidecar, which also keeps the "files stay plain" promise.

ONE MARKER CARRIES EVERY INVISIBLE PER-PAGE FACT. The row-129 marker grew attributes instead of gaining a sibling syntax: `<!-- page:13 continued -->`, `<!-- page:13 bookmark -->`, `<!-- page:13 bookmark=""Eigenvalues"" -->`, and they compose. Old files parse unchanged because "no attributes" was always the ordinary case, and the split stride stays 3 because the second capture group is now the whole attribute string. A name is escaped on write — & " and > — and escaping > is what makes --> unrepresentable, so a bookmark name can never terminate the comment it lives in. The model stores the name UNescaped, or a rename round-trip would grow &s.

A BOOKMARK NEEDS NO ADJACENCY RULE, which is the whole difference from a link. A link is a relationship BETWEEN two pages, so every re-key has to ask whether the relationship survived; a bookmark is a property OF one page, so it just follows it — insert shifts it, reorder maps it, and delete DROPS it (handing it to a neighbour would leave a bookmark pointing at a page nobody marked). Merge import carries it by chapter offset with no conditions at all.

THE LABEL IS DERIVED, NOT STORED (the user asked for the derived form plus renaming). A row reads the page number plus the page's first note line, falling back to the chapter it sits in, falling back to nothing — computed at display time, so editing your notes cannot leave a label describing what used to be there. Renaming stores a name that then wins; committing the derived text unchanged deliberately stores NOTHING, or the first note line would freeze into the file. Renaming is inline (F2 on the selected row, or the pen button on it), never a dialog: it is a one-word edit. It reads own_text, not get — labelling all five slides of a run with the run's body helps nobody (row 129's trap in a new place).

THE MENU ENTRY IS THE BUTTON'S UNDERSTUDY. `_sync_bookmark_chrome` is the single place that decides: _MODE_CHROME answers "does this mode have it", the collapse level answers "is there room", and the menu entry appears exactly when the button has been collapsed away. Two places deciding is how a verb ends up offered twice or not at all. Both list widgets come from ONE builder (`_new_bookmark_list`, registered in `_bookmark_lists`) for the same reason the toolbar badges are generated: a second implementation is how the popover and the menu come to disagree about what is bookmarked.

BOTH MODES? NO — the second stated exception after row 129, and for the same reason: a text-first page is one endless sheet with no page structure to mark. Said loudly here per the parity rule. Bookmarking a LINE of the sheet is a real feature, just a different one (it needs its own re-keying rules when the text is edited); row 130 territory if it ever comes up.

REOPEN WHERE YOU LEFT OFF lives in recent.json, NOT the sidecar (the user's call after being shown the trade). A sidecar is created only once you actually write something, so storing the reading position there would drop a .md beside every PDF you merely glanced at — breaking a documented promise to fix a smaller problem. recent.json already holds a per-path record that is pruned when the file vanishes, so the cost is its own limit: a document older than the last 15 reopens at page 1, which is what it did before anyway. Two traps, both now guarded by tests: loading a document fires a page-0 change, so `_restoring_page` stops it erasing the position it is about to restore; and `_remember_recent_page` updates in place WITHOUT re-ordering the list, or "recent" would come to mean "whatever tab I scrolled in last". An explicit #page=N still wins, because it is applied after open_file.

Ceiling: one small atomic write per page turn — flipping a deck end to end writes recent.json once per page. Coalesce on a timer if it ever shows up in a profile; a crash would then lose the last few seconds.

column2: Stylus/touch input: the device TOOL as a key in the bindings table (pressure, barrel buttons, palm)
column5: Sidemark routes every press purely on BUTTON NUMBER (Bindings.tool_for), so a stylus tip, a fingertip and a resting palm are one and the same to it: all three are button 1 and all three draw. Measured 2026-07-31 with extras/input_probe.py on a Goodix GXTP7380 (27C6:0111) integrated stylus+touchscreen (TUXEDO convertible, Hyprland/Wayland). FINDINGS - these are expensive to re-derive, re-measure only if the hardware changes. (1) Gdk.InputSource LIES. Every stylus event reports src=MOUSE on device 'Logical pointer for GXTP7380:00 27C6:0111 Stylus', because GTK delivers the LOGICAL pointer; only the seat enumeration says PEN. So event.get_device().get_source() - the obvious API - is useless for routing. event.get_device_tool() is the truth: non-None with a Gdk.DeviceToolType on every stylus event, None for the real mouse ('Core Pointer') and for touch. (2) Pressure is real: 0.0533..0.9993, smooth ramps, and already meaningful AT BUTTON_PRESS (0.05/0.32/0.99 on different strokes), so there is no stroke-start ramp artifact to work around. Gtk.GestureStylus down/motion/up delivers it. This is what unblocks row 26. (3) NO TILT. xtilt/ytilt/dist/rot are present as AXES but flat zero in every one of 1177 sampled lines - a presence check would pass and a tilt feature would silently do nothing. Test for a nonzero VALUE. Rules out tilt-driven behaviour on this class of panel. (4) The pen's two barrel buttons are different KINDS of thing, and this is the load-bearing finding. One switches the pen's tool type to ERASER - PROXIMITY_OUT then PROXIMITY_IN 20ms apart, every following event carrying tool=ERASER with button=1 - and sends no button number at all; it fires while HOVERING, before the tip lands. The other sends a plain button=2 with press=0.0000, independent of the tip, and can be held mid-stroke (mods=0x300). So one is a tool IDENTITY and the other is a MODIFIER on the tip. The second must NOT become its own row in the table: today it arrives as BTN_MIDDLE, which means a hover-press of your thumb fires the lasso. (5) Palm rejection is MOSTLY FREE. The compositor suppresses touch while the pen is in proximity - four pen strokes with a hand resting on the glass produced zero touch events. The hole is the LEADING edge: the palm lands before the tip does, and one 1-point touch got through 0.5s before PROXIMITY_IN. Note PROXIMITY_OUT fires after EVERY stroke (you lift a few mm between letters), so a suppression window must be a timeout after the last proximity, never a raw boolean. (6) This pen has no eraser END - flipping it over produces ordinary TOUCHSCREEN events, the plastic acting as a finger. The ERASER-flip button covers that role better anyway. DESIGN: add a source dimension to Bindings keyed off get_device_tool(), with values pen/eraser/touch/mouse; defaults tip->pen, eraser->eraser, finger->pan. Touch defaulting to PAN is the real palm fix - a palm that pans instead of drawing makes the leading-edge leak harmless, and a proximity timeout closes the rest. Full plan in notes/stylus-input-plan.md. FOLLOW-UP MEASUREMENTS (2026-07-31, extras/input_probe.py --followup), answering what the first pass could not: (7) A GestureDrag DOES see the device tool at drag-begin, via gesture.get_current_event().get_device_tool() - tool=PEN/ERASER for the stylus, None for touch and mouse. The plan's main risk is cleared: the source can be read exactly where routing happens, and no capture-phase source-stamping is needed. (8) The eraser flip MID-STROKE is delivered as a synthetic BUTTON_RELEASE + PROXIMITY_OUT + PROXIMITY_IN + BUTTON_PRESS about 10ms apart, with pressure never dropping (0.7812 at the release, 0.7872 at the press) - the pen never left the glass. So a tool flip splits one physical stroke into two logical ones and needs NO mid-drag tool handling at all; it arrives as a fresh drag-begin with the new tool. The cost to watch: it manufactures a pen LIFT that did not happen, and the pen lift is exactly the separator row 126 (circle to lasso) relies on to tell a dwell-snap from a lasso conversion. Check a barrel flip cannot hand the lasso a stroke the user was still drawing. (9) Barrel button 2 pressed AFTER the tip does not interrupt the drag - it arrives as its own BUTTON_PRESS with mods=0x100 and later events carry 0x200. But pressed BEFORE the tip it CLAIMS the GestureDrag (drag-begin btn=2) and the following tip press gets NO drag-begin at all (observed: tip press with mods=0x200 and no drag). So 'barrel+tip' is NOT a single chorded drag-begin and BUTTON2_MASK cannot simply be read off the gesture state. The barrel must be tracked as a HELD modifier by the capture-phase legacy controller and merged in _chord_state - exactly the pattern the window already uses for held KEYS because touch events do not carry modifiers - and the drag gesture must DENY a pen button-2 press so the tip's press can start a fresh drag. (10) A bare barrel click while hovering is a clean button-2 press/release with pressure EXACTLY 0.0, which is what distinguishes it from a tip press; today it reaches the router as `middle` and fires the LASSO. The eraser button while hovering produces no button event whatsoever, only a proximity flip to tool=ERASER. (11) PALM, and this SIMPLIFIES the plan: libinput ends a palm-shaped contact BY ITSELF after ~110ms (TOUCH_END, not TOUCH_CANCEL) with the hand still flat on the glass and the pen a full second away, and not one touch event arrives during a pen stroke. So the leading-edge hole is a ~110ms tap, which with touch bound to PAN is a few pixels of drift. The planned proximity grace window and the TOUCH_CANCEL retro-cancel are BOTH unnecessary and are dropped - touch->pan is the whole fix. (12) Both barrel buttons together: the eraser flip does not engage at all (tool stayed PEN throughout). Do not design a two-button chord on this hardware. DESIGN REVISED 2026-07-31 (user's call) - the source-dimension table above is SUPERSEDED, keep the findings, drop the table shape. The pen's ends do not need their own table: they are ALIASES OF MOUSE BUTTONS. Pen tip -> left, eraser barrel + tip -> right, other barrel + tip -> middle, finger -> a new 5th button identity with its own stripe colour (default pan). The bindings table, chord ids, persistence, badges, tooltips, popover and toolbar binding surface are then COMPLETELY UNTOUCHED - one new function maps an event to a button identity and every existing consumer already speaks in button identities. Three things fall out for free: the shipped defaults (left pen / right eraser / middle lasso) ALREADY ARE the pen workflow with zero new default rows except the finger; the colour stripes teach the pen mapping because the eraser barrel literally wears the right-button colour; and rebinding the pen is rebinding a mouse button, already built and persisted. THE COST, and it is real: the pen tip cannot hold a different tool from the left mouse button - they are one identity - so 'mouse-left pen, pen-tip highlighter' is inexpressible and you switch with a toolbar tap instead, which changes both.
