That is consistent with the one-table law rather than an exception to it. Implementation shrinks to six sites (BTN_FINGER + its name/label/colour, one DEFAULT_BINDINGS row, button_for_event(), both press routers, and the legacy controller for the barrel held-flag + denying the pen's button-2 drag claim). If you find yourself editing Bindings/chord_id/from_json/chord_label/_refresh_tool_bindings you have drifted back to the superseded draft. Full plan in notes/stylus-input-plan.md. SHIPPED 2026-07-31 as designed above (the aliasing design, not the source-dimension draft). Six sites: BTN_FINGER=11 with its name/label/stripe colour; one new DEFAULT_BINDINGS row (finger: pan); button_for_event(); track_barrel(); both press routers (PDFCanvas._on_drag_begin, TextPageView._on_press_begin) resolving the button through button_for_event; and the legacy controller both canvases already had for the thumb, which now also tracks/denies the barrel. Bindings, chord_id, from_json, chord_label and _refresh_tool_bindings were NOT touched, which was the design's own success criterion. Tests: TestButtonBindings' row-135 block (the mapping, the shipped defaults being the pen workflow, the finger as an ordinary rebindable button, barrel tracking vs a mouse middle-click), TestToolModes.test_the_stylus_routes_through_the_table_as_mouse_buttons + test_a_finger_rebound_to_the_pen_draws_again, and TestTextPageLasso.test_the_stylus_routes_the_same_way_on_a_text_page for parity. Two things worth knowing for the next session: (a) a bare mock.Mock() gesture returns a TRUTHY Mock from get_current_event(), which button_for_event reads as a real touch sequence - every hand-rolled gesture fixture in the suite now sets get_current_event to None explicitly, and a new one must too or its plain drags silently become finger-pans; (b) on the TEXT page a right press is deferred (the context menu owns a clean right click), so the eraser barrel resolves one drag-update later, not at press - correct existing behaviour, but it means a TAP with the eraser barrel opens the context menu. Left alone deliberately rather than forking the router on device; revisit only if it annoys in practice. NOT VERIFIED ON HARDWARE - every one of these is a gesture. IMPLEMENTATION CORRECTION found before shipping: the barrel tracker needs its OWN CAPTURE-phase EventControllerLegacy (_on_barrel_event), not a branch on the thumb's controller. Both existing legacy controllers default to BUBBLE, which runs AFTER the gestures on the same widget - so the drag would have already claimed the barrel press and the deny would do nothing. The thumb's controller stays bubble on purpose: button 10 reaches no gesture, so it never needed capture, and changing its phase would risk a proven path for nothing. SHIPPED-BROKEN AND FIXED SAME DAY, the lesson worth keeping: A NEW DEFAULT BINDING REACHES NOBODY WHO HAS EVER CUSTOMISED THEIR TABLE. Bindings.from_json builds purely from what was saved (which is what makes an unbind stick), so `finger: pan` existed only for a fresh install; the user's finger did nothing on a PDF and dropped through to the caret on a text page, and the giveaway was the missing purple stripe - pan wore no plain button, visible in the [input] bar log line. Worse, the test that was supposed to cover this asserted that a table of only left/middle/right 'behaves exactly as today', which PASSED and locked the bug in: a backwards-compatibility test must assert what SHOULD reach the old table, not that nothing does. Fix: settings.json also stores `button_defaults_seeded`, the list of default KEYS ever offered. A key missing from that list is new since the table was written and is seeded once; a key on the list but absent from the table was deliberately cleared and stays gone. Do NOT merge DEFAULT_BINDINGS over the saved table on load - that resurrects every binding the user ever removed. One-time ambiguity on the FIRST migration only, and it is unavoidable: with no prior record there is no way to tell 'never offered' from 'removed', so any default the user lacks is treated as new and seeded once (for this user that also restored alt+left: text). From this version on the record exists and the question cannot recur. KNOWN HARDWARE QUIRK, deferred to its own session (user, 2026-07-31): on this laptop PALM DETECTION STOPS WORKING WHILE THE CHARGER IS PLUGGED IN. Almost certainly electrical - a capacitive digitiser picking up charger noise, so libinput's palm heuristics stop firing - rather than anything in Sidemark, which is why it is recorded here and not treated as a code bug. Re-measure with extras/input_probe.py on AC vs battery before touching any code: the question is whether the TOUCH_END libinput normally sends after ~110ms still arrives when plugged in. TOOLBAR DECISION REVERSED by the user, 2026-07-31, and the reasoning is worth keeping because the first answer sounded right. The plan said the toolbar stays SOURCE-BLIND so a finger tap binds LEFT, on the argument that binding the finger would make you lose panning every time you picked a tool by touch. The user's correction: it is not permanent - `pan` is in TOOL_BAR_ORDER, so a finger that was just given the pen is ONE finger-tap on `pan` away from panning again - and two-finger gestures must survive regardless, which they do BY CONSTRUCTION: pinch zoom/pan lives on GestureZoom and never consults the table, and _on_pinch_begin already discards any stroke the first finger began. So the bar now binds WHAT YOU TOUCHED IT WITH, which is also what row 132's own law actually says: a finger tap binds `finger`, an eraser-barrel tap binds `right` (free, via button_for_event), and only the pen TIP is the plain pick because a tip press IS a left press. The decision was lifted out of the press closure into module-level toolbar_binding_for(event, raw_button, ctrl, shift, alt) -> (chord|None, swallow_click) so it is testable and lives in ONE place. The swallow flag is a SEPARATE question from which chord to bind and must not be folded into it: GTK does not cancel GtkButton's own primary-only click gesture when our capture controller claims the press, so a `clicked` arrives anyway - and a TOUCH TAP reaches that gesture exactly like a left press does, which is why a finger tap must swallow or it binds the finger AND steals the tip.

column2: Hardware input report: extras/probe_input.py --report + a GitHub issue template
column5: USER IDEA (2026-07-31), out of the row 135 measuring session. When someone's stylus, touchscreen or extra mouse button does not work, neither side can guess what their hardware sends - row 135 is the proof: the docs' obvious API reported the wrong thing, and the four facts that decided the design took a derivation pass out of 1177 raw event lines. Promote extras/input_probe.py into extras/ beside probe_thumb.py (same family, same PyGObject 'event is None' quirk) and add a --report mode that walks the checklist and prints a Markdown block of DERIVED OBSERVATIONS: tool types seen and which button/proximity pattern produced each, button numbers, whether pressure exists and actually VARIED, whether tilt is nonzero (not merely present - row 135's axes exist and are all zero, so a presence check lies), and whether any touch arrived while the pen was in proximity. Observations only, never conclusions: the reporter cannot be asked to interpret their own hardware, and the one thing the script cannot know is what they EXPECTED each button to do - so the issue template must ask that. Plus .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/hardware.yml pointing at the one command. THE VALUE IS THE SUMMARY, NOT THE LOG: a reporter who pastes 1177 raw lines has handed the maintainer homework. It also makes a prefilled issues/new?body=... URL feasible, which caps out around 8KB - a summary fits, a raw log never will. Do NOT have the script file the issue itself (needs auth, and an outbound action should be deliberate). Must not emit hostname, username or file paths, and should SAY so in its own output or nobody will paste it. Sequenced AFTER row 135 on purpose: the summary should report the fields the new table actually keys on, and building it first means rewriting it once. Expect low volume (a couple a year) - it earns its place by collapsing a six-message back-and-forth into one paste, so keep it to one script and one template, not a framework.

column2: --new / --new-text: start on a blank document from the command line
column5: USER REQUEST (2026-07-31). `sidemark --new` opens a blank PDF page, `--new-text` a blank text-first page. Both mirror the EXISTING menu items (☰ New / New text page) by calling the very same actions (_on_new_pdf / _on_new_text_page) rather than reimplementing them, so the flag cannot drift from the menu entry it mirrors. Window policy is the SAME as opening a file: a tab in the window you were last using (_reuse_target), else a new window - so `--new` from a terminal lands beside what you are already reading instead of littering the desktop. --new-text shipped alongside --new (which is all the user asked for) because both menu items exist and shipping half of a pair is the asymmetry the user has called out before. TWO TRAPS, one of which shipped broken and was caught by the user in the real app: (1) open_new_window() queues _open_scratchpad on the idle handler whenever it is given no path, so a fresh window opened for --new got the scratchpad AND the blank page, as two tabs. The fix is a `blank=` parameter on open_new_window: a launch that asked for a blank document gets THAT INSTEAD OF the scratchpad, because the scratchpad is what an EMPTY launch means and nobody asking for a blank page asked for two documents. Do not 'fix' this by queueing the blank doc after the scratchpad - that is what produced the bug. (2) A path WINS over --new (`_parse_open_args` returns new=None whenever a path is present): naming a file and asking for a blank one is contradictory, and opening the file you named is the safe reading - the blank page is one click away in the menu, the file you meant might not be. Surfaces updated together, since a flag nobody can discover is a flag nobody uses: --help text, README's command-line block, and the bash completion in extras/sidemark.bash. Tests: TestSingleInstanceArgs covers the parser including the path-beats---new rule; the window behaviour (one window, one document, no scratchpad) was verified by launching the real app, which is the stronger check here since it is idle-handler ordering that a headless test cannot meaningfully drive.

column2: Delete button on a lasso selection (red cross beside the loop/box chip)
column5: USER REQUEST (2026-07-31): circling strokes with the pen should let you REMOVE them without reaching for the keyboard - which is the whole point on a convertible folded flat, where Delete is not available at all. A bare red cross - no ground - sits directly BELOW the row-125 mode chip, on the same vertical. Below rather than beside: the chip already sits diagonally out from the box's top-left corner, so going further left walks it off the screen on a selection near the page edge, while the space below is the box's own left margin and is always there; sharing the chip's x also makes the two read as one small stack of verbs instead of two unrelated dots. ONE POLICY FOR BOTH CANVASES, exactly like the chip it rides with: lasso_delete_centre / lasso_delete_hit / draw_lasso_delete are module-level and shared, and lasso_delete_hit simply defers to lasso_chip_hit so the destructive button can never be HARDER to hit than the harmless one beside it. It appears under the same condition as the chip (a selection that still has its LOOP); a boxed or click-selection reaches Delete from the keyboard. LIGHTER THAN THE CHIP ON PURPOSE (user's call after seeing a filled disc: 'more light weight'): the chip is a filled control you toggle, this is a mark you tap once. COLOUR and SHAPE are what separate them - red strokes vs an accent-on-white square - and that is the only guard on a destructive target touching a harmless one; it never needed a disc to do that. A test asserts the two hit regions do not overlap and that neither steals the corner resize handle. The paint is light but THE TARGET IS NOT: lasso_delete_hit still covers the full chip-sized square, so it stays as easy to hit with a pen as the control above it - do not shrink the hit box to match the ink. It carries a white underlay stroke under the red so it survives dark ink or a pasted photo; invisible against the page, and the alternative is a control that vanishes exactly where you most want to delete something. It calls delete_selected_strokes(), the same op the Delete key produces, so there is ONE delete verb and one undo entry rather than a second path that could drift. Both press routers test it just before the chip and claim the press, and selection_grab_at includes it so a press on the button is never read as a grab or a fresh loop. Tests: TestLassoSelect (removes exactly what was selected, one undo entry restores it; no overlap with the chip or the corner handle; rides with the chip) and TestTextPageLasso for the sheet - the parity law, a delete button on a PDF and not on paper would read as a bug. NOT yet verified by hand: it is a pen target, and whether 16px is big enough to hit first time is the user's call. FOLLOW-UP (user, same day): tapping EITHER little control - the delete cross or the row-125 mode chip - and drifting a few px before lifting used to leave a stray stroke beside the button you just pressed. A PEN TAP ALWAYS JITTERS, so a press that a control consumed has to kill the REST of the gesture, not just the press: both branches now set the surface's already-existing 'this drag means nothing' flag (PDFCanvas._ignoring, TextPageView._ink_ignoring). Without it the drag-update falls through every branch of _on_drag_update to the drawing one, which is the LAST branch - so any consumed press that forgets this draws. The bug predates the delete button: the chip had it since row 125 and nobody noticed, because a mouse click does not move. Worth remembering when adding any further tap target to a canvas. The regression test drives begin+update+update+end and was CHECKED TO FAIL when the flag is removed (an extra stroke appears, 3!=2 and 2!=1) - a test that taps without dragging would have passed against the bug.

column2: Handwriting quality: interpolate then denoise (Taubin), pressure width, smear trim, hover lead-in, arc prediction, page rulings
column5: USER REPORT (2026-07-31): "my handwriting does not look good", with two observations that turned out to BE the diagnosis: "when I write slow it looks good, but on fast writing the o's will get small", and a screenshot of an 'o' drawn as a visible 12-gon. Both were right, and the first has an exact formula. THE BUG: _smooth_points was 4 Laplacian passes at factor 0.25, asked to do two different jobs at once. Laplacian is a DIFFUSION and diffusion destroys curvature: a loop of N samples loses about 1 - 2f(1 - cos(2pi/N)) of its radius per pass. Measured on a true circle of r=6: -19.0% at 12 samples, -8.2% at 20, -2.3% at 40. So the damage scaled with HOW FAST YOU WROTE, which is exactly the symptom. And because nothing interpolated the sparse samples, the smoother was the only thing rounding the corners - and the only way a diffusion can round a corner is by pulling it inward. THE DESIGN is three jobs kept deliberately apart (conflating any two is how this happened): (1) resample_ink - INTERPOLATE, centripetal Catmull-Rom walked at fixed arc length. Catmull-Rom because it INTERPOLATES: the curve passes through every point the pen reported, so filling gaps can never move the line off where you drew it. 'Centripetal' (knots spaced by sqrt(chord)) is what stops it looping out past a sharp corner. The arc-length walk both fills a fast stroke's gaps and thins a slow one's clusters, so what reaches step 2 no longer depends on pen speed. (2) taubin_smooth - DENOISE, lambda shrink alternating with mu = -1.06*lambda inflate. New result: -0.3%/0.0%/+0.1% at 12/20/40 samples. (3) width_profile - SHAPE. TRAP, cost an hour and a real bug: the Laplacian must be the MIDPOINT form c + f*((a+b)/2 - c), NOT c + f*(a+b-2c). The two differ by 2x, which puts the operator's eigenvalues in [0,2] rather than [0,4], and Taubin's lambda/mu are only a low-pass filter on the former - with the doubled form the mu pass AMPLIFIES the Nyquist frequency and smoothing a zigzag made it worse. It passed the circle test while broken (a smooth circle has no high-frequency content to blow up) and was caught only by test_smoothing_reduces_jitter. TRAP: lambda is capped at 0.5 by stability, so the PASS COUNT is the only knob that deepens the stopband - 6 pairs removed 20% of measured noise, 20 removed 26%, past that it flattens; the cost is a passband ripple that makes a loop GROW (+0.5% at 20, +2% at 70), the right direction to err but not far. TRAP: a big zigzag is NOT jitter - once resampled it is a long-wavelength shape, and Taubin preserving it is the SAME property that keeps a fast 'o' round, so denoising must be tested against a smooth arc plus per-sample noise, never a zigzag. NOTE the 'Smoothing' slider is now the DENOISER only; resampling always runs, because turning interpolation off would only bring the facets back. PRESSURE (unblocks row 26): pressure_for_event() is the sibling of button_for_event(). A stroke's 'press' list is NOT raw pressure - it is the finished per-point WIDTH FACTOR in 0..1 with the end taper folded in, painted as width*factor. One concept instead of two: it lets a mouse stroke taper without a second flag beside it, and makes 'has a profile' mean exactly 'is freehand' at render time (a snapped rectangle or an imported annotation has none and stays flat). draw_ink_stroke is THE ink painter - all SEVEN painters route through it (page render, live stroke, presenter mirror, both copy-render PNGs, both lasso glows, the text-page PDF export); with a profile it builds a closed OUTLINE and fills it once, because per-segment strokes would double-darken where they overlap. 'grow=' is how the lasso glow haloes a tapered stroke without disagreeing with it at the tip. PERSISTENCE: a PDF ink annotation has ONE width - the row 26 blocker - so the profile rides in the annot's /Contents behind INK_PROFILE_TAG. Sidemark reloads the taper exactly; every other reader shows constant-width ink. Chosen over splitting a stroke into per-width-band annotations, which would have cost the lasso, the eraser and the control points. Text sheet: a 'press' key in the -ink.json sidecar. Both guarded by a LENGTH match, so a mismatched profile loses the taper rather than shifting every width along the stroke. THE SMEAR TRIM IS ASYMMETRIC, and this is the load-bearing insight - it came from the user reframing their own request: they wanted a minimum-pressure threshold for "clearer breaks between letters", then noticed "sometimes the stroke will be captured too late". Those are OPPOSITE problems at opposite ends of one stroke. The END is a real smear (the pen unloads before leaving the glass and trails into the next letter). The START is already CLIPPED, not smeared - the digitiser reports no contact until its own hardware threshold is crossed, so the first sample already carries real pressure (row 135 measured 0.05/0.32/0.99 at BUTTON_PRESS) and the ink before it was never captured. A symmetric gate would therefore have made the second complaint strictly worse while fixing the first. trim_light_tail() trims the falling edge only; the live per-sample gate that existed briefly was removed for exactly this reason. It also stops at the first sample above threshold rather than filtering, because a dip in the MIDDLE is the pen still writing. Off by default. LATENCY, two prototypes, and only one of them invents anything. The HOVER LEAD-IN is free real data, from the user's question "the position of the mouse before I draw should be available because it gets tracked even if I do not touch the glass, right?" - correct, a stylus is tracked in proximity, so the app already knows where the pen was in the milliseconds before contact was admitted. That IS the ink 'captured too late' was missing. hover_lead_in() walks BACKWARDS from the press and stops at the first sample too old or too far from the one after it - stopping on the gap is what keeps a pen that swooped in from across the page from drawing its approach. Recovered points get pressure 0.0 (they were genuinely below the contact threshold), so the taper treats them as the lightest part of the stroke. On by default. The PREDICTION is a guess and is therefore confined to the screen: _live_stroke() adds the predicted tip, the commit path reads current_stroke which never contains it, so a bad guess flickers for one frame and can never reach the file. Off by default. It extrapolates along an ARC, not a line (user asked to integrate curve information, and it matters more than expected): heading and turn rate are estimated over the window and the lead integrated as constant-speed circular motion. Straight extrapolation is wrong exactly where the lead is most visible - out of the curve of an 'o' the velocity points along the TANGENT, so a linear guess leaves the letter and is yanked back on the next sample, reading as the tip stuttering. Measured against a traced circle, mean error tangent vs arc: 0.913/0.189 at 8ms, 3.728/0.554 at 24ms, 7.653/0.885 at 40ms. Clamps: PREDICT_MAX_TURN (a noisy curvature estimate must not spiral) and PREDICT_MAX_PX. PREDICT_MAX_MS is 120, deliberately past anything sane at the user's request - the useful value is only findable by feel, and the top of the range is where you SEE what the guess is doing. PAGE BACKGROUNDS (user request): plain/lines/squares/dots, drawn into the page CONTENT at creation by draw_page_background, not painted under it at render time - a background you write on is one you hand in, so it must print, export and open ruled anywhere else. Ceiling: fixed at creation; changing it later would mean marking which pages are ours, i.e. the optional-content machinery row 118 warns about, and it is not worth it to re-rule a page you can simply make again. Text-sheet parity was offered and DECLINED for now (a grid under Markdown text may just look busy). An ink STABILIZER (pulled-string lag) was also offered and declined - it adds the very latency the user is unhappy about. NOT VERIFIED: every part of this is a gesture, so it is the user's to judge; stroke-onset recovery (extending backwards along the initial tangent when the first sample arrives hot) is written up but NOT built, because it invents ink - measure with extras/input_probe.py first. SECOND PASS 2026-08-01, after the user tried it - five findings, three of them user hypotheses that were RIGHT. (A) SMALL WRITING was the only thing being mangled, and it was a SCALE bug the user guessed before I did ("maybe the smoothing can be automatically tuned based on the size of the stroke"). Every length in the pipeline is really 'a fraction of a letter' and only looked like a constant because it was tuned at one size: a fixed 1.0-unit spacing implies a fixed ~1.2-unit smoothing radius, which is a few percent of large writing but a QUARTER of a small x-height, so small cursive was averaged into mush while the same settings barely touched big writing. ink_feature_size + adaptive_spacing fix it, and because a fixed pass count over a fixed spacing IS a fixed smoothing radius, one number scales both effects. Fidelity is now scale-invariant: an 'o' holds to -0.6% at r=1.5 and -0.7% at r=20. The measure is the bbox's SHORT SIDE - a cursive run's x-height is what must survive, the diagonal is only how long the word is - and the degenerate fallback must stay SMALL: at diag*0.15 it wins above ~6.6:1, which ordinary cursive exceeds, and the measure would then grow with WORD LENGTH, the exact opposite of its purpose. (B) The i-DOT problem was a bug introduced by the taper in the first pass: INK_TAPER_LEN was 2.5 units at EACH end, so any stroke under 5 units long was pure ramp and never reached full width - i-dots came out at 45-56% thickness. INK_TAPER_FRAC caps the ramp at a share of the stroke itself; dots now reach 1.00. The lesson generalises: a length expressed in page units is a bug waiting for a mark smaller than it. (C) PREDICTION FLICKERED because the estimate is rebuilt from scratch on every motion event, so consecutive guesses disagree by more than the pen actually moved. Damped with an EMA (PREDICT_SMOOTH). Damping the OFFSET and not the point is what makes it safe - the anchor still tracks the pen exactly, so the lag being hidden is not re-introduced. (D) The POINTER is now hidden for drawing tools under a STYLUS (_hide_pointer): an arrow trailing a few mm behind the nib is exactly what gives the lag away, and it destroyed the illusion the lead was buying. Never hidden under a mouse, where the pointer is all the hand has. (E) The HOVER LEAD-IN did not help in the hand - kept as an option, defaulted OFF, as is prediction. CAPTURE AND REPLAY, so ink tuning stops being guesswork: SIDEMARK_CAPTURE_INK=<path> appends every finished stroke's RAW samples (pre-interpolation, with pressures and the settings in force) as JSON lines, and extras/ink_replay.py measures, sweeps and re-renders them. Its key statistic is SAMPLE SPACING / FEATURE SIZE, and it is what answers 'is this fixable in software or is the hardware just too coarse?': above ~0.25 the digitiser is undersampling the writing and interpolation is carrying the result (writing bigger is the real fix), below ~0.06 the pen oversamples and whatever roughness remains is tremor, so denoising is the lever. Measure before touching a constant again. THIRD PASS 2026-08-01, MEASURED ON REAL HANDWRITING (41 strokes, kept at notes/ink-capture-2026-08-01.jsonl because /tmp does not survive a reboot; re-analyse with extras/ink_replay.py). READ THIS BEFORE CHANGING ANY INK CONSTANT. (1) SMALL WRITING IS A HARDWARE CEILING, and now it is a number rather than a guess. The digitiser samples at a roughly constant SPATIAL density however big you write, so samples-per-letter collapses as the writing shrinks: feature size 4.7 -> spacing 2.09 -> ~3.1 samples per feature; 11.0 -> 2.40 -> ~4.3; 21.5 -> 3.76 -> ~6.4; 93.2 -> 3.66 -> ~26.7. Three samples per x-height is not a smoothing problem, it is an INFORMATION problem - no filter can reconstruct a letter that was never measured. So the answer to 'is this fixable in software or is the hardware too inaccurate' is: for small writing, the hardware. What software can do, and now does, is interpolate smoothly between the few real points and not destroy them. Corollary worth telling a user: writing bigger roughly DOUBLES samples per feature from tiny to medium (a bigger letter takes longer to draw), while ZOOMING IN does not help at all - the digitiser samples in physical space, so letter and spacing shrink together in document units and the ratio is unchanged. (2) THE SMOOTHING SLIDER IS NEARLY INERT ON REAL INK, AND THAT IS CORRECT: sweeping it end to end moved mean arc length by 0.5% (100.5% -> 100.0%). At 3-6 samples per feature there is no redundancy - every sample is signal, so there is nothing to average away and anything removed would be shape. The adaptive spacing already backs the smoothing radius off as writing shrinks, which is exactly why the slider goes quiet where it should. DO NOT 'fix' this by strengthening the denoiser; on this data that can only destroy letters. A stronger denoiser is only meaningful on OVERSAMPLED input (large slow writing, ratio below ~0.06). (3) THE SMEAR IS REAL AND MEASURED: every one of the 41 strokes ends in a pressure ramp to exactly 0.00 (e.g. 0.73, 0.60, 0.27, 0.12, 0.05, 0.00) while starts come in already loaded (first sample 0.23 and rising). That is the asymmetry the design assumed, confirmed: the last ~4-5 samples of every stroke are the pen unloading and none of the starts are. Suggested starting value for Smear trim: 0.15-0.25. Also this pass: a DOT BOOST (INK_DOT_BOOST 2.1, fading to 1.0 by INK_DOT_LEN 5.0) because a dot at exactly the stroke width reads as a speck beside its own stem; the POINTER is hidden while a stroke is in flight and restored on lift (_hide_pointer/_apply_cursor) - tying it to the STROKE rather than the selected tool is what makes it safe with a mouse, since the pointer can only vanish while a button is already held, and an earlier stylus-detection version silently did nothing because a hovering pen does not reliably deliver motion events; and prediction is DAMPED across frames. TRAP found the hard way: `flat` (the highlighter) must NOT skip the pipeline - it drops pressure, taper and dot boost only. Making it return early broke resampling for highlighter strokes and was caught only because two geometry tests used flat=True to mean 'geometry only'. GENERAL LESSON, now made twice: a length expressed in PAGE units is a bug waiting for a mark smaller than it - the fixed taper ate i-dots, the fixed spacing ate small writing. Check anything measured in document units against a 3-unit mark before shipping it. PERSISTED (2026-08-10), the follow-up this row's settings always needed: the pen popover's values were session-scoped, so a value chosen by hand was gone on restart - which would have annoyed the moment one was liked, and the live-smoothing and prediction A/Bs are exactly the sessions that choose one. PEN_SETTINGS is the one table behind both directions: every PDFCanvas loads the values at construction and the window writes them to every open canvas AND to settings.json (nested under "pen") on each change. A text sheet needed nothing - TextPageView already reads its session's canvas through get_smoothing/get_predict_ms/etc. Doing it this way also closed a hole that predated the popover: a new tab's PDFCanvas took the HARDCODED defaults, so picking red and then opening a second file handed you the stock blue pen back, and only pen_color was ever pushed onto a canvas (once, at window build, from the theme accent). The accent is now the fallback for an unpicked colour rather than an assignment over the loaded one, and it is applied per TAB. Every value is validated on the way in against the popover widget's own range - settings.json is a plain file a user can edit, and a junk shape_snap or a predict_ms of 1e9 must fall back or clamp rather than reach the ink pipeline or leave a scale unable to show what was loaded. # ceiling: one small settings write per scale step, so dragging a slider writes the file a few dozen times; debounce if it ever shows up in a profile. PREDICTION CAN NOW BE GRADED ON REAL INK (2026-08-10), which it could not be before: the capture recorded no per-sample TIMES, and prediction is the one part of the pipeline that reads the clock - so the 41 real strokes that settled spacing, smoothing and the taper could say nothing at all about the lead. capture_raw_stroke now writes a `samples` list beside `pts`: the same stroke in SCREEN coords with a timestamp each, which is exactly what predict_point sees live (pts is document units and untimed, so it cannot carry this). Collected in _note_sample, which is already called once per stroke sample on both canvases, and only while capturing - a diagnostic that grows a list on every motion event is not off. Old captures simply lack the key and still replay. extras/ink_replay.py --predict is the grader: it walks each stroke sample by sample with the SAME PREDICT_WINDOW and the same EMA on the offset as the live path, and against the pen's actual later position scores three things - `lag` (the last reported sample, i.e. no prediction, which is the error prediction exists to cancel and so the denominator for everything else), `arc` (what Sidemark draws) and `linear` (straight extrapolation, what the arc claims to beat). It reports recovery, p90, how often prediction made it WORSE, and a breakdown by curvature quartile, because the sharp turns are where an extrapolation of any kind overshoots. THE CAVEAT THAT KEEPS IT HONEST, and it is in the docstring: ground truth is the DIGITISER's later report, so this grades how well the guess tracks the pen's path, not how much lag the hand perceives - which also includes the panel's own reporting delay and the compositor's. A prediction can score perfectly here and still feel late, so the A/B in the hand is not replaced by it. USER OBSERVATION the same day, still unexplained: 20 ms is barely felt; a FINGER needs no prediction at all while the pen does. Three candidate reasons, only the first of which is about latency at all - a pan has no reference point (nothing must appear AT the fingertip, whereas the nib is a physical marker sitting beside the ink), a finger occludes its own contact point, and a pan is one transform of an already-rendered surface against a stroke going through the pipeline and a redraw. Whether the pen's ACTUAL latency is higher than touch on this Goodix panel is unmeasured; extras/input_probe.py is where to answer it before blaming software. FIRST GRADING ON REAL INK (2026-08-10, 29 strokes, 314 graded samples) AND THE THING IT FOUND. THE HEADLINE IS NOT PREDICTION: the pen's samples arrive every 33.2 ms, range 33.0-34.6 across 26 strokes - a 30 Hz clock, not hardware jitter, on a 60 Hz display, so ink updates every OTHER frame. The one stroke the session log identifies as a FINGER came in at 18.5 ms (~54 Hz), which is exactly the user's report that a finger feels quick and the pen does not. n=1 for the finger, so that half is a hint, not a result; the 30 Hz is solid. This reframes the whole ink-feel question: sample spacing / feature size measured 0.337 here (UNDERSAMPLED), so the denoiser has no redundancy to work with and prediction has almost no signal to extrapolate from, and at least one full 33 ms sample of the felt lag is simply waiting for the next report. Chase the rate before tuning any filter. Open question, not yet measured: is 30 Hz the PANEL or our delivery? _now_ms is wall-clock at handling time, so the capture measures DELIVERY. A mouse stroke is the clean control (no digitiser at all), and live smoothing running per motion event is the obvious suspect if we are dropping frames. PREDICTION AS SHIPPED IS WORTHLESS AT THIS RATE: recovery of the no-prediction lag was 0.1% at 10 ms, 4.4% at 20, 4.0% at 30, and NEGATIVE at 40 (-2.0%) and 60 (-5.7%); it made the error worse on 40-45% of samples; by curvature quartile at 60 ms it was -0.9% / +23.4% / -0.4% / -43.6%, i.e. worst exactly at the sharp turns the user suspected. BUT THE ARC IS NOT THE CULPRIT - it beat linear extrapolation at every lead and in every curvature quartile, so the arc choice (row 139's original measurement) holds. THE DAMPING IS: undamped recovery is 22.2% / 22.8% / 23.1% / 13.1% / 9.0% at the same leads, and undamped is worse-than-nothing on 31-36% of samples against the damped 39-45%. PREDICT_SMOOTH is 0.3 PER EVENT, which at 30 Hz is a time constant near 100 ms - five times the lead being smoothed, so the offset drawn is computed from a pen position 100 ms old. It is a rate-dependent constant expressed per event, which is bug-shaped rather than a design choice; a time-based constant would not change meaning with the report rate. Do NOT simply turn damping off: it was added from a HAND judgement about jitter, and accuracy and stability are different properties. MEASUREMENT CAVEAT that cuts against the above and must be kept with it: ground truth is the digitiser's own later report, and truth at t+lead is LINEARLY interpolated between samples 33 ms apart, which straightens exactly the curvature the arc model exists to capture - so the truth is biased toward straight lines, flattering lag and linear and penalising arc. The arc is probably better than -43.6% at high curvature. The bias shrinks as the rate rises. ALSO SETTLED HERE: do not reach for a Kalman or constant-acceleration model yet. At 30 Hz with a 5-sample window this is an INFORMATION limit, not a modelling one - the measured ceiling even undamped is ~23% recovery, and a richer model has more parameters than the data supports. Fix the damping's units, re-measure, and only then ask whether a model earns its complexity. device_source_for() was added so a capture names its device ("stylus"/"touch"/"mouse") and ink_replay reports the rate per device; it is CAPTURE-ONLY and deliberately not part of button_for_event, because a source dimension on the binding table is the design row 135 superseded.

column2: Number-set symbols, ruling on pages added mid-document, Ctrl+Shift+O for recents
column5: Three small asks in one pass. (1) NUMBER SETS: \R \N \Q \Z \C render as the double-struck letters, each with a long spelling beside it (\realnum \natnum \ratnum \intnum \compnum) so the symbol is findable when the initial has slipped your mind. These are the only single-LETTER commands in _MD_SYMBOLS and they are safe for the same reason every other entry is: a command runs to the first non-letter, so \Real is an unknown command and not 'R'+'eal'. Nothing else was needed - one table serves the editor, the callout markup and the PDF export. (2) RULING ON ADDED PAGES: the ruling was baked only by the blank-document path, so a document started on squared paper went plain at page 2 - reported as 'when will ruling:dots be applied?'. The fix is the one draw_page_background always promised: blank_pdf_file() is now module-level and every blank page in the app comes from it (New, --new, row 130's edge pull, and add_blank_page). insert_page CANNOT do this - it makes an empty page and the ruling is page CONTENT, so the new page is built by cairo at the CURRENT page's size and merged with insert_pdf. That is safe here only because the source has no image layer to strip (row 123's trap). The setting keeps its meaning - it is what a blank page is ruled with at the moment it is made - so a page added today is ruled per today's setting and row 139's ceiling (a page's ruling is fixed once made) is unchanged. (3) Ctrl+Shift+O opens the recent list. It pops the single menu popover and then switches its stack to the recent page, in that ORDER: the popover resets itself to 'main' on show, so choosing the page first lands you on the main menu (#63's stack design is what makes a second popover not an option).

column2: Only the expression under the caret falls back to source (and a click lands on the symbol)
column5: Reported as: clicking into a line with rendered symbols leaves the caret at the column you hit rather than the symbol you aimed at, and the whole line un-renders. Both are the same cause - the cursor line reverted to source WHOLESALE, so the text moved out from under the click and the caret was then guessed back with a common-prefix/suffix heuristic that is only right when the caret is past every symbol on the line. Fix has two halves, and the second is what makes the first safe. (1) _symbolize_map returns the rendered text AND an index map back to the source (one entry per rendered character; every character of a substitution points at the START of what it replaced, which keeps the map non-decreasing and makes both directions a lookup). The caret is now PLACED through the map, so a click lands on the \command the glyph came from. (2) Only the expression the caret TOUCHES (from just before the backslash to just after the last letter) is left as source; everything else on the line stays rendered. Extended to the tag-rendered constructs for the same reason - the script the caret is in shows its ^/_, the bold run it is in shows its **, nothing else does. THE TRAP: the caret's line is now partly rendered, so an edit CAN land on a glyph (backspace at the start of the open expression), and the old rule - trust the stored source only if it still renders to exactly this line - would then throw the source away and freeze every OTHER symbol on the line as a literal glyph in the .md. _line_source splices the edit onto the source through the index map instead, so deleting a rendered symbol deletes the command it came from. That also fixes the same latent hole on non-cursor lines. A SELECTION still opens the whole line: its two ends are two expressions and a selection re-shaping itself as it grows is worse than a line that settles once. _line_originals is now (source, rendered, imap, open span) - the open span is what tells the next pass that a line the caret has left is not already done. Cursor-move rehighlighting is gated on the line holding something renderable (_MD_RENDERABLE_RE), since moving along a line now matters and walking a line of prose must not re-highlight the buffer on every keypress. Row 128's two mark tests still hold, with the click moved onto the glyph - that is now the case where the line changes under the caret.

column2: Marked text opens in full, a terminating space is eaten at end of line, triple-click takes the whole line
column5: Three follow-ups from using row 141. (1) EVERYTHING MARKED opens, not just the two ends: a selection de-renders every line it covers, because what is selected is what is about to be cut or replaced. _rehighlight computes the covered line range once and _render_open_line takes whole=True for those; _highlight_line's caret_in returns True on a marked line so the tag-rendered constructs (scripts, **, [[ ]]) open with it. Trap: the rehighlight gate in _on_cursor_moved skips a caret move within a line with nothing renderable on it, which left the other lines of a just-dropped selection open - it now always reschedules while a selection was open. (2) THE TERMINATING SPACE AT END OF LINE is eaten like any other. Typing `\beta ` rendered the glyph but left the space visible, so the caret stood a gap away from the beta and the gap closed itself on the next keystroke - the caret appearing to jump backwards. Two regexes now: the strict one, and _MD_SYMBOL_END_RE whose lookahead also accepts end-of-line. It is end of LINE, not end of string: rendering runs per code/link segment and per protected-span split, so at_end is threaded through _symbolize_map/_symbolize and only the last text segment of a line gets the end rule (the callout markup renderer had to be told the same, or `\alpha `x`` lost its space). The touch test that decides whether an expression stays open uses _MD_COMMAND_RE - the command WITHOUT its terminating space - so a caret standing after the space means you are done and the glyph belongs on screen; without that split, typing the space would keep the command open instead of rendering it. (3) TRIPLE-CLICK selects the paragraph (blank-line delimited) rather than GtkTextView's logical line, which on a wrapped sheet is a fragment of what looks like a line. Bubble phase so it runs after the view's own selection and replaces it; a blank line is its own paragraph so a triple-click there does not swallow a neighbour. FOLLOW-UP after using it, two corrections and one bug. (2b) SCRIPTS obey the same rule as commands: `a_i ` and `b^2 ` at the end of a line eat their terminating space too. It is needed wherever the space was FORCED on you - an unbraced script runs to the first non-alphanumeric, so `a_ib` subscripts "ib" and you have to type `a_i b`; that makes it exactly the `\alphax` bargain, and half the maths behaving differently from the other half is not a rule anyone can hold while writing. _MD_SCRIPT_END_RE is the end-of-line twin of _MD_SCRIPT_RE, iter_scripts takes at_end (threaded through the callout markup renderer per segment, same as _symbolize), and the caret test in _highlight_line now uses script_body_end - the script WITHOUT the space it ate - for the reason the command test uses _MD_COMMAND_RE: otherwise typing the space holds `_i ` open under the caret instead of rendering it. (3b) TRIPLE-CLICK takes the whole LOGICAL line - everything up to the newline, however many rows it wraps onto - not the blank-line paragraph shipped first, and not GtkTextView's own "line", which is the DISPLAY line. (3c) The bug behind "the selection disappears after a split second": GtkTextView's triple-click starts a selection DRAG with LINE granularity, anchored to two anonymous marks on the line, and re-derives the selection between them on every motion event. _buf_replace_line (the de-render rewrite that a selection triggers) deletes and re-inserts the line, collapsing both anchors onto its start - so the first flicker of the hand re-selected an empty range. Two fixes, both worth keeping: _buf_replace_line now carries EVERY mark on the line across, not just insert/selection_bound (row 128 generalised - it walks by column, because forward_char reports failure when it lands on the buffer's end iterator, which is where the last line's marks sit); and the triple-click handler DENIES the view's internal GestureDrag, since that drag's granularity is the display line and it would otherwise snap our whole-line selection back to one wrapped row on the next motion event. (3d) And the selection has to be applied from an IDLE, after the press, not inside the click handler: controllers on one widget fire NEWEST FIRST, so GtkTextView's own click gesture - installed before ours - runs AFTER it and lays its display-line selection on top of ours. Shipped once selecting in the handler, which is why the first cut still selected the wrapped row: the handler was running the whole time and being overwritten. The idle is also the only place the drag denial works, since the drag only holds the sequence once the press is over.

column2: The line is smoothed while you draw, not only once you lift
column5: Reported as: while drawing, the line is raw and pointy and only becomes smooth once the pen is lifted. It was: the live path deliberately skipped the pipeline, on the stated grounds that 'resampling on every motion event would cost more than it could possibly show'. Both halves of that were measured against the 41 captured strokes in notes/ and both are false. COST: the whole commit pipeline is 1.7 ms per motion event on the longest real stroke (87 samples), against a 16.7 ms frame. CRAWL - the real worry, since denoising is a GLOBAL filter and a re-settling line behind the nib would be worse than a pointy one: appending one sample re-indexes up to 203 of 245 resampled points, which looks fatal in a diff and is nothing, because those samples are SLIDING ALONG A PATH THAT IS NOT MOVING. Measured as SHAPE - distance from each point to the other polyline - the settled body shifts by a median of 0.0% of an x-height, p90 0.19%, worst 1.3%. That distinction is the whole finding and is why the test compares shape and never index-aligned points: an index-aligned test fails against correct behaviour. live_ink_stroke() is the result, beside finish_ink_stroke and sharing its steps. It skips exactly two, both because the stroke is not over: capture_raw_stroke (that file is one record per STROKE, not per motion event - routing the live path through finish_ink_stroke would have spammed it on every frame) and trim_light_tail (mid-stroke the falling edge is just where the pen IS, so trimming would eat the tip and hand it back the moment you pressed harder). The tail is therefore the one place live and committed still differ, and it is the last millimetres of a stroke you have not finished. Verified live-vs-committed deviation over the body is 0.0000 of an x-height - they are the same line. THREE traps. (1) A SNAPPED stroke must be exempt live exactly as it is at commit: the dwell already settled that geometry and denoising a recognised rectangle rounds the corners it was just given. _live_stroke tests _straight_mode. (2) The predicted tip is appended AFTER smoothing, via a `lead` argument, never before - taubin_smooth pins its endpoints, so a guess passed through the filter drags the last REAL samples onto it. It still never touches current_stroke, so it still cannot reach the file. (3) Cost is O(n) per event and INK_MAX_POINTS is 3000, so past LIVE_SMOOTH_MAX_PTS (600) only the TAIL is re-shaped: 3000 samples costs 4.0 ms instead of ~17. The join needs no blending because resampling starts at the first point and denoising holds both endpoints, so head and tail still meet at the sample they were split on. The head is simply un-denoised until commit - which is what the entire live line used to be, so the degradation floor is yesterday's behaviour. _live_stroke was already shared by class assignment (TextPageView borrows PDFCanvas's), so both modes got this at once; the one thing needing an adapter is the smoothing setting, which the canvas holds as an attribute and the sheet behind a getter - hence _smoothing_now(), matching the existing _finish_stroke adapter pattern. FOLLOW-UP: prediction (row 139) is deferred until this has been judged in the hand - both act on the line near the nib, so judging prediction against the old pointy live line would have to be redone anyway. FIRST HAND TRIAL (2026-08-09), and the trade-off it exposed. The user's report: 'feels a bit slower', and - the sharp observation - 'the line will only be updated once the pen sends a new point, that feels quite shaky'. Two candidate causes, one measured dead and one measured true. NOT LAG: the drawn tip sits exactly on the pen's latest sample, gap 0.000 doc units at every sample of all 41 captured strokes, so the resample walk does land the final point and nothing is trailing behind the nib. IT IS THE TAIL RE-SETTLING: the last 15% of the line moves a median of 0.21% of an x-height per new sample, p90 1.2%, worst 6.6% - against EXACTLY 0.0000 for the old raw polyline, which by construction cannot move because appending a point never disturbs the points already there. So the user's diagnosis is right and the shakiness is real and inherent: denoising is a global filter, the samples are sparse (~3 per x-height writing small on this panel), and so the tip visibly re-shapes on every report. This is the COST side of live smoothing and it was not visible in the pre-ship measurements because those deliberately excluded the tail as 'expected to move'. The lesson generalises: measuring the settled body answered whether the ink CRAWLS and said nothing about what the hand is actually watching, which is the last centimetre. Shipped a 'Smooth while drawing' checkbox rather than picking for the user, because the two failure modes are opposite and only feelable: OFF, the line never moves once drawn but re-forms on release; ON, it is already the line you keep but the tail wriggles. Same wiring as the other pen-popover settings (canvas attribute + get_live_smooth getter on the sheet), and the committed ink is identical either way - the switch changes only what is on screen mid-stroke, which a test pins. NOT YET DONE, the obvious follow-up if the wriggle is the verdict: damp the tail across frames (blend the newly computed last stretch toward the previous frame's) - the same shape of fix as PREDICT_SMOOTH, and it trades tip fidelity for stability rather than removing the effect. Also this session: INK_DOT_BOOST 2.1 -> 2.8 (asked for bigger a third time). SMEAR TRIM was tried and the user felt no difference at any setting - left at its default and NOT tuned; it is a real measured effect on the captured pressure data but evidently below the threshold of what this hand notices, so it should not be tuned further without a reason to. Pointer hiding was judged GOOD and is accepted. VERDICT (2026-08-10): live smoothing ON is accepted - 'very good right now'. The A/B was written the same sentence each way and the wriggle the first trial exposed is no longer what the hand notices; the tail-damping follow-up above is therefore NOT needed and should not be built on speculation. The two spot checks passed with it on: a half-page single stroke shows no seam where LIVE_SMOOTH_MAX_PTS splits head from tail, and a rectangle snapped mid-stroke keeps sharp corners while drawing continues, which is the _straight_mode exemption working. Default stays ON. This closes the gate on prediction (row 139), which was deferred behind it.

column2: A dot is round, and the same size however the digitiser sampled it
column5: Reported across four sessions as 'the dot on an i is too small', answered three times by raising INK_DOT_BOOST (1.0 -> 1.6 -> 2.1 -> 2.8) and never fixed, because the boost was the wrong knob every time. Settled by CAPTURING the user's own writing (SIDEMARK_CAPTURE_INK, 162 strokes incl. three rows of deliberate taps, kept in notes/) and measuring, which found TWO defects the multiplier could not touch. (1) SIZE DEPENDED ON A HARDWARE ACCIDENT. finish_ink_stroke has two paths - under three samples it returns early with taper=False, three or more goes through the pipeline WITH the taper. A dot is nothing but ENDPOINTS, and the taper multiplies each end by INK_TAPER_MIN (0.4) whatever its length, so capping the ramp's LENGTH via INK_TAPER_FRAC never saved it. Measured on 62 real dots: a two-sample tap painted 2.33 wide, a three-sample tap 0.96 - the SAME tap of the SAME pen, 2.4x apart, decided by nothing but how many samples the digitiser happened to emit. Raising the boost scaled both branches equally, so it could never fix the INCONSISTENCY, which is what actually reads as wrong. Fixed by making the taper skip any mark short enough to be a dot, so both paths use one test; cliff 2.42x -> 1.26x, ordinary ink unchanged at 0.97. (2) A DOT WAS PAINTED AS A TEARDROP, which is what the user finally photographed. The last raw sample of a tap reports pressure ~0 - that is the pen LEAVING THE GLASS, not the shape of the mark - so per-point widths drew one end at the pressure floor and the other at full boost: 2.47x apart at the median across 64 real taps, 2.86x at worst. On a mark of near-zero LENGTH, an outline with two different radii is not a lozenge but a crescent with a bite out of it, which renders as a pac-man. A DOT HAS NO DIRECTION, so it can have no width variation along it: the profile is flattened to its PEAK, the pressure the dot was actually made with. trim_light_tail cannot do this job - a tap under three samples returns before it runs, and trimming a two-sample mark leaves nothing to draw. Ends now differ by 1.00x. The rendered before/after is unambiguous and was the thing that ended the argument - measure, then LOOK. STILL OPEN, deliberately: marks between INK_DOT_LEN (5.0) and ~12 units get no boost at all, and some of those are dots that slid. INK_DOT_LEN is also the one length in the ink pipeline that is FIXED rather than scaled to the writing (cf. ink_feature_size). Not touched because an i-dot that slid cannot be told from a t-crossbar or a comma by geometry, and boosting all short marks would fatten those too - it needs a decision about what counts as a dot, not a constant. Also: INK_DOT_BOOST is at 2.8 partly because it was compensating for both defects above, so it should be RE-JUDGED downward now rather than assumed correct.

column2: Audit the test suite, and restructure CLAUDE.md using it as the instrument
column5: Raised by the user after a session where the suite's cost became the bottleneck: 905 tests, ~140 s, a warm laptop, and 'usually they never fail - not sure if they are specific enough'. Both halves are real and they are separate problems. COST, measured: the window tier is 299 of 905 tests (33%) and 87% of the runtime - ~410 ms each against ~30 ms for the rest. Partly addressed already by flipping run_tests.sh's default to the fast tier (the expensive one now needs --full), since a bare run is what anyone reaches for by reflex; and by writing down that CI runs the full suite on every push and PR, so the laptop rarely needs to. What is LEFT is the tier itself. conftest.py marks per CLASS - a test is 'window' if its class source mentions PDFEditorWindow/Adw.Application/PresenterWindow - so one sibling that builds a window drags every cheap test in the class into the slow tier. Measured: 26 window-tier tests have bodies of <=6 lines, including pure-logic ones (TestCallouts.test_callout_belongs_to_nearest_preceding_anchor, TestShareToPhone's IP checks). Splitting those classes is free speed with no risk. VALUE, the sharper half. The failure mode is not 'tests that check constants' but tests that assert WHAT THE CODE SAYS instead of WHAT THE USER GETS. Three specimens found in one pass, all the same mistake in different coats: (a) test_both_erasers_share_one_radius_policy asserted erase_radius(30) == 15.0 + 3.0 - restating the helper to itself, touching NEITHER canvas, so the row 116 regression it is named for would sail straight past. Rewritten to drive both erasers and compare what they DELETE, and verified to fail when one canvas is given its own formula. (b) an assertion echoing INK_DOT_BOOST, which can only fire when somebody changes it on purpose - a speed bump on intentional change, no net under an accidental one. (c) a point-count standing in as a proxy for 'the line was resampled', which broke on a correct change and would have missed a real one. Also near-unfalsifiable: TestShareToPhone's tailscale check passes trivially on any machine without Tailscale, and test_lan_ip_is_a_string would pass on a WRONG address. WORTH KEEPING AS COUNTER-EXAMPLES: test_focusing_the_sheet_does_not_scroll_it (a property half that always runs plus a gesture half that skipTests when the frame clock is dead, with the reasoning in the docstring so nobody 'fixes' the skip), and test_thumb_drag_export_notes_and_multipage, which bundles four behaviours into ONE window build - the opposite of the usual advice, correct here because the build is the cost. The pass to do: walk the window tier class by class asking 'what would this catch, and would it catch it?', split classes to free the cheap tests, and delete or rewrite what cannot fail. Expect it to shrink the tier and improve it at the same time. SECOND HALF OF THIS ROW: RESTRUCTURE CLAUDE.md, using the audit as the instrument. At 1077 lines / 12.1k words it is too big to act on, but the user's framing is the right one and better than 'trim it': the problem is STRUCTURE, not bloat. Split by WHEN A THING IS READ. 'Architecture in one minute' is 543 lines - half the file, and the title is now a joke - and it interleaves two kinds of content with opposite retrieval patterns: ARCHITECTURE is read once to orient (what exists, how it is shaped), PITFALLS are looked up just-in-time when you touch the thing they describe. Mixed, the just-in-time material is buried inside orientation prose and does not fire at the moment it is needed. THE EVIDENCE THIS SESSION, which is what the restructure should be built on: the FACTUAL content works and the PROCESS rules do not. 'One table, not two' visibly shaped the code written (live_ink_stroke landed as a shared helper with a _smoothing_now adapter BECAUSE of it); the ink-pipeline notes were used repeatedly. Meanwhile the test-cadence rule was in context from the first message and was broken repeatedly within the hour - not unread, but with no retrieval cue, competing continuously against the pull of wanting a result, at line 563 of 1077. What actually fixed that was flipping run_tests.sh's default: A TOOL CHANGE, NOT A SENTENCE. So the third category is process rules, which belong in TOOLING wherever they can be encoded and in prose only when they cannot. A fourth force: per-subsystem reasoning is increasingly DUPLICATED between CLAUDE.md and the code comments this project already favours (INK_DOT_BOOST's comment, width_profile's docstring and CLAUDE.md's ink section now overlap - made worse in this very session). Duplication drifts and the loser is whoever reads the stale copy. CLAUDE.md should carry the INVARIANT PLUS A POINTER ('the taper must not touch a dot - see width_profile'), not the argument. WHY DO IT DURING THE AUDIT (the user's idea, and a good one): the audit walks the codebase class by class, so it is a natural instrumented pass - note per area whether CLAUDE.md helped, was silent, or was STALE. That beats editing from an armchair, which is judging by reading, i.e. the exact method that mis-predicted both the crawl and the taper today. THE TRAP IN IT, which must be respected or the pass does damage: a test audit is a BIASED SAMPLE. It exercises the testing and per-subsystem-behaviour sections heavily and things like the PDF image layer or session proxying barely, so 'I never used this' means UNOBSERVED, not USELESS. Only sections the audit actively exercised earn a verdict; everything else is untouched by default. This is the same error as measuring a stroke's settled body, finding it still, and concluding the line was fine when the TAIL was what the hand was watching. And the restructure is a deliberate pass AFTER the notes are in, never live edits during the audit.

column2: The notes panel's empty slot stays open on a PDF with no sidecar
column5: Reported: opening a PDF that has no .md sidecar leaves a wide EMPTY strip on the right of the window -- the notes panel is not there (no editor, no 'Notes' header) but its space is. The intent is already in the code and already runs: _open_pdf does _set_notes_shown(self.notes_model.has_content()) and a PDF with no notes therefore starts collapsed. It is overwritten a moment later. TWO causes, and fixing either alone leaves the other's path broken. (1) _set_notes_shown() hides the WIDGET and never moves the DIVIDER: it does _notes_box.set_visible(shown) and then only on the shown branch sets a position. That is safe for a child of the paned, but _notes_box is NOT the paned's end child -- _sheet_box is (row 130 keeps the sheet in the notes' slot so the page can slide in and out), and _sheet_box is never hidden anywhere in the file. So the end child is always visible and always claims exactly what the position says, however empty it is. Contrast _on_notes_toggled's OFF branch, which animates the position out to w BEFORE hiding -- that is why the Ctrl+backslash toggle looks right and the automatic collapse does not. (2) _init_pane_position re-applies the default 62% split afterwards. It guards on _text_mode only, not on whether the notes are shown, and it wins on ordering: open_new_window calls win.present() and then win.open_file(path) SYNCHRONOUSLY, so the hide happens first and the realize-time idle fires after it and puts the divider back. Cause 2 is the fresh-window path; cause 1 alone is the open-into-an-existing-tab path (open_file_in_tab does not re-run _init_pane_position, so the divider simply stays wherever the PREVIOUS document left it -- a no-notes PDF opened after one with notes shows the same empty strip). Fix belongs in _set_notes_shown's hide path (collapse the divider to the full width, matching what the toggle already does) with _init_pane_position additionally asking whether the notes are visible rather than only whether we are in text mode. Trap for whoever writes it: _on_pane_position reads an extreme position as row 130's mode switch, so any programmatic collapse must go through _mark_pane_programmatic() -- the show path already does, and a hide path that forgets it will silently enter full-notes/sheet mode on every open. Second trap: do not 'fix' this by hiding _sheet_box, which would break the sheet slot. Regression test wants both paths: a window opened on a no-notes PDF, and a no-notes PDF opened as a second tab after one with notes; assert the paned POSITION (the model), not pixels -- a full run has no live frame clock. SHIPPED: _set_notes_shown's hide path now pushes the divider out (the show path already placed it), and _init_pane_position applies the default split only when the notes are actually visible -- otherwise it collapses at the REAL width, which is why the idle still has to act rather than just skip: _set_notes_shown runs before the window knows how wide it is and can only guess 1280. Tests: test_no_notes_leaves_no_empty_slot (fresh window, and the idle re-run on top) and test_a_second_tab_without_notes_closes_the_slot_too (the tab path, which never re-runs the idle); both checked to fail before. They read the paned POSITION, never the allocation. KNOCK-ON, worth knowing: entering the full-notes sheet from a PDF whose notes were collapsed now ANIMATES from the window edge instead of setting 0 directly, because _settle_pane_at only animates when the distance is >4px. test_the_page_side_stays_collapsed_after_realize asserted a literal 0 and was reading that animation rather than the idle it is about; it now asserts the idle did not MOVE the divider, which is what its docstring always claimed.

column2: Pen input arrives at half the rate of touch (30 Hz vs 137 Hz)
column5: MEASURED 2026-08-10 on 100 real strokes captured with the device label (see row 139 for the harness). THE PEN'S SAMPLES ARRIVE AT HALF THE RATE OF A FINGER'S, THROUGH THE SAME CODE PATH: median interval between samples was 33.4 ms for the stylus (~30 Hz, 44 strokes), 7.3 ms for touch (~137 Hz, 34 strokes) and 49.5 ms for a mouse (17 strokes), on a 60 Hz display. This is what the user reported by hand and could not have been guessed: 'with the finger I do not need [prediction] at all as this is very quick, only the pen has delay'. THE STRUCTURE OF THE NUMBERS IS THE FINDING. Expressed in display frames, the stylus arrives at 2.00 frames per sample and the mouse at 2.97, each within 0.03-0.04 of a WHOLE frame, while touch sits at 0.44 frames with a deviation of 0.35 - i.e. pointer motion is locked to the frame clock and touch is not. GTK delivers a stylus as the LOGICAL POINTER (the row 135 finding), so the pen is subject to pointer motion compression and a finger is not. TWO THINGS THIS RULES OUT. (1) Our pipeline is not the ceiling: touch pushes ~137 Hz through the same canvas, the same live smoothing and the same redraw, so nothing downstream caps us at 30 Hz. (2) Live smoothing costs nothing measurable - the deliberate with/without groups came out at 34.0 ms and 33.5 ms, so the feature accepted the same day is not paying for this. AND ONE THING IT ESTABLISHES: the pen is not a 30 Hz device. The fastest stylus strokes, all on an empty page early in the session, came in at 16.5-16.7 ms - exactly ONE frame - so the hardware can deliver 60 Hz and 30 Hz is not a hardware ceiling. WHAT IS STILL OPEN, and the capture cannot answer it: _now_ms is wall-clock at HANDLING time and pointer events are frame-locked, so this measures DELIVERY. Whether pen samples are being DISCARDED by motion compression, or the device simply reports ~30 Hz most of the time, needs the raw device: `sudo libinput debug-events --device /dev/input/eventN` while drawing (neither libinput nor evtest is installed here, and the user is not in the `input` group, so an agent cannot run it). A weak correlation with ink already on the page (34 -> 30 -> 27 -> 30 Hz across the session) is NOT strong enough to claim the redraw degrades with stroke count; re-measure before believing it. WHY THIS OUTRANKS PREDICTION, and closes row 139's loop: prediction is a workaround for a low sample rate. Graded per device on this same capture, it recovers 6.3% of the lag at 20 ms on the stylus but is catastrophically counterproductive on touch (-1255% at 20 ms, worse on 88% of samples) - because at 7 ms per sample there is almost no lag left to cancel and any guess is larger than the error it replaces. That is precisely why a finger needs no prediction. Doubling the pen's rate would help the felt lag, the denoiser (spacing/feature was 0.337 = UNDERSAMPLED for the pen against 0.08 for touch) and prediction all at once, and is worth more than any tuning of the three. ANSWERED, and it is OURS (2026-08-10, extras/device_rate.py reading the evdev node directly, 15 s of continuous drawing each). RAW HARDWARE RATE: stylus 7.51 ms median (133 Hz), p10 7.37 / p90 7.65 - a tight hardware clock, 1753 motion reports; touch 10.00 ms (100 Hz), p10 9.80 / p90 10.20. So the PEN IS THE FASTER DEVICE at the panel, and the story is the exact inverse of how it feels: touch reaches the canvas at close to its full rate while the pen arrives at 30 Hz, i.e. WE DISCARD ABOUT 78% OF THE PEN'S SAMPLES. The panel is not the limit and there is nothing to fix in the hardware. CAUSE: GTK compresses POINTER motion to one event per frame and a stylus is delivered as the logical pointer (row 135), while touch events are not compressed - which is exactly the frames-per-sample signature measured earlier (stylus 2.00 frames, mouse 2.97, touch 0.44). TWO SEPARATE LOSSES, and they must not be confused. (1) RESOLUTION: everything between the frames is thrown away, which is the whole of the undersampling that every ink constant has been tuned around - spacing/feature 0.337 for the pen against 0.08 for touch. Gdk.Event.get_history() exists precisely for this: it returns the GdkTimeCoord trail that was compressed away since the last delivered event, and it is available in this GTK (verified). Reading it recovers the full 133 Hz for the stroke geometry. (2) LATENCY: the newest sample is still only as fresh as the frame it arrived on, and the measured 33.4 ms is TWO frames, so the canvas is running at ~30 fps during a stroke, not 60. The fastest strokes in the capture - all early, on an empty page - hit 16.5 ms, one frame, which points at redraw cost growing with ink on the page. get_history does NOT fix this half: it improves the SHAPE, not the age of the tip. Do not sell one as the other. HALF ONE SHIPPED (2026-08-10): motion_history() reads Gdk.Event.get_history() in both drawing routers and walks the recovered trail into current_stroke BEFORE the event's own point, so a stroke is captured at the pen's rate instead of the frame's. TWO TRAPS, both silent if wrong. (1) GdkTimeCoord axes are in SURFACE coordinates while a GestureDrag reports WIDGET ones, so every recovered sample would land offset by the canvas's position in the window - a header bar's height too high. The offset is derived from the EVENT's own position, which is available in both spaces at once, rather than from widget geometry. A test caught this by having an unrealistic fake position, which is worth remembering: the fixture was wrong and the code was right, and the failure looked identical to the bug. (2) coord.time is the EVENT clock, an arbitrary 32-bit millisecond base, NOT GLib.get_monotonic_time() - mixing them makes prediction's velocity estimate explode. Only the difference from the current event is meaningful, so motion_history returns an AGE and _note_sample takes an age_ms; stamping a frame's worth of recovered samples as simultaneous would read as an infinite speed. Junk is dropped rather than drawn: a coord without the X/Y flags is not a position, and a wrapped 32-bit time would otherwise place a sample seconds in the past and drag the stroke to it (MOTION_HISTORY_MAX_AGE_MS). The whole thing is guarded like capture_raw_stroke - recovering extra samples is a bonus and failing to must never cost the user the stroke - which a mock-object event in an unrelated test proved was not theoretical. The press list is kept in LOCKSTEP with the points (a history sample with no pressure axis borrows the event's), because a length mismatch loses the taper for the whole stroke. INK_MAX_POINTS needed no change: it widens the resample SPACING rather than truncating, and the output count is a function of arc length, not of how many samples came in. STILL OPEN, and deliberately not sold as fixed by this: the newest sample is only as fresh as the frame it arrived on, and 33.4 ms is TWO frames, so the canvas renders at ~30 fps mid-stroke while an empty page manages 16.5 ms. That is the half the hand feels as lag, and it is a redraw-cost question. RE-MEASURE THE INK CONSTANTS AFTER THIS: every one of them was tuned against a 30 Hz capture of a 133 Hz pen, so the undersampling verdict (spacing/feature 0.337) and 'never strengthen the denoiser for small writing' were both conclusions about a sampling rate that no longer holds. CONFIRMED IN THE APP AND RE-MEASURED (2026-08-10, 23 fresh strokes). The canvas now sees 8.0 ms between stylus samples (125 Hz, range 7.6-8.8) against 33.4 ms before, and the raw sample spacing fell from 3.29 to 0.85 document units. User's verdict: 'wow, that made it way better'. THE RATIO THAT RETIRES A DOCUMENTED RULE: spacing/feature is now 0.091 - 'reasonable sampling' - against 0.337 (UNDERSAMPLED) before, and that is with a SMALLER hand (median feature 8.4 units against 14.2). So the conclusion recorded in row 139 and in CLAUDE.md, that small writing is an INFORMATION limit and the denoiser must never be strengthened for it, was a fact about the 30 Hz the canvas was RECEIVING and not about the pen. It is void; the method (measure the ratio, do not guess) is what survives. THE DENOISER IS NOW NEAR-INERT, measured rather than felt: across its whole range Taubin moves the committed ink 0.11% -> 0.16% of an x-height, against 0.44% -> 0.48% at 30 Hz, i.e. 0.0 and 1.0 now differ by 0.05% of an x-height. The user noticed this unprompted ('stroke smoothing does almost nothing because all is smooth already') and the numbers agree. WHY: the denoiser was never mainly removing tremor, it was cleaning up what INTERPOLATION invented between sparse samples, and there is little left to invent - the shaping is now done by resample_ink. Deliberately NOT changed as a result: no constant was retuned. The pipeline is in a good regime, an inert filter is harmless, and there is no measurement saying any change would improve anything. Do not widen the slider's range to make it 'do something'. PREDICTION RE-GRADED at the new rate: 13.5% recovery at 10 ms, 13.0% at 20, 3.5% at 40, still worse on 33-42% of samples. Better than the 0.1-4.4% it managed at 30 Hz but still not compelling, and it stays OFF by default. Its one remaining known defect is that PREDICT_SMOOTH is per-EVENT and so changes meaning with the report rate; fix that before judging it again. BUG FOUND BY THE USER'S SESSION LOG, fixed same day: gdk_event_get_history ASSERTS the event is MOTION_NOTIFY or SCROLL, and a finger drag delivers TOUCH_UPDATE - so every touch stroke printed a Gdk-CRITICAL per event. Nothing was lost (touch is not compressed, which is why a finger already arrived at full rate) but the console spam was real. motion_history now checks the event TYPE first. The test that was supposed to cover this passed for the WRONG REASON: its fake touch event had no get_history method at all, so the AttributeError guard caught it and the type check was never exercised. KEEP THE SMOOTHING SLIDER (user's call, 2026-08-10) even though it is now near-inert on this hardware: another panel may still be in the old sparse regime, where it is exactly the control that is needed. The future home is a separate/advanced settings page, not deletion. THE LATENCY HALF, MEASURED (2026-08-10). Every committed stroke is re-outlined and re-filled on EVERY frame - the page itself is cached as a surface and blitted, but the ink is not. Benchmarked on the user's own committed strokes (median 150 points after resampling): 0.164 ms per stroke, dead linear. 25 strokes 3.9 ms, 50 strokes 7.9, 100 strokes 16.4, 200 strokes 33.2, 400 strokes 67.9 - and that is stroke painting ALONE, before the page blit, images, lasso, anchors and the live pipeline. The 16.7 ms frame budget is gone at ~100 strokes. This matches the field data exactly: the session that measured 33.4 ms between samples saved 100 ink annotations, and the strokes that hit a full 60 Hz were all on an EMPTY page. So the felt lag is a redraw cost that grows with the notes on the page, which is also why it gets worse the longer a lecture goes on. NOT the live pipeline: measured at 2.0-2.5 ms per frame on a real stroke even now that motion_history feeds it ~4x the samples, and capped at 9.0 ms by LIVE_SMOOTH_MAX_PTS for an absurd 1800-sample stroke. THE FIX is to cache committed ink into its own surface beside _page_surface and blit it, so a frame costs O(1) plus the live stroke instead of O(strokes). Invalidation is the whole risk and it is the same list _page_surface already has, plus every ink mutation: add/erase/undo/redo/move/resize/recolour, page change, zoom (the surface is scale-dependent, hence _surface_scale). Compositing is safe - each stroke's alpha is baked into the layer, so overlapping translucent highlighter still double-darkens exactly as it does when painted one by one. SHIPPED (2026-08-10): committed ink is now a cached SURFACE beside _page_surface, blitted per frame. Measured on the user's own committed strokes: per-frame cost went from 4.1 / 16.4 / 65.6 ms at 25 / 100 / 400 strokes to a FLAT 1.42 / 1.50 / 1.78 ms - one blit plus a 0.03-0.39 ms fingerprint. TWO DESIGN DECISIONS WORTH KEEPING. (1) The cache is keyed on a FINGERPRINT of what would be painted, not on a list of invalidation call sites. There are a dozen ways a stroke changes here (draw, erase, undo, redo, move, resize, rotate, reshape, weld, recolour, grid re-space, paste) and a cache keyed on remembering all of them goes stale on the thirteenth - and a stale layer is the ONLY bug this design can have. The fingerprint samples INK_SIG_SAMPLES=5 points per stroke, which is what catches a control-point drag on an interior vertex; an endpoints-only signature misses exactly that. invalidate_ink() is the escape hatch. (2) An APPEND is detected as a prefix of the old signature and painted onto the existing layer. Found by measuring, not by reasoning: the first version repainted in full on every change, which is O(strokes) = 80 ms at 400 of them, arriving exactly when you LIFT THE PEN - i.e. it would have traded a steady lag for a hitch at the worst possible moment. Committing a stroke now costs 0.16 ms at 100 strokes and 0.55 ms at 400. Erase/undo/move/recolour/page/zoom still rebuild, correctly: a surface can only gain ink, not lose it. NOT DONE: the text sheet still repaints per frame - its ink is on an overlay with a different substrate, so this does not transfer for free. USER REPORT that this does NOT explain, and it is the honest limit of the whole thread: there is still delay on the FIRST line, on an empty page where the stroke cost is zero. That is the structural pipeline and mostly not ours - up to 7.5 ms waiting for the next pen report, up to 16.7 ms of frame quantisation, one to two frames of compositor latency, plus panel response, i.e. 30-60 ms end to end before Sidemark does anything wrong. The old capture confirms the app itself is already at the frame limit on an empty page (16.5 ms per sample = 60 fps). THE ONE SOFTWARE LEVER LEFT FOR IT IS PREDICTION, which makes this the moment its known defect is worth fixing: PREDICT_SMOOTH is an EMA weight per EVENT, so its time constant changes with the report rate - at 30 Hz it was ~100 ms, five times the lead it was smoothing. It should be a time constant in ms applied per elapsed dt. Fix that, re-grade with ink_replay --predict, and only then judge it in the hand. USER'S IDEA, built the same day: extras/latency_probe.py measures the end-to-end lag by chasing a moving dot. A dot sweeps at a known speed, the user keeps the pen TIP on it, and the time offset that best aligns the dot curve with the reported pen curve is the lag. The sweep is a SINE and not a triangle: a triangle's velocity flips instantly at each end, which no hand can follow, and the tracking error there would swamp the lag. WHAT IT HONESTLY MEASURES: the WHOLE loop - pen, app, compositor, panel, eye, hand, pen - and it cannot separate the display half from the input half. The user's own tracking is inside the number, and because a predictable sweep is one people ANTICIPATE, the result is closer to a lower bound on the machine than an upper one.
