So the number to trust is a DIFFERENCE: run it twice changing one thing (prediction on/off, a compositor setting, another machine) and the human term is roughly constant, so the delta is real even when the absolute is soft. It reports the fit RESIDUAL beside the lag for exactly this reason - a hand that was not really tracking must be visible as a bad fit rather than as a confident wrong number, and --selftest checks both halves against known lags without hardware (a wrong fit looks exactly like a fast machine). Deliberately imports nothing from sidemark, so it measures the platform and can be pointed at another toolkit or machine for comparison. INK LAYER VERIFIED IN THE APP (2026-08-10, the user's hand): erase, undo/redo, lasso-move with no ghost left behind, zoom in/out staying sharp and in register, page turn, and drawing on a page that already carries a lot of ink. The fingerprint-keyed cache holds. LATENCY PROBE, first run, and the bug it exposed in ITSELF: it exited immediately with '1 dot frames'. A UNIT MISMATCH - _now() returns MILLISECONDS (which is what the fit works in) while --seconds and --period arrive in SECONDS, so the run-length test fired on the second frame and closed the window after 4 ms. Worth recording for two reasons. First, the symptom reads as BROKEN HARDWARE rather than as a bug in the measuring tool, which is the failure mode every diagnostic has and the reason --selftest exists (it passed throughout - it exercises the fit, not the window). Second, it was found by REPRODUCING it under the headless weston the test suite already runs, not by reading the code: two plausible wrong guesses (the tick callback's argument count, an exception swallowed by GTK) were both eliminated in a minute by running them. The fix names the units in the fields themselves (_run_ms, _period_ms) so the two cannot be mixed again. Also fixed while there: the probe now reads get_history() too, or it would sample the pen once per FRAME and report the frame rate as the pen rate - the exact confusion this whole row is about - and it uses ONE controller, since a GestureDrag beside the motion one puts every sample into the fit twice. FIRST REAL RUN, and the user's correction to the METHOD (2026-08-10). The run fitted 93 ms with residual 0.263 - correctly self-rejected as a poor fit, which is the guard earning its place on the first try. The user's diagnosis was right and better than the design: a back-and-forth SWEEP changes speed through every cycle, fastest at the centre and stopping dead at each end, and a reversal is the hardest thing there is to track - so the hand's error peaks exactly where the measurement lives. Default path is now a CIRCLE at constant angular speed: no reversals, one speed, so the hand settles in and its error becomes a steady phase offset, which is precisely what the fit reads. The fit is now 2D (error is the distance, so both axes constrain the lag at once; a line degenerates to the axis that moves), the default period slowed from 1.6 s to 3.0 s and the amplitude from 380 to 260 px, and a faint GUIDE RING is drawn under the dot - you cannot anticipate a path you cannot see, and anticipation is exactly what keeps the human term out of the number. --path line keeps the old sweep. The report also prints the dot's speed in px/s and px per 10 ms, without which a lag in milliseconds is unreadable. SEPARATE FINDING FROM THE SAME RUN, worth chasing: the probe's own frame interval was 22.5 ms, ~44 fps, in a window drawing ONE DOT on a 60 Hz panel. That is not Sidemark - it is a trivial GTK4 window - so something in the compositor/renderer path is not presenting at the panel's rate, and it is 22.5 ms of the latency budget rather than the 16.7 assumed everywhere above. Worth re-running the probe against GSK_RENDERER variants and with Hyprland's tearing/direct-scanout options before concluding anything about prediction. MEASURED END TO END, AND MY OWN ESTIMATE WAS WRONG (2026-08-10). I had put the machine at 40-60 ms. Two independent methods agree it is about 110 ms. (1) The probe fitted 125 ms with residual 0.069, and the user reports staying ON the ball, so the human tracking term was near zero and the number is almost entirely machine. (2) THE USER'S OBSERVATION, which is the isolation the probe could not provide: the MOUSE CURSOR following the pen sits ~1 cm behind the nib, and behind the ball, with the same delay felt in Sidemark. At 64 px/cm (1920 px across a ~30 cm panel) and 569 px/s that is 64/569 = 112 ms. The two agree. WHY THE CURSOR OBSERVATION SETTLES OWNERSHIP: the cursor is drawn by HYPRLAND, not by Sidemark and not by GTK. If it lags the nib by as much as the ink does, the bulk of the latency is below the application and no work in Sidemark can recover it. It also suggests a SOFTWARE cursor - a hardware cursor plane updates at input rate and would not lag like this - so cursor:no_hardware_cursors is the first Hyprland setting to check. 110 ms is far more than a composited path should cost (a frame is 16.7 ms), so something there is buffering several frames deep. GSK RENDERER IS A FREE WIN, measured: the DEFAULT (Vulkan) ran the probe's window at 24.4 ms per frame (41 fps) drawing ONE DOT on a 60 Hz panel, while GSK_RENDERER=gl gave 16.9 ms (59 fps) and =cairo 16.7 ms (60 fps). End-to-end lag fell from 125 ms to 107/105. That is ~8 ms per frame the default renderer is losing on this hardware, and it applies to Sidemark for free - same toolkit, same compositor. NB `ngl` is a RENAMED value (it is `gl` now) and silently falls back, so a test using it is not testing what it says. CALIBRATION OF THE PROBE ITSELF, via --inject-lag: 0 ms -> 125, 100 ms -> 200, so a 100 ms injection moved the fit by 75. Deltas are real and directional but UNDER-REPORT by roughly 25%, and the mechanism is the hand: shown a visibly larger delay the user anticipates harder, and their own lag shrinks to absorb part of the injection. So the renderer's true benefit is likely nearer 25 ms than the 20 measured, and any future delta from this tool should be read as a floor. The capture now also counts motion EVENTS per stroke, so ink_replay reports the canvas's FRAME rate beside the pen's report rate. Samples arrive per pen report and events arrive per frame, so the two together say which of the two a stroke was limited by - and that is the measurement that settles a renderer or compositor A/B, which by feel is ambiguous (the user's verdict on GSK_RENDERER=gl in the app was 'feels similar, maybe a tiny bit faster', which on a ~20 ms change out of ~110 is exactly what a real but small improvement feels like and is not something to hardcode a renderer on). WHERE THE LATENCY LIVES, SETTLED (2026-08-10): UPSTREAM OF THE COMPOSITOR. Forcing a HARDWARE cursor plane (cursor:no_hardware_cursors 0, so the cursor is not composited at all) left the ~1 cm gap to the nib unchanged, and forcing SOFTWARE cursors (1) made no difference either. So the ~110 ms is spent before anything is drawn - the Goodix digitiser's own processing, libinput, and panel response - and neither Sidemark nor Hyprland can recover it. Note the option is a NEGATIVE (0 = use hardware cursors = fast, 1 = no hardware cursors = software, 2 = auto), which is easy to test backwards; the user's first run was at 1. PREDICTION CANNOT BRIDGE IT, and this closes the question rather than deferring it again. Re-graded on 133 Hz ink with the damping bug fixed: recovery of the lag error is 11% at a 10 ms lead, 10% at 20, 1% at 40, -11% at 60 and -29% at 80, and it makes matters worse on 33% of samples at 10 ms rising to 63% at 80. The lag needing masking is 110 ms, where a guess is far worse than none. THE REASON IS INFORMATION, NOT MODELLING: a pen stroke changes direction on a ~100 ms timescale and a letter takes 200-400 ms, so predicting 110 ms ahead is guessing the second half of a letter that has not been written - kinematics cannot know whether a curve is closing an 'o' or leaving into an 'l'. A Kalman, constant-acceleration or learned predictor fits more parameters to a future that is not in the data and hits the same wall. Prediction's realistic ceiling here is masking ~20 ms of 110, at the cost of overshoot at every cusp. Decision: keep it off, keep the bug fix, build nothing further. THE BUG FIX, which was worth making regardless: PREDICT_SMOOTH was an EMA weight applied PER EVENT, so its meaning drifted with the report rate - a ~92 ms time constant when the canvas saw 30 Hz, five times the lead it was damping, which is most of why prediction measured as useless. It is now PREDICT_SMOOTH_MS, a real time constant applied over elapsed dt, meaning the same thing at any rate; ink_replay applies the identical damping so it grades the filter the app actually runs. CHOOSING ITS VALUE EXPOSED A TRADE-OFF NO METRIC CAN SETTLE: swept at a 20 ms lead on real ink, recovery falls monotonically with damping - 41% undamped, 31% at 10 ms, 25% at 15, 19% at 20, 10% at 30 - so ACCURACY alone says use none. Damping exists for STABILITY, which no error metric measures, and was added because the tip visibly jittered - a complaint from the 30 Hz era, when consecutive guesses disagreed wildly. At 133 Hz they agree far better, so less is needed. Set to 15 ms with the sweep recorded in the comment; re-judge in the hand before moving it.

column2: A second finger must stop the first from drawing, until every finger lifts
column5: Reported: two-finger panning sometimes leaves a POINT of ink behind, and the user's read was that the finger which was on the glass longer keeps drawing. Confirmed as far as static analysis goes; the exact GTK sequence hand-off needs the panel (no touch injection on this machine). PRECONDITION, and why this is not the shipped behaviour: the user's settings.json binds finger -> pen (a touch-only drawing setup). With the shipped default finger -> pan a stray touch cannot draw at all -- that IS row 135's palm rejection -- so this bug only exists for a table that has moved the pen onto the finger, and any fix must keep working for that table rather than leaning on the default. TWO holes, one certain and one likely. CERTAIN -- TextPageView has NO pinch protection at all. Its GestureZoom connects only 'begin' and 'scale-changed'; there is no 'end', no 'cancel', and its _on_sheet_pinch_begin does not discard the stroke the first finger has already started. PDFCanvas connects all four and does discard (_on_pinch_begin clears current_stroke and sets _ignoring). So on a text sheet -- and on a PDF shown as one sheet, row 130 -- the first finger's stroke lives through the whole two-finger gesture and commits on lift. That is a dot. The sheet's router also CLAIMS the sequence for a drawing tool before the pinch is recognised, which is a second reason not to rely on the pinch gesture firing at all. LIKELY -- on PDFCanvas the guard is one-shot and the next press tears it down. _on_drag_begin's FIRST statement is self._post_pinch = False, and _drag_end consumes _post_pinch at the first lift. So 'the finger left over from a pinch pans until it lifts' holds for exactly one finger and exactly as long as no new drag-begin arrives. GtkGestureDrag is single-point, so the second finger is never its sequence; if GTK hands the drag to the surviving sequence when the first lifts, that begin routes straight through the table to `pen` and the remaining finger draws. This matches the report's shape and is the piece to verify on hardware. WANTED (the user's call): once two fingers have been down, EVERY touch pans and never draws until all fingers are up. Implement as a latch on the touch SEQUENCE COUNT shared by both surfaces, not as more pinch begin/end bookkeeping: the count is true whether or not GestureZoom recognises, whether or not a router claimed the first sequence, and whichever finger lifts first. Clear it only at zero touches, and do not let a drag-begin clear it (that is precisely today's bug). The first finger's in-flight stroke must be discarded on the second touchdown on BOTH surfaces -- the sheet does not do this today. Testable headless by feeding the latch synthetic sequence begin/end pairs; the gesture itself is not. SHIPPED: TouchLatch + attach_touch_latch, one shared helper, on both surfaces. It counts live touch SEQUENCES off a capture-phase legacy controller (track_barrel's reason: the gestures below take a sequence for themselves, so the raw stream is the only honest count) and latches `multi` from the second touchdown until the LAST lift -- not until the pinch ends, which is while a finger is still down and is exactly when the survivor used to draw. Both press routers return early while multi is set, and _on_drag_begin no longer clears _post_pinch when a finger is still on the glass. The latch also fires _on_second_finger, which abandons the in-flight stroke -- the PDF canvas did that from the pinch gesture already, the sheet did not do it at all, and now both do it from the touch stream so it happens even when GestureZoom is starved (row 150). Tests are in TestPinchZoom, fast tier, driven with synthetic sequence begin/end pairs; the surviving-finger one carries a positive control (the same press reaches `pen` once every finger is up) so it cannot pass against a finger that never draws. NOT verified on hardware: whether GTK actually re-begins the drag for the survivor is what made this 'likely' rather than 'certain', and the fix is correct either way -- but if a dot still appears, that assumption is where to look first. 2026-08-11, REOPENED AND REALLY FIXED. Shipped dead, and the traceback the user pasted is the whole story: PyGObject hands EventControllerLegacy a NULL event for some events (the trap already recorded for the pane drag), TouchLatch.handle dereferenced it, and an exception in a signal handler is silent apart from a traceback -- so the latch stopped counting fingers and every guard built on it quietly did nothing. Guarded, and the controller's own get_current_event() is the second chance at the same event. SECOND cause, ordering: capture-phase controllers of ONE widget run in the order they were ADDED, and a gesture that claims a sequence returns STOP, so the sheet's latch -- attached after the press router -- could never see the touches the router had taken. It is now the FIRST controller on the sheet. Lesson for anything built on a raw event stream: it can be perfectly correct, unit-tested, and never once run.

column2: A stroke drawn on a text page is truncated to whole pixels when it is stored
column5: Reported: on a text page the line is smooth while the pen is down and goes 'low res' the moment it is released; on a PDF page it does not. The user's guess -- that it is how the sheet STORES strokes -- is exactly right, and it is one line. _commit_stroke does buf_pts = [self._overlay_to_buffer(x, y) for x, y in pts_overlay], the INT helper, whose own docstring says 'rounded to whole pixels. Fine for hit-testing; use _overlay_to_buffer_f to STORE geometry'. This is the trap CLAUDE.md already records ('geometry you STORE must not go through the int-truncating coord helpers'), in the one place that was missed: the initial commit of a freehand stroke. Every RE-anchor path -- move, rotate, resize, the lasso loop -- already goes through the float helper via _anchor_stroke_at, whose comment is literally 'truncating each point to a whole pixel is what made a rotated stroke go lumpy'. Only birth was wrong. WHY IT READS AS 'low res on release' and not as a small offset: the truncation is INDEPENDENT per point, so it is uncorrelated +-1 px noise -- precisely the high-frequency content taubin_smooth has just removed, re-injected AFTER the denoiser, where nothing can take it out again. Measured on an arc at the small-writing sample density from row 139: max deviation 1.41 px, rms 0.91 px, and max per-segment ANGLE error 142 degrees. The angle is the visible part -- resample_ink walks at a spacing that scales with the writing, so writing small puts consecutive samples 1-2 px apart, and a 1 px lattice then makes neighbours collide or zigzag. The curve becomes a staircase, and it is worst exactly where row 139 says there is no redundancy left to spend. It PERSISTS: pts are stored as (bx - r.x), int minus int, so the sidecar holds integers and a reload cannot recover the fraction. Ink already committed is degraded for good. The PDF canvas is unaffected because it stores PDF-space floats via _screen_to_pdf -- no integer lattice anywhere on that path. That asymmetry is the whole bug report. FIX: _commit_stroke should call _anchor_stroke_at(pts_overlay), which already returns exactly the (mark, pts) pair it currently builds by hand and does the int() only for the get_iter_at_location lookup, where ints are the API. That removes the duplication rather than adding a guard. DELIBERATELY LEFT: two other callers of the int helper store geometry but harmlessly, because they shift a whole object by at most 1 px with its internal geometry intact -- the image paste and the multi-object paste origin. Do not 'fix' them reflexively; the rule is about geometry that is truncated PER POINT. Test: commit a stroke on a sheet from float overlay points and assert the stored pts are not all integers -- or better, that the stored polyline's per-segment angles match the input's within a tolerance. Do not assert exact coordinates (that pins the anchor arithmetic, not the precision). SHIPPED: _commit_stroke now anchors through _anchor_stroke_at, which is where the float conversion already lived -- the fix is a deletion, not a guard. Test: test_a_stored_stroke_keeps_the_shape_it_was_drawn_with, checked to FAIL on the old code (per-segment angles off by more than 5 degrees) and pass on the new. Ink already in a sidecar stays degraded; the fraction was never written.

column2: Two-finger zoom on a text page is starved by the press router, and selects text instead
column5: Reported: on a text page two-finger zoom SOMETIMES does nothing and the first finger selects text instead. Same root as row 148 seen from the other side, and the two should be fixed together. The sheet's router (_on_press_begin) is capture-phase on the Overlay and resolves EVERY press through the binding table with no idea that a touch may be one of two. It then does one of two things, and NEITHER leaves the sequence available to GestureZoom: it CLAIMS (a drawing tool -- with this user's finger -> pen, the common case) so the router owns sequence A and the zoom, which needs two sequences, only ever gets B; or it DENIES (finger unbound, or resolved as `text`), and the TextView's own selection drag takes sequence A instead -- same starvation, plus the visible symptom, which is text being selected. GestureZoom never reaches two points, so it never begins, so nothing zooms. PDFCanvas is reliable here for a reason that is pure luck: its _on_drag_begin never calls set_state at all, so both sequences stay available and the pinch recognises normally. The sheet cannot simply copy that -- it claims on purpose, because the TextView below it would otherwise take the press (see the reachability notes in CLAUDE.md). That asymmetry IS the bug. The 'sometimes' is the timing: it works when the second finger lands before the router has resolved the first, or when the first lands somewhere the router does not claim. This is why the fix for row 148 belongs in the same place. A latch on the live touch-sequence COUNT serves both: while more than one touch is down the hand belongs to the pinch -- nothing draws (148) and nothing is claimed or denied as a tool press (this row). The hard part, and what to design deliberately rather than discover: the router cannot wait to see whether a second finger is coming without adding latency to every single-finger stroke, and a sequence already denied to the zoom is probably not re-acquirable retroactively. Two candidate shapes, neither validated: claim the first touch as now but ABANDON it (discard the stroke, release the claim) the instant a second sequence begins, and see whether GestureZoom still recognises from that point; or treat a TOUCH press differently from a pointer press in the router, deferring only the claim (not the tool resolution) until the stroke has moved far enough that it cannot be the start of a pinch. Measure which one the panel actually supports before writing either -- this is a GTK sequence-state question, not a Sidemark one, and it needs the hardware. Note the sheet's pinch is CAPTURE phase where the PDF canvas' is BUBBLE; worth re-checking that too when this is touched, though the starvation above is the story. PARTIALLY ADDRESSED with row 148's latch, and the design question is now SHARPER rather than answered. What shipped: a second finger no longer draws, and the survivor's fresh press is CLAIMED and dropped instead of routed. What did NOT ship: the zoom still cannot recognise, because the router still holds the first sequence. REJECTED, after working through it: releasing the claim (set_state DENIED on multi). It is the obvious move and it is wrong -- the claim is what keeps the TextView off the press, so releasing it hands the caret a click in the middle of a pinch, which IS this row's reported symptom. Do not try it first. The promising shape instead: the latch already sees every touch event with coordinates, so the SHEET can drive the zoom itself from those positions -- centroid and spread, the arithmetic _on_sheet_pinch_scale already contains -- and never depend on GestureZoom getting a sequence it cannot have. That is a real piece of work and it was deliberately not done blind: it needs the panel to confirm the touch stream carries what it needs and to judge the feel. The PDF canvas needs none of this and must stay as it is: its router never claims, so its GestureZoom is never starved. 2026-08-11, DONE, along the candidate route (drive the zoom from the latch's own touch positions); the rejection held -- releasing the router's claim is still not the fix. TouchLatch now keeps each live finger's POSITION (surface coords) beside the count, and the sheet computes centroid + spread itself: _on_touch_multi records base zoom, base scroll and the start centroid, _on_touch_move applies spread/spread0 through _apply_pinch. That arithmetic is shared with the touchpad path -- GestureZoom stays, because a touchpad pinch carries no touch sequences at all and the latch can never see it; the gesture stands down while the latch holds real fingers, so there is one pinch and two ways in, not two pinches. Surface->widget conversion takes the origin ONCE per gesture (_surface_origin), never per point: only the centroid needs widget coords, and the scale ratio is translation-invariant. Parity extra: the survivor of a lift keeps PANNING until it lifts too, which is the PDF canvas' _post_pinch. STILL OPEN, deferred by the user: the TextView's own touch text-selection popup can still appear under a pinch, because with the finger unbound (or bound to `text`) the router DENIES and the TextView takes the sequence before any second finger exists. The user's idea is to let that selection UI belong to the finger only when the finger's tool IS the caret. FIRST VERSION IN THE HAND, 2026-08-11: it zoomed, and everything else about it was wrong -- 'jumps a lot, zooms to the top left, still marks text'. Four causes, and the theme is that a SHEET IS A REFLOW, not a scale factor like the PDF canvas. (1) It ran once per touch EVENT: a zoom here is a font change and a full relayout, and the panel reports several times faster than that, so events piled up and each queued its own deferred correction. It is now one tick callback, once per frame, reading wherever the fingers are then. (2) The 'top left' was GtkAdjustment CLAMPING: a scroll value set during a zoom-in is clamped against the extent of the layout that exists, and the relayout is async, so every frame's target was truncated. The driver now keeps its own float scroll and re-applies it at the top of the next frame, when the extent is real. The PDF canvas never meets this -- its offsets are plain floats with no clamp and no layout. (3) Base-relative arithmetic amplified both of the above; it is incremental now, each frame measured against the last, so a short step cannot drag the gesture off. A lift re-bases (_touch_anchor is the centroid or the one finger left) instead of continuing against a spread the hand no longer has. (4) 'Still marks text' was the second finger: a GtkGestureDrag is single-point and IGNORES a second sequence, which is not the same as denying it, so it sailed past the router into the TextView. The latch now swallows the second and further fingers (consume_extra) -- never the first, whose release the router's drag still needs. Also learned, and it is the general lesson: abandoning the stroke at the second TOUCHDOWN is not enough, because GTK can cancel the first finger's drag when another controller takes the sequence and that fires drag-end with the pen in hand, committing the mark drawn before the pinch. The guard belongs at the COMMIT as well (_press_end): the hand decides, not the gesture that noticed. AND the abandon has to reach ink the finger ALREADY COMMITTED. Reported on the sheet after the four fixes above: the mark made before the second finger landed was still there. Abandoning the LIVE stroke only helps while it is still live, and GTK can end that drag early -- another controller taking the sequence cancels it -- so by the time the second finger lands the stroke is committed and there is nothing left to abandon. _commit_stroke now REMEMBERS a stroke drawn by a finger while a finger is still down (_touch_strokes), and _on_second_finger takes it back off the page together with its ('add', ...) undo op -- an undo entry left behind would restore a stroke the user watched vanish. Three things keep that from eating real ink: it is armed by _capture_device == 'touch', never by the touch count, so a palm resting during a PEN stroke arms nothing; the record is cleared when the glass empties (the latch's on_end now fires for a one-finger hand too -- it means 'the glass is empty', not 'the pinch is over'); and it is cleared again at any fresh press with at most one finger down. So the ink is revocable only for the hand that drew it. PDF-only asymmetry, deliberate: the canvas already behaved, because its pinch gesture is not starved and the abandon lands while the stroke is still live.

column2: A finger left over from a two-finger gesture on a text sheet should keep panning
column5: Deferred, LOW priority, and only worth doing if it starts to feel wrong in the hand. When a two-finger gesture on a text sheet loses one finger, the SURVIVOR should go on panning until it lifts too -- the hand is still on the glass and still driving, so the gesture should degrade to a one-finger pan rather than end. Today the pinch ends when the count drops below two: the survivor arrives at the router as a brand-new press (GtkGestureDrag is single-point, so the second sequence is not a continuation of the first) and is routed through the binding table like any other press -- with finger:pen that is a fresh stroke, which row 148's guard then correctly refuses to commit while the hand is still down. So the piece that is missing is not the lift handling (TouchLatch already re-bases on the finger that is left, which is what makes a lift change only HOW MANY fingers make the gesture) but a decision that a survivor whose hand began a pinch keeps panning instead of being re-resolved against the table. The natural shape: while _post_pinch holds -- it must not be cleared while a finger is still down -- treat the survivor's press as a pan whatever the table says, and stop at the last lift. That is a deliberate exception AT the router, so it belongs beside the two that are already there (Shift+lasso adds, a live selection is grabbable with any tool) rather than as a fork of the table. Verified 2026-08-11: everything else in the row 150 pinch is accepted in the hand -- zoom is smooth, the fingers look stationary, the sheet does not throw to the top-left and the second finger no longer marks text. This is the one piece that was never built. PDF pages are unaffected: a finger there pans already, so there is nothing to degrade to.

column2: Name a bookmark as you make it, and confirm removing one
column5: Reported together with the outline and search work, then refined the same day: ENTER is what creates the bookmark, Escape creates nothing (the user's call -- 'that feels more natural'). Three changes to the row 134 bookmark, all about the moment one is created or destroyed. (1) Adding opens a name field with the derived label already in it and SELECTED, so the first keystroke replaces it and Enter alone keeps the suggestion -- a bookmark you have to go and rename afterwards is one you name never, and the field is never an empty box you have to think of something for. The field IS the add: nothing touches the model until Enter, so a cancelled add leaves the page unmarked and does not even make the file dirty, and there is no create-then-undo to get wrong. (The first version stored the mark on the click and let the popup edit it, which kept Ctrl+B a strict one-key verb; it was rejected in the hand.) Committing the suggestion UNCHANGED stores no name, so the label goes on being derived (row 134's rule) instead of freezing today's first note line into the file. Two consequences worth keeping: the header toggle flips itself on the click that opens the field, so cancelling has to put it back (the popover's closed handler), and if no chrome is on screen to anchor the popover to, the bookmark is created unnamed rather than silently not at all. (2) Removing asks first, through one confirmation that every path routes into (_drop_bookmark; _do_drop_bookmark is the confirmed action) -- deliberately with NO 'don't ask again', unlike the page-drop dialog: the guard exists because the name is stored nowhere else and an opt-out is one stray click from removing it for good. A cancel must re-sync the header toggle for the same reason as above. (3) A popover, not a modal, for _begin_rename's reason -- a one-word edit -- and anchored to whichever chrome is on screen, because the header button collapses into the menu on a narrow window and a popover parented to an unmapped widget never appears at all. FOLLOW-UP 2026-08-11, from use: clicking the bookmark button again must NOT offer to delete -- it opens the list scrolled to that page with the name selected, because a stray click on a toggle should not put a confirmation dialog in front of you. Removing lives where it reads as destructive (the list's cross, the outline row's menu), and both still ask. In the outline a DOUBLE-CLICK renames: F2 works too, but only once the list has keyboard focus, and a single click activates the row and takes focus with it -- so by hand the key alone meant click, click again, then F2. Two GTK criticals fixed with it, both of the same family: unparent() inside a popover's own `closed` handler re-enters (unparent can emit closed), so every on-the-fly popover now tears down through _drop_popover, which unparents once; and a rename's focus-leave is delivered AFTER the fact, so a list rebuilt in the meantime left finish() removing a child from a box that no longer owned it. Both print gtk_widget_get_parent: assertion 'GTK_IS_WIDGET (widget)' failed and neither is fatal, which is why they shipped. THIRD critical, reported and this time REPRODUCED (rename via double-click in the outline, then click away): the focus-leave commit was tearing the entry out of its row and rebuilding the list INSIDE GTK's focus change -- i.e. destroying the very widget focus was leaving. GTK then goes on walking a widget with no parent and asserts once per iteration for ever: measured at 3.5 million lines and a killed process, not the handful that scrolls past. The leave now defers to an idle; Enter and Escape are not inside a focus change and stay immediate, and the edit's token makes whichever arrives second a no-op. Note the first attempt deferred the COMMIT rather than the teardown and changed nothing -- the flood starts at the moment focus moves, which is what says the teardown is the culprit. A test pins the deferral (the edit must still be standing when the handler returns) and was checked to fail against the unfixed code; the criticals themselves are invisible to the suite, which is why all three of these shipped.

column2: Bookmarks appear in the outline, and can stand in for one
column5: Your bookmarks are outline entries too, shown with a star, and they ALONE are enough to make the outline worth offering: a lecture deck almost never carries a TOC, and it is exactly the document you bookmark your way around (the user's call). So the Outline/Pages switch now appears when the document has a TOC OR bookmarks, and a 'Bookmarks' tick-box appears beside it -- only when there are some, since a filter for a kind of row the document contains none of promises something that is not there. Persisted app-wide as outline_bookmarks, like show_comments: it is a preference about how you read, not a fact about one file. THE TRAP, and why the merge is not a sort: bookmarks are merged INTO the outline's own order (each one emitted before the first entry that starts after its page), never sorted with it. chapter_no -- the drag index into chapter_spans -- counts entries in TOC order, so re-sorting the whole list by page looks identical on a well-formed outline and silently hands a chapter drag the wrong span on one whose entries are not in page order. A bookmark on the same page as an outline entry follows it: the entry names the page, the bookmark names your place in it. The star is the whole signal that the text is YOURS -- an indistinguishable row would have the outline claiming a title the PDF never contained. POSITION MARKER, revised 2026-08-11 after use: the first version marked the containing entry at half strength, and in the hand that was too little to find while presenting -- you are usually BETWEEN entries, so the mark you see most is the weak one. Now a rule carrying the page number is inserted BETWEEN the two entries the page falls between, and only an exact page match still highlights a row (solid bar, bold title). The containing entry keeps a faint tint, which is what says which section the gap belongs to; two strong marks would compete. The line counts EVERY row -- chapters, sub-entries and bookmarks alike -- since 'the entry above me' is whatever is actually above me in the list, and ignoring the star rows would point at a chapter several screens up. It is inserted and removed rather than moved, so a second stale line cannot exist, and it is neither selectable nor activatable because a row you could click would be a destination that does not exist. Every walker of the outline rows has to skip it (getattr _here_marker), which is the one cost of putting chrome in the list itself rather than drawing it.

column2: Search a large PDF without blocking every keystroke
column5: Reported as: typing in Ctrl+F lags on a large PDF while it scans for results I have not finished asking for. The old _on_search_changed scanned EVERY page synchronously before returning, so on a 400-page file that is most of a second of dropped input per character -- and all of it thrown away by the next keystroke. Now the first match is found synchronously within a 25 ms budget and jumped to, and the remaining pages are scanned in 8 ms idle slices, so the count climbs while you carry on typing. Pages are scanned from where you ARE, forwards, then wrapping, so the first hit found is the one you would have gone to anyway and the background half is filling in what is behind you. Details that are load-bearing: the flat match list is ordered by PAGE and rebuilt as hits arrive, never in the order the scan found them, and the current match is re-found by IDENTITY so a hit landing ahead of it renumbers the label without moving you; the label carries a trailing ellipsis while the scan is incomplete and 'not found' is not flagged until it finishes, or every long document flashes red at a term that is in it; stepping off the end of a PARTIAL result set finishes the scan first, since wrapping to match 1 with pages unread would silently skip everything between here and the end; a tail of <=8 pages is finished on the spot rather than deferred, which keeps an ordinary document's count final the moment you stop typing. The idle callback reads its state through the ACTIVE-session proxies, so it parks itself when its tab goes to the back and _activate_session starts it again -- otherwise a background tab's scan writes its hits into the front document's table.

column2: Ctrl+F re-selects the term instead of clearing it
column5: Ctrl+F on a bar that already holds a term now SELECTS it rather than clearing it, and the term survives closing the bar. Typing replaces it (what you want most of the time) and Enter searches it again (what you want the rest of the time); clearing can only be undone by retyping. Two things this needs. grab_focus selects only when focus ARRIVES, so pressing Ctrl+F with the caret already in the entry did nothing at all -- the explicit select_region is there for exactly that case. And _hide_search keeps the text while dropping the results, so Enter on a reopened bar has a term but no matches: _step_search re-runs the search instead of stepping through nothing, which is what makes Enter 'search this again' rather than a dead key.

column2: The page counter and bookmark toggle follow a tab switch
column5: Reported: switching tabs does not update the page counter -- it still reads the page count of the document you left until you turn a page -- with the right question attached, which was whether the update is triggered everywhere it should be. The page counter and the bookmark toggle belong to the WINDOW, not to the tab, and both were driven only by the canvas's on_page_changed callback. Every structural change (add, delete, insert, reorder, merge) goes through PDFCanvas._load_page, which fires it, so those were all fine and the count is re-read rather than adjusted. A TAB SWITCH is the one that changes which page is in front without any page changing, so it fired nothing. Fixed by putting both in one _sync_page_chrome() that the page-change callback and _activate_session both call -- the same one-table rule as everywhere else: two paths that paint the same chrome are two paths that come to disagree. The bookmark toggle had the identical bug and nobody had noticed: it went on describing the previous tab's page.

column2: Ctrl+R brings back every tab and the view you were reading in
column5: Reported: Ctrl+R reopens only the selected tab, and the view state (outline open, side panel) is lost -- with the user's own suggestion, which is what was built: pass the state on the command line. _reload spawns a STANDALONE process so the reload re-reads the code from disk, and it was passing exactly one path (self._path or self._notes_path, the ACTIVE tab) plus --page, so nothing else could come back. Now session_state() records every tab that has a file, the page each is on, which was active, and the window's view state (outline revealer + Outline/Pages choice, notes panel, divider position, size, maximised), and --restore hands it to the child. The state goes through a temp FILE rather than argv: it is a structure, and the alternative is a public multi-tab command line -- a contract to keep for ever for a flag whose only caller is Ctrl+R. The file is CONSUMED (read once, deleted whatever happens), so a stale session cannot be restored twice or linger in the temp dir, and neither an unreadable state nor a file that has since been deleted is fatal: a poor reload beats a crash on startup, so both fall back to opening what still exists. THE TRAP: the divider position must be applied from a LOW-priority idle. _init_pane_position is a realize-time idle that applies the default 62% split, so anything setting the position before it runs is silently overwritten -- the priority is what puts the restore after it. The outline view choice is applied to every tab, since it is a preference about how you are reading and one tab disagreeing with the next looks like the setting failed. Two things deliberately NOT done, both awaiting the user's call: an UNTITLED tab (a blank never saved) has nothing on disk to name, so it is dropped -- keeping it means writing it somewhere first, which is session persistence rather than a reload; and the dirty prompt is still the single-document one, so several unsaved tabs are not yet asked about together. Multiple WINDOWS are out of scope: Ctrl+R replaces the window it was pressed in. FOLLOW-UP 2026-08-11: the reload asks about EVERY dirty tab, not just the one in front -- a reload replaces the whole window, so a tab you never looked at would lose its edits without being mentioned. Asked one tab at a time (each is a different file with a different answer, and a single 'save all?' cannot offer 'discard this one, keep that one'), bringing each tab to the front so the dialog stands in front of the file it names. Cancelling ANY of them abandons the whole reload: saving half a window's work and reloading anyway is the one outcome nobody asks for. Untitled tabs are still dropped -- accepted by the user.

column2: Hide pages: skipped when paging, presenting and exporting
column5: Requested: hide pages from the thumbnail view, right-click showing Hide or Unhide (Unhide when the selected pages are all hidden), working on one right-clicked page AND on the existing multi-selection. The user's call on what hiding MEANS: skipped when paging in the editor, skipped when presenting, and left out of an export -- i.e. PowerPoint's 'hide slide', not a sidebar filter. And on how it looks: a hidden page stays in the strip, dimmed with a marker, because that is the only way to select it again and bring it back. STORAGE: the page marker, as ' hidden', beside continued and bookmark (rows 129/134) -- and it RANGES the way continued does, since hiding a block of slides is one fact about a run. The range coalescing is now one rule (same attributes, no body, not bookmarked) instead of a special case for continued; a bookmark still breaks a range because it names ONE page. Like a bookmark it needs no adjacency rule: it follows its page through every re-key and through a merge, and a deleted page takes it with it. THE TRAP that cost a test: skipping must be resolved ONCE per navigation. _nav_page resolves a target and then called the canvas's _flip_page, which resolved it again -- paging from page 1 over a hidden 2-4 landed on 7 instead of 5. _flip_visible is now the single resolving entry (scroll-past-edge uses it too) and _flip_page takes a plain delta. The canvas has no notes model, so it asks the window through a next_page_for hook, which takes the SESSION rather than reading the active-tab proxies. Navigation is skipped only when it is RELATIVE: clicking a thumbnail, a link or a bookmark still opens a hidden page, which is what keeps it reachable and editable. An export drops the page AND its notes page -- a notes page for a slide nobody receives is a puzzle. _pages_acted_on is the one rule for which pages a per-page verb applies to (the selection when the clicked row is in it, else that row alone), shared with the drag-export so the two cannot say different things. The menu offers the verb that CHANGES something rather than both, so a mixed selection needs no thought. PDF-only, like bookmarks: a text-first page is one endless sheet with no page structure.

column2: Rename and delete the document outline headings too
column5: Requested right after row 153 landed: the document's OWN outline headings should rename and delete with the same gestures as bookmarks -- double-click to rename in place, right-click for both verbs. To the reader the sidebar is one list, so one set of gestures; what differs is only what the verbs write to. _begin_rename therefore no longer knows what it is renaming: the ROW carries _rename_read/_rename_write, and a bookmark writes a name into the notes model while a heading writes a title into the PDF's own outline (set_toc, which means the FILE changes and a save is what makes it stick). _attach_row_menu is likewise one builder for both kinds of row. Two decisions worth keeping. An EMPTY title is refused rather than written -- a heading with no text is unreachable in every other reader, and deleting is its own verb one line below in the menu. And deleting a heading PROMOTES its sub-headings by one level explicitly, rather than leaving it to normalize_toc: that clamps each level to at most one deeper than the entry above it, so the first orphan is promoted and its siblings then hang UNDER it -- the children of a deleted chapter would silently become children of each other. A test caught exactly that. The pages themselves are never touched; the dialog says so, and says how many sub-headings survive. EXTENDED the same day, from use: the right-click menu also changes an entry's PAGE and adds a heading or SUB-heading, and a double-click opens the title and the page together. The new heading takes the page of the ROW you clicked, never the page you are viewing (the user's call: otherwise it would not appear where you clicked), and a SIBLING lands after that row's own children rather than between a heading and them. It is created named ('New heading') and opened for typing, because unlike a bookmark an outline entry with no title is unreachable in other readers, so something has to be there if you walk away. Bookmarks got the page field too -- moving one is re-marking the page you meant, which is otherwise remove-then-add-and-retype -- and it refuses to land on a page that already has a bookmark, since one of the two names would lose silently and there is no undo for a name. The page field REPLACES the page number while editing rather than sitting beside it: the row would otherwise show the page twice, and the one you must not type in looks just as editable. THE BUG that made it unusable, and the reason to remember it: clicking the page field committed the rename and closed the row. The guard that keeps a move between the two fields from counting as 'clicking away' asked each entry has_focus() -- and a GtkEntry delegates focus to an internal GtkText child, so the entry itself NEVER has focus, even while you type in it. It asks the WINDOW for its focus widget now and tests ancestry. Both writes go through one set_toc: doing them separately rebuilds the sidebar under the edit that is still running.

column2: Both dwells demand a stillness no hand has
column5: Reported from the browser port and confirmed to be the same in sidemark.py: the two hold gestures "have to be too precisely not moving". A hand holding a pen against glass for half a second does not stop moving, it DRIFTS -- so a tolerance measured in single pixels is a tolerance nobody has. CIRCLE_LASSO_SLOP_PX is 6.0 (sidemark.py), tested from the press origin in PDFCanvas._on_drag_update and TextPageView's press router; the web port had NO tolerance at all on that hold (any motion event cancelled it) and re-armed the SHAPE dwell's timer on every motion event, so a shaking hand reset that clock for ever and the dwell could never fire. Fixed there as HOLD_SLOP_PX = 16.0 governing both holds, and the desktop should follow. THE TWO MEASURE FROM DIFFERENT ORIGINS AND THAT IS THE DESIGN: circle-to-lasso from where the press LANDED, so a slow drag across the page can never turn into a selection; the shape dwell from wherever the pen was last moving, because you draw a shape and then stop, and the hold has to begin where you stopped. Do not 're-base' the lasso anchor to fix a slow drag -- that is the one case the origin anchor exists to reject. On the desktop this is a one-token change to the constant plus the same rolling anchor for the dwell arm; check the tests that name the slop, and re-judge in the hand rather than by the number, since 16 was chosen on a 1.5x display. DESKTOP FOLLOWED, 2026-08-13. One constant, HOLD_SLOP_PX = 16.0, replacing CIRCLE_LASSO_SLOP_PX and governing BOTH holds on BOTH surfaces -- the web port's name and value, so the two cannot drift. The desktop turned out to have the SAME second defect the web port had, which the report did not name and reading the constant alone would have missed: _arm_straight_timer() was called on every motion event, so the shape dwell's clock restarted per event and a drifting hand could never outrun it -- the tolerance was not the only thing making the dwell unreachable. _arm_straight_timer now TAKES the point it is anchored at (_straight_anchor, cleared by _cancel_straight_timer, which every press begin and end already calls) and the motion handlers re-arm only once the pen has travelled past the slop from it, moving the anchor there. The press point stands in until the pen has moved once. The two origins are unchanged and commented AT the constant: lasso from the press, dwell rolling. Tests: four new, each verified to FAIL against the defect it names -- three on the canvas and one on the SHEET, because the two surfaces re-arm from their own motion handlers and a fix that reached only one of them would be invisible (drift must not restart the dwell -- and it counts re-arms, never GLib source ids, which are ints GLib is free to reuse once a source is removed; travelling must restart it from where the pen got to; and a hold survives 7-11 px of drift, the band the old 6.0 rejected). STILL TO JUDGE IN THE HAND: 16 was chosen on a 1.5x display, so the number is a starting point, not a result.

column2: Reopen the last document; heading marks and \sqrt in notes
column5: Three small things from real use, in one change. (1) AN EMPTY LAUNCH REOPENS WHAT YOU WERE LAST READING, not the scratchpad. The scratchpad had been what an empty launch meant, which is right on the first run and wrong on every later one: the document you were working in yesterday is what you come back for. That inverts one thing -- the scratchpad had been deliberately EXCLUDED from recents as 'noise', and it is now the recents list's own last resort, because with the launch repurposed the list is the ONLY way into it. So it is created and seeded at the TAIL of recent.json on startup (_seed_scratchpad_recent), never at the front -- at the front it would be 'the last document' and every launch would reopen it, i.e. the behaviour this replaces -- and _add_recent PINS it against the 15-entry cap, dropping the oldest ordinary file instead. _open_last_document walks the list and stops at the scratchpad entry, since nothing below it is newer. (2) 'RECENT' NOW MEANS LAST USED, NOT LAST OPENED. Opening A then B and then working in A left B at the top, so a launch handed back the file you happened to open first. Every close refreshes the entry (_touch_recent, from _remember_closed for a tab and from _destroy_all for a window -- oldest first with the ACTIVE tab last, so the document you were looking at wins). _add_recent already preserved the stored reading page, so the position survives the bump. (3) A SECOND BARE LAUNCH SKIPS WHAT IS ALREADY ON SCREEN (_documents_open_elsewhere, walking every window of the app). Asked for as soon as (1) shipped, and it is the same request read properly: opening a second Sidemark with no file means 'give me ANOTHER document', and by then the newest recent is the one already in front of you, so handing back a second view of it helps nobody. It reads every window rather than this one because a NEW window is empty and its own tabs can never be the answer. If the scratchpad itself is open the fallback is a fresh blank sheet, not a second view of it: the scratchpad is a FILE, and two windows saving one .md loses writing. (4) HEADING MARKERS OPEN FROM ANYWHERE ON THEIR LINE. Row 141's rule is that only what the caret TOUCHES falls back to source; '## ' was following it literally and revealed only from inside the marker, so a caret at the end of a heading could not see why the line was big. It is the exception, and the reason it is safe is the reason it is needed: a heading marker is a property of the WHOLE line, it is the one construct whose source you cannot read off what it renders, and revealing it only pushes the line sideways -- nothing on it re-renders. ASCII ARROWS WERE BUILT AND THEN REMOVED THE SAME DAY, and that is the part worth keeping. '->' had been rendering as a long arrow and stopped; it was never a Sidemark feature, it is a FONT LIGATURE (JetBrainsMono Nerd Font, which is what 'font-family: monospace' resolves to here), and it stopped because of a font-cache problem that a REBOOT fixed. The substitution built in the meantime worked and was still worse: a ligature spans BOTH cells, so a one-glyph arrow comes out visibly shorter than the '->' it replaces -- the user's own report. A two-glyph box-rule-plus-arrow matched the width (measured by rendering it: one unbroken run of ink across both cells, the same extent as the ligature) and was still a worse answer than the font's own. Do not re-add it: if the arrows vanish again the question is about the font, not about _MD_SYMBOLS. WHAT SURVIVED from that branch is '\sqrt' -> the radical sign, asked for explicitly as 'not very beautiful but better than nothing': the sign ALONE, no overbar, so '\sqrt x + 1' cannot say where the root ends and '\sqrt{x+1}' shows its braces. An overbar would have to be DRAWN -- a combining U+0305 per character sits at the wrong height on most fonts, the same wall \vec hit. Ported to web/src/mathrender.js with \sqrt in the vector corpus.

column2: The caret follows you between the page and the notes sheet
column5: The caret follows you across the divider, in both directions. Row 130 made the notes panel and the one-page sheet the same notes seen two ways, but crossing between them always landed you at the top: going in, the sheet opened at offset 0 whatever page you were reading; coming out, the page you got back was whatever page the canvas happened to still be on, which is where you STARTED, not where you had read to. Both directions now translate one position into the other. THE TRANSLATION IS TWO PLAIN FUNCTIONS ON THE TEXT (note_offset_for_page / note_page_at_offset, beside parse_note_sections), reading ONE marker table: the sheet is the whole sidecar, so a page index and a character offset are two coordinate systems for the same notes, and two readings of the markers is exactly how the caret comes back on a different page than it left. A range marker (page:13-40) answers for every page in it. GOING IN, the lookup asks for the RUN, not the page (row 129): a linked page has no body of its own, it shares the run start's, so that is the text to go to. The caret lands on the first character of the body; on the marker itself when the page is marked but empty, which reveals the marker (row 141's cursor-line rule) and so says which page you are on; and where the section WOULD be inserted when the page has no notes at all. COMING OUT, TWO OF THE THREE ANSWERS CANNOT COME FROM THE OFFSET, which is why the session remembers the page the sheet was opened at and the offset it was opened at (_full_notes_from / _full_notes_caret). A shared body says the RUN and not which of its pages you were reading, so the page you came from wins whenever it is in the caret's run -- the whole of the user's 'for annotations that belong to several pages, go back there'. And a caret that never MOVED has learnt nothing since it was placed, which is also the only honest answer for a page with no notes: its caret was parked in somebody else's section, so reading a page off it would send you somewhere you never were. A caret above the first marker (the ![[embed]] line) is no page at all and falls back the same way. Otherwise the caret's own marker wins, including over the page you came from. THE ORDER ON THE WAY OUT IS LOAD-BEARING: go_to_page fires on_page_will_change, which COMMITS the notes panel, so the panel has to be holding the page you are leaving before the page turns -- _restore_note first, then the jump. Leave it out and the panel writes back what it held before the sheet ever opened, silently reverting that page's sheet edits (a test pins it). The page follow is confined to the ACTIVE session for the same family of reason: the canvas's callbacks are window methods reading the active-session proxies, so turning a background tab's page writes its chrome onto the tab in front. SCROLLING THE SHEET IS NOT scroll_to_mark: the view is a non-scrollable child inside the viewport (the endless-paper wrapper), so it holds no scroll of its own and the position has to be translated into the ScrolledWindow by hand (TextPageView.scroll_to_offset). Retried while the view reports no height -- entering the view sets the text, shows the sheet and animates the divider in one frame, the thumbnail strip's trap exactly. Text-first pages are untouched: they have no pages to follow. FIX (2026-08-13): the sheet opened at the caret's page but did not SCROLL to it. `scroll_to_offset` retried while the view had no allocation, but that is only the first of two lags — the ADJUSTMENT still describes the extent it had before the text changed, so `upper - page_size` is 0 ('the whole sheet is on screen'), and a value set against a stale upper is silently clamped short. It now retries on a zero span too, and re-reads the value it actually took. And a THIRD wait, which is why the first fix was not enough: the layout SETTLES after the value sticks — entering the sheet sets the text, shows it, animates the divider and re-wraps every line to a new width — and a GtkAdjustment does not carry its value along when the text under it moves. Measured 373 px of drift on a 40-page sidecar between the first successful application and the settled layout. The scroll is now re-applied at 60/200/500 ms; SIDEMARK_SCROLL_DEBUG=1 traces which of the three waits it is in.  FOLLOW-UP (2026-08-16, shipped on the WEB, owed to the desktop): the caret should keep its EXACT offset, not just its page. Both buffers hold the SAME body — the panel shows a page's notes, the sheet shows them inside the whole file — so the offset within that body is the same number on both sides and only where the body STARTS changes; landing at the top of the right section is still landing somewhere you were not, and a divider you can cross without losing your place is one you will cross mid-sentence. Clamp to the body's length or a long position walks into the next page's marker. Second half: a linked run (row 129) should light up as a WHOLE in the sidebar, since inside one there is no single answer to which page you are reading — the page you are on keeps the solid outline, and a run of one is left looking exactly as it does now.

column2: A \command can be a super/subscript body (x^\alpha)
column5: DONE (2026-08-13): a \command's GLYPH is a script body. `x^\alpha` is `x^α` by the time the script grammar runs (the editor rewrites the line, symbols first), and α is not [A-Za-z0-9] — so `x^\alpha`, `e^\lambda`, `x_\mu` rendered as no script at all, the one maths idiom the grammar could not write. _MD_SCRIPT_BODY is now [A-Za-z0-9 + every value in _MD_SYMBOLS]. WHY THIS AND NOT A WIDER RULE: the user asked whether to stop breaking scripts at special characters generally (only at brackets, or not at all now that a script's terminating space is eaten). Rejected, and the reason is worth keeping: `x^2+y^2` typed without spaces is the most common line in a physics note and would silently become x^{2+y}; `/` ruins `x_1/x_2` and `dx/dt`; `*` is Markdown's own emphasis marker; and `,` `.` `=` `)` must break, so 'brackets only' is strictly worse than what we had. A whitespace rule does not survive punctuation hugging a script (`a_i , b` shows the space, since the eat only fires before an alphanumeric). Above all, widening the rule RE-RENDERS notes already written — the source is never touched, but a semester of x^2+y^2 would start reading wrong. This change cannot: every symbol value is non-ASCII and single-character (asserted in a test), so nothing that renders today changes meaning — only text that rendered as literally nothing starts to render. The terminating space deliberately did NOT grow the same way: nothing forced the space in `x_i \alpha`, so it stays visible. Ported to web/ (SCRIPT_BODY in src/mathrender.js) and graded by the shared vectors — extras/export_math_vectors.py grew four cases. Tests: TestLatexFormatting.test_a_command_can_BE_a_script, test_a_space_you_were_not_forced_to_type_survives_a_symbol, test_the_script_body_can_not_swallow_markdown.

column2: One rule for a rendered expression's terminating space (and Backspace over it)
column5: DONE (2026-08-13), two changes to the same rule, both from writing real notes. (1) THE TERMINATING SPACE IS EATEN BEFORE ANY CHARACTER. It used to depend on whether that character could have CONTINUED the expression — a letter for a command, an alphanumeric for a script — so `\alpha a` closed up while `\alpha 1` and `\alpha +` kept their space. Three lines that look like the same construct rendering three ways, with the reason visible only to somebody who knows which characters can follow a backslash. The user asked for it and was shown the cost first: `\alpha + \beta` now reads "α+ β", and an equation that wants its operator spaced asks with two spaces (the escape that already existed). A rule you can SEE beats a rule that is right. Consequence worth knowing: with nothing left for the rule to depend on, the whole at_end / _MD_SYMBOL_END_RE / _MD_SCRIPT_END_RE split is gone from both sides and from the vectors — the end of the line, the end of a `code` segment and an ordinary letter all terminate alike. Applied to SCRIPTS as well as commands, because 'commands and scripts obey one rule' is the invariant; that is what makes `x^2 + y` read "x^2+ y", and it is a one-line revert if it ever grates. (2) BACKSPACE OVER THE EATEN SPACE. Reported as: write `\alpha + b`, hold Backspace, and the α disappears in ONE keystroke — expected was to land on a de-rendered `\alpha`. Cause: once the space is eaten the caret stands behind a character nothing is drawn for, so GTK's Backspace lands on the glyph in front of it and splicing that through the index map removes `\alpha ` entirely. `_open_eaten_terminator` reveals the line first and then returns False, so the deletion itself is an ordinary buffer edit (dirty tracking, undo). It is deliberately DELETE-ONLY: typing the terminator must still settle the expression (that is what the caret test's 'span without its space' rule is for), and the two directions want opposite things. Forward Delete needs nothing — a caret in FRONT of the glyph is inside the command's own span, so the line is already open there. Web port unaffected: CodeMirror keeps the source in the document, so nothing is ever spliced back. Tests: TestLatexFormatting.test_backspace_takes_the_eaten_space_not_the_glyph, test_backspacing_up_to_a_symbol_stops_at_it, test_an_ordinary_backspace_is_left_alone, test_the_space_is_eaten_wherever_the_command_ends, plus the updated space expectations across TestLatexFormatting/TestCalloutMarkup and web/test/math.mjs.

column2: Links point at names (bookmarks/chapters), preview on hover, and say when they are dead
column5: DONE (2026-08-13). The linking feature (row 99) worked and nobody could find it, and what it pointed at did not survive editing. Four changes, one design. (1) A LINK POINTS AT A NAME. `[[#Eigenvalues]]` / `[[l2.pdf#Chapter Two]]` resolve against a document's BOOKMARKS (row 134) and its outline HEADINGS — the two things in Sidemark that already have a name and a page. This is the fix for the real defect: nothing re-keys a `#page=N` when a slide is inserted, a chapter is dragged (row 123) or two decks are merged, so a semester of links quietly drifts, while a bookmark just follows its page. The page forms are still parsed and followed FOR EVER — notes already written are full of them, and a link that stops resolving is worse than a syntax we would not choose again — they are simply not what the picker suggests. `document_anchors()` indexes a document that is NOT open without a window: headings from the PDF, bookmarks parsed out of the sidecar's page markers (an unnamed one carries the derived label, row 134's rule), cached on BOTH files' mtimes because the things that change anchors are not all ours (another window, another tab, an editor). The OPEN document is read live instead (`_own_anchors`), or a bookmark you just made — the one you are about to link to — would not resolve until you saved. Earliest page wins a repeated name ('Summary' is a heading in every chapter). (2) ONE RESOLVER. `_resolve_note_link` answers for following, for the strike-through and for the preview; two of those would drift, and a link that looks live and does nothing is the worst of the three. (3) AN UNRESOLVABLE LINK IS STRUCK THROUGH and greyed — never while the caret is in it, because a target is unresolvable for most of the time you spend typing one and a line that strikes itself out under your hands reads as your mistake. Memoised per view with a 5 s TTL rather than invalidated (what it resolves against changes outside this window), plus an explicit drop from `_populate_toc`, which is exactly the list of edits that make a dead link live. (4) DISCOVERABILITY. ☰ 'Link to a page…' / Ctrl+K inserts `[[]]` and opens the picker — an entry that DOES the thing teaches the syntax by leaving it on screen — and ☰ 'Copy link to this page' is row 100's link-to-here, naming the page by its bookmark or heading when it has one. The picker offers this document's names first, then This page, then files; a `#` in the query switches to the anchors of whichever file is named before it, so picking a file and typing `#` walks straight into its bookmarks. (5) HOVER PREVIEW: resting on a link renders the page it leads to (450 ms, cached by file+mtime+page). A link is a promise about a page you cannot see and following one costs you your place, so a wrong guess is expensive twice. TRAP worth keeping: showing a Gtk.Popover in the headless test compositor KILLS weston — it took out the rest of that run, and every window test after it failed with GTK's 'couldn't be initialized', blaming itself. Tests reach the picker and the preview through an UNPRESENTED window (`_run_in_window(present=False)`), which is what the existing `get_mapped()` guard is there for. run_tests.sh also learned to drop a stale socket, which is the same failure with a different cause. NOT DONE, deliberately: backlinks ('what links here', row 100 item 4) — it needs a cross-file index and an invalidation story, and is only worth building once naming targets proves itself in real notes. FOLLOW-UPS from the first hour of real use (same day): (a) THE WAY BACK. Following a link costs you your place, so `_link_return` remembers where the click came from and the notes header offers '↩ Back to p.N' — only while you are still on the page the link put you on. Asking 'am I where the link left me?' is what retires the offer with no timer and no stale jump. (b) TWO DEAD HIT-TESTS, one cause: `buf.get_text(..., include_hidden_chars=False)` compared against a line OFFSET, which always counts the hidden characters. `_link_target_at` therefore could not match `[[...]]` on any line whose brackets were hidden — i.e. every line except the caret's — so the hand cursor, Ctrl+click and the hover preview were all dead in normal use while testing fine with the caret on the line; and `_cursor_line_and_col` shifted the `[[` query by one per marker, so the picker stopped opening on a line that already had a link or a rendered symbol. Found by DRIVING THE REAL APP (a probe script that opens a window, calls _on_link_motion at a link's coordinates and screenshots) after the user reported 'hovering does nothing' — no unit test could have: the seam it broke at is the buffer, and the tests constructed their iters directly. `_link_at_iter` is split out so the rule can be tested without a laid-out widget. (c) BOTH POPUPS ANCHOR TO THE LINE (halign START), not to a point: given a zero-height anchor GTK centres the popup and flips it back over the text you are reading — the `[[` you just typed, or the link you are hovering. (d) Bookmarks are listed before headings: a bookmark is a place YOU named, a heading is one the author did and a deck has dozens. (e) `link_target_to_here` always names the file, because the clipboard does not know where it will be pasted and a bare `#name` would resolve against whatever document receives it — a link that works and goes to the wrong place. PREVIEWS (the hover one and the inline `![[embed]]` one) were built, shipped and then PULLED the same day after a crash — see row 166, which carries their whole design. What stays from this row: named anchors, the one resolver, the strike-through, the picker, Ctrl+K, copy-link-to-here and the way back.

column2: Show the page a [[link]] leads to (hover, and ![[embeds]] inline)
column5: DEFERRED (2026-08-13), built and pulled the same day. Showing the page a [[link]] leads to, so you can tell whether it is the slide you meant without losing your place. Two forms shipped and both were removed at the user's word after Sidemark ABORTED while editing notes: `Gtk-ERROR: Byte index 31 is off the end of the line` from gtktextbtree.c, i.e. a GTK-level fatal, immediately after a hover. NOT diagnosed. The leading suspect is mine and is worth checking first: `_insert_link_target` read `ls.get_line()` from an iterator INVALIDATED by the two buffer edits just above it, to insert the `!` that made a picked target an embed — a stale GtkTextIter is undefined behaviour and this is the only new code on that path. Second suspect: `Gdk.Rectangle(x=…, y=…)` silently ignores its arguments in this PyGObject (a DeprecationWarning in the crash log), so the tooltip's tip_area was (0,0,0,0) and GTK re-queried on every motion event. WHAT WAS RIGHT, and should be kept if this is rebuilt: (1) The MARKER decides, never the caret. A caret-keyed preview cannot be read — it appears and vanishes as you move, and the reflow shifts the line you were reading. `![[target]]` is the marker: Obsidian's embed syntax and already Sidemark's own (a sidecar's first line is `![[lecture.pdf]]`). The user proposed `[[!target]]`, which is neither. (2) The space is a TAG (`pixels-below-lines`, one tag per height), so the notes below MOVE DOWN and the picture never lands on the writing. It cannot be a paintable in the buffer — that is a real character, and this buffer IS the .md source, spliced back through a character-to-character index map. (3) The hover form must be a TOOLTIP (`query-tooltip`), never a popover: a popover is a real surface, so near the pointer it takes the crossing, the view gets a LEAVE, the preview hides and it oscillates — the symptom was 'it only appears when I click'. (4) Renders memoised per target string (the highlight pass runs per keystroke over every line), pages of unopened documents cached by file+mtime+page, one preview per line. BEFORE REBUILDING: reproduce the abort first, with a long real sidecar and non-ASCII text, and fix the stale iterator regardless. The removed code is in git: 285b885, f280e87, and the tooltip half of 8ee8091. ROOT CAUSE FOUND AND FIXED (2026-08-18), and it was never the previews. GTK's `get_iter_at_location`, handed a y BELOW a line's text, gives up and answers 'the end of that line' — computed as the line's RAW byte count but converted as a VISIBLE line index (gtktextlayout.c, `gtk_text_layout_get_iter_at_position`, the `y > display->height - margins` branch, into `gtk_text_iter_set_visible_line_index`). On a line carrying invisible characters the index overshoots by exactly the hidden bytes and GTK calls g_error: the process dies where it stands, no exception, which is why the log simply stopped mid-session. In this buffer nearly every line has hidden characters — a page marker, a `[[`, the source behind a rendered symbol — so it was our hit tests that met it. Reproduced in a BARE GtkTextView in ~40 lines (an invisible tag, a `pixels-below-lines` tag, probe the space below the text): nothing about Sidemark is required, and the same sweep dumps core on a real MarkdownNotesView and is clean through the fix. That also explains the shape of the report: `pixels-below-lines` is the plainest way to create space below a line, so the embed gap made it easy to hit — but the previews were pulled and it still fired on hover alone, because any vertical slack (a tall glyph's row, a stale height on a long sheet) does the same. The 805-page sidecar was circumstantial. FIX: `MarkdownNotesView.iter_at_buffer_xy` clamps the y into the band the paragraph's display ROWS actually occupy before GTK sees it — measured with `get_iter_location`, which converts iter->index and is safe, in the same layout GTK is about to use, so the two cannot disagree. Every pointer->iter hit test in the notes view and the sheet (8 call sites: link hover, task boxes, ink and image anchoring, paste, the context menu, the export page split) goes through it; a bare `get_iter_at_location` on this buffer is now a bug. Two traps in writing it: the band must NOT come from the end-of-line iter (it sits on the newline and reports a 0x0 rect, which collapses the band and rejects clicks on the text — a 1.3x-tall task box is what noticed), and the regression test runs in a SUBPROCESS, since a regression does not fail an assertion, it takes the interpreter with it. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS ROW: design (2) above — the gap as a `pixels-below-lines` tag — is safe to rebuild on now, and the 'reproduce the abort first' precondition is met.

column2: Import the PDF's own images as Sidemark objects
column5: Asked for by the user after they assumed PDF-mode images were missing entirely -- they are not (row 118 shipped both modes), but every route IN was the clipboard: dropping a .png is refused by classify_import_paths as 'not a PDF or PowerPoint' and there is no menu entry. Following that, the real question turned out to be the more interesting one: can a picture that arrived WITH the PDF become one of our objects? The user's own framing is the acceptance test -- 'if I open the pdf in a browser it would look the same as long as I do not move the objects'. THE DESIGN IS THAT THE PROMISE IS CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED. A placement is importable only if it round-trips BIT-IDENTICALLY, and three things rule that out. (1) Z-ORDER: our layer is APPENDED, so anything we place draws above the whole page -- invisible for a figure with nothing over it, wrong for a watermark under the text. (2) A ROTATED placement: _layer_bytes_for BAKES a tilt into fresh pixels because a PDF placement carries no free angle, so a rotated import would come back RESAMPLED -- softer and bigger, which is the promise broken quietly. Only an axis-aligned, unflipped, unskewed placement can be re-placed by reference. (3) An image used MORE THAN ONCE, anywhere: importing marks the xref /OC ours and ownership is what strip_image_layer acts on, so REUSING the object for a logo that is also page content on 40 other slides would strip it from all of them on the next save. That was first built as a REFUSAL and the refusal was wrong -- measured over 12 real lecture PDFs, sharing is the NORMAL case (70 of 124 placements, i.e. every template logo), and refusing it left the feature working on 38% of real pictures. It is an argument for giving the import its OWN COPY of the object, not for declining: one re-encode, the original untouched, the other pages keep their placement. Same answer for the same image drawn twice on ONE page -- two placements, two objects, two rects, so moving one does not move the other. After the change: 121 of the same 124 placements are importable, and the 3 that are not are the rotated ones. The lesson is the general one about measuring on real documents instead of constructed ones -- every rejection rule in the first version was defensible in the abstract and one of them was rejecting the majority case. The classifier reads (2) off the placement and copies rather than refuses for (3). NOTHING can read (1) off a placement, so nothing tries: render_matches RENDERS the page as it is and as it would be SAVED and compares the pixels. That is the only check that tests the actual promise, and it catches in one step everything a static rule would have to enumerate -- soft masks, blend modes, clipping paths, a caption over a figure. All candidates are tried together first (one render pair, the answer on almost every page) and only a page that fails pays for the per-image bisect; the surviving set is then re-tested AS A SET, because two images that each look fine alone can still swap order against EACH OTHER once both are on top. content_placements is a real tokeniser, not a regex: 'Do' appears inside strings a page is drawing, a matrix can be built across operations, and an inline image's binary data can contain anything. It tracks the CTM through q/Q/cm and spans ONLY the '/Name Do' -- removing exactly the one paint operation can never corrupt the page, where deleting the enclosing 'q ... cm ... Q' would take a transform the next operator may share. TRAP FOUND BY TEST, worth keeping: PyMuPDF hands out a FRESH resource name when it re-places an existing xref, so counting placements by NAME reports 'drawn once' about a picture that is on the page twice -- the count is by XREF, because ownership is a property of the object. Second trap: _load_page clears the selection (it is per-page and transient), so the re-render has to come BEFORE selecting the imported images or there is nothing to drag. The REPORT is half the feature: an import that takes three of five pictures and says nothing teaches that Sidemark is unreliable, when it in fact declined the two it could not have kept identical. Undo restores BOTH halves (the objects and the page's content stream) or the picture vanishes off the page altogether. PDF-ONLY and that is not a parity gap: a text-first page has no page content to import from. DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: text and vector art (a different feature with no model behind it -- see the note below), whole-document import (the menu entry is about the page you are looking at), and the OTHER half of the gap that started this, inserting an image from a FILE (drop + a menu entry), which is small and still open. VALIDATED ON A REAL DECK, and it immediately paid for the render check. Of the three images in the user's own seminar presentation, all three passed the classifier and two FAILED the render -- both because they carry a SOFT MASK (/SMask, i.e. transparency) and extract_image returns the base image WITHOUT it, so importing them naively would have put an opaque block where a logo with a transparent background had been. Nothing in the design anticipated soft masks; the pixels caught it anyway, which is the whole argument for checking rather than enumerating. Fixed by import_image_bytes, which recomposes base+mask into an RGBA PNG -- shared by the trial and the commit path, or the trial stops predicting the save. That costs the by-reference re-placement (new bytes, so _xref is 0 and the save re-encodes once), which is the right trade: a transparent picture is the common case in a real deck.
