Two of the three now import; the third is a 5360x5435 image squeezed into 128x140 points, where recomposing changes 1.0% of the rendered pixels by up to 65/255 -- a real difference from resampling, correctly refused. ceiling: the trial render is ~1.3 s for an image that size, and the per-image bisect pays it once each, so a page of huge pictures is slow; IMPORT_MAX_TRIALS bounds the COUNT but not the size. TWO FIXES FROM ONE REAL FILE (a scanned, image-only PDF the user tried and it refused). Both were the import telling the truth about a defect that was NOT the import's. (a) THE TRIAL MUST PLACE THE IMAGE THE WAY THE SAVE WILL. _trial_page re-encoded from bytes while _write_image_layer re-places BY REFERENCE, so for a scan -- one big JPEG with an ICC profile -- the trial dropped the profile, shifted every colour, and reported 'it would look different' about its own extra step. It now uses the TRIAL's own copied xref (insert_pdf brings the object across, profile and all) and mirrors the save's xref/stream/oc call exactly. This also fixed the seminar deck's third image, a 5360x5435 picture that had been failing purely on resampling. (b) A PRE-EXISTING BUG IN THE IMAGE LAYER, older than this row and nothing to do with importing: page.insert_image treats the rect as a SUGGESTION -- by default it fits the picture inside at the picture's own aspect and CENTRES it. Our rect is the truth, because row 122's side handles stretch one axis on purpose, so every non-uniformly stretched image was being written letterboxed and displaced: the saved PDF did not match the canvas, in a way no test caught because the file still looked plausible. The scan made it visible (a full-page image came back 788.4pt tall instead of 792, shifted 1.8pt down) only because there the distortion was the whole page. Fixed with keep_proportion=False in _write_image_layer and the trial; the regression test asserts the placement MATRIX, since that is the only place the shift shows. Both files now import completely.

column2: Text objects on the page (type on a PDF, real text in the file)
column5: PLANNED, not started -- the full plan is notes/text-objects-plan.md, approved by the user 2026-08-14. Reached by asking about EDITING THE PDF'S OWN TEXT, which was analysed and REJECTED with the user's agreement: a PDF stores positioned glyph runs, not words, so subset fonts mean you often cannot type a character the document never used, there is no reflow, and encodings with no ToUnicode CMap cannot be round-tripped -- the failure mode is silent layout damage in a file you hand in. Do not reopen that without a new reason; deleting text (redaction) is separable and reliable if the narrow need appears. WHAT IS BUILT INSTEAD is the thing people actually want from it: putting YOUR OWN text on a page -- a label on a diagram, a correction over a typo, a caption. Sidemark cannot do that at all today; you can draw a letter with the pen and paste a picture of words, but you cannot type on a page. THE USER'S THREE DECISIONS: replace #56 (the Ctrl+Alt+right-click standalone text box) entirely; edit IN PLACE on the page rather than in the notes panel or a popover; and -- their own framing, which became the design -- 'render it as a pdf object but still make it editable for sidemark, similar to the drawings'. THAT ANSWER IS BETTER FOR TEXT THAN FOR DRAWINGS: insert_textbox takes oc=, so page text goes into the SAME optional-content layer images already use (row 118) -- sidecar is the truth, the layer is a render target regenerated on save -- and where an image is pixels and ink is an annotation, this is REAL TEXT another reader can select, search and copy. TWO LIMITS, BOTH MEASURED HERE ON PyMuPDF 1.27.2, both the same shape as the image layer. (1) Base-14 fonts cannot encode maths: alpha/beta/sum/reals/arrow written with helv come back from get_text() as '?????'. THIS IS A LIVE BUG TODAY, not a new constraint -- _NotesWriter and _draw_export_callout use helv, so exporting notes containing \alpha already produces ?. An embedded Unicode font fixes it and doc.subset_fonts() takes the cost from 650 KB to ~25 KB per file. That is phase 0 and is worth doing on its own whatever happens to the rest. No single INSTALLED font covers what is needed -- NotoSansMath has the symbols but renders 'ab' as superscripts, NotoSans misses the sum/arrow/leq/integral, LiberationSans misses the reals sign, DejaVu is absent -- so it probably means shipping one font with the package. Using that same font for the Pango layout is what keeps canvas and PDF identical by construction. (2) insert_textbox rotates only in multiples of 90 (rotate=45 raises ValueError), so a freely tilted box rasterises exactly as _layer_bytes_for already does for a tilted image. WHAT IT REUSES rather than builds, which is why this is Medium and not Hard: rich text on cairo ALREADY EXISTS -- _note_box_layout drives _notes_to_pango_markup into a PangoCairo layout, so a text object gets \alpha, x^2 and \hat{x} for free and nothing else in this class of app does that; the whole image object template (hit-test, bbox, handles, rotate knob, clipboard, undo ops); the OC layer machinery; and the tool tables, which generate badges, stripes and tooltips from one entry. THE RISK IS PHASE 3: nothing on either canvas has ever accepted typed characters, the sheet's ink overlay is deliberately non-targetable and its router DENIES so the caret keeps the press, and set_scroll_to_focus is off because a focus grab there jumps the sheet mid-press (row 128). Phases 0-2 are useful without it and the fallback is a popover editor. One thing to CONFIRM with the user before phase 5: the recommendation is that legacy textbox markers keep rendering read-only rather than being migrated, because converting them would rewrite the user's .md to fix a feature nobody has complained about. PHASE 0 HAS LANDED on its own (2026-09-11, row 191): the export embeds DejaVu Sans, so `_NotesWriter` and the callout/anchor/text-box drawing no longer turn the notes grammar's maths into `?`. The font helper (`_export_font`/`_export_measure_font`) is the one phase 1 was to share, so a text object should draw through it rather than resolving its own. Phases 1-5 are unstarted.

column2: Diagnose GTK aborts and UI freezes from the log (faulthandler, a GLib log bridge, a main-loop watchdog)
column5: A crash with NO trace in the log, and the fix is diagnostics rather than a cure. 2026-08-14: the user's session died while dragging the divider from PDF into text mode on an 805-page document. The session log simply STOPS -- no ERROR, no traceback -- because a GTK abort kills the process from C: there is no Python exception, so sys.excepthook never runs. coredumpctl had the answer the log could not: SIGABRT through g_log_writer_default <- gtk_text_iter_set_visible_line_index <- gtk_text_view_get_iter_at_location, called from a Python signal handler under the main loop. In sidemark.py the only handler on that path is MarkdownNotesView._link_target_at, reached from _on_link_motion -- i.e. moving the pointer over the notes buffer. That is row 166's crash ('Byte index N is off the end of the line'), and this proves it SURVIVED the pull of the link/embed previews: the hover hit-test still calls the same GTK path, so 166's leading suspect is confirmed live in shipped code. Suspected mechanism, NOT proven: entering the full-notes view fills one buffer with the whole sidecar and _rehighlight then walks every line rewriting the ones whose rendering changed, which churns GTK's line-display cache; a motion event landing while the invisible-tag bookkeeping is out of step asks for a visible byte index past the end of a line. The document's size is why it bit here and not in a page's notes panel. WHAT SHIPPED (diagnostics only, no behaviour change): (1) faulthandler.enable() pointed at the session log -- it catches SIGABRT/SIGSEGV and writes the PYTHON frames, which is what names the handler; (2) a GLib log writer func bridging GTK's own messages into the log, with the Python stack, flushed immediately because the abort is microseconds away; (3) breadcrumbs on the suspect path -- the full-notes switch logs the sheet's char/line count, a big buffer replacement is logged, and a render pass over REHIGHLIGHT_SLOW_MS is a warning. FOUR THINGS MEASURED, each of which the obvious implementation gets wrong. g_log_set_handler does NOT see these: modern GTK logs through the STRUCTURED API (g_log_structured_standard in the crash stack), so only a writer func sees both paths. The writer CANNOT suppress a crash -- glib aborts in the caller ABOVE it whatever it returns (verified against a fatal critical), so the hook is purely additive; it still delegates to g_log_writer_default so stderr and the journal are unchanged. FLAG_FATAL is NOT set on the way in -- glib decides fatality after the writer returns, so an always-fatal critical arrives as a plain level 8; classify on LEVEL_ERROR (g_error, fatal by definition, which is what the real abort was) and give a critical a stack too. And g_log_set_writer_func may be called ONCE per process: the second call is itself a g_error, so the install is guarded -- an unguarded re-install aborts the app with exactly the crash the hook exists to explain (found by the test suite doing it twice). PyGObject hands the writer the raw GLogField array, so field values are gpointers read out with ctypes; the structured path also carries CODE_FILE/LINE/FUNC, which names the GTK source line that gave up. NOT FIXED: the crash itself. The next occurrence should now arrive with GTK's message, the GTK source line, the Python handler and the sheet size in the log -- which is what a fix needs. If it recurs, the first question is whether _link_target_at can be skipped while the view is mid-relayout. ALSO IN THIS ROW, from the same session: a MAIN-LOOP WATCHDOG, for a second symptom the user reported -- Sidemark freezing for a split second while typing, after which every character appears at once. That is a blocked main loop: the events were never lost, they were QUEUED while the loop was busy, which is precisely why nothing inside the app can see it. Only a thread OUTSIDE the loop can. _watchdog watches a STALL_BEAT_MS heartbeat and, once the loop is STALL_WARN_MS late, samples the MAIN thread's Python stack via sys._current_frames() until it comes back, then reports the busiest frames. Naming the frame is the entire point -- 'stalled 400 ms' is the symptom the user could already see. Rate-limited, because the shape to expect is work repeating on every keystroke; the thread never touches GTK; SIDEMARK_NO_WATCHDOG=1 turns it off. The prime suspect for the typing freeze is _rehighlight, which walks EVERY line of the buffer per keystroke -- hence the REHIGHLIGHT_SLOW_MS warning, which should name it directly. Verified by hand against a deliberate 600 ms block: 'main loop stalled 612 ms -- busiest: a_render_pass_over_every_line (15/15)' plus the full stack. NOT started in the test suite: _loop_beat frozen at the end of one test's main loop makes every later moment look like a permanent hang, and a stray warning breaks any test counting assertLogs records -- the pieces are tested instead. One knock-on, found because the first stall test DELETED its own log: a clean exit removed the log unless an ERROR was recorded, and every diagnostic here is a WARNING in a session that then exits perfectly cleanly. The keep rule is now WARNING and above (all 22 warning sites in the file are something having gone wrong), with _prune_logs bounding the directory at LOG_KEEP.

column2: Autosave only writes what changed (the typing freeze)
column5: FOUND BY ROW 169's WATCHDOG, on its first day, from the user's own log: 'main loop stalled 923 ms -- busiest: update_timing_test, fz_transform_point, pdf_new_text_string' with a stack straight into _autosave_tick -> _write_autosave_for -> canvas.save_copy. The user had reported Sidemark freezing for a split second while typing, with the characters all landing afterwards; that is the signature of a blocked main loop, and the autosave timer is what was blocking it, every 60 s. MEASURED on the user's 806-page, 59 MB deck: rewriting the 212 ink annotations 420 ms, document.save() 86 ms, ~506 ms total (923 ms in the app, under load). Note the page count is NOT the story -- a plain save of the same file from disk is 94 ms. The cost is _write_ink_annotations deleting and re-creating EVERY stroke in the document on EVERY tick. THE FIX IS 'ONLY SAVE WHAT CHANGED', and the direction of the default is the design: _mark_dirty(pdf=True) is the default and every unaudited caller keeps paying for a full snapshot; the notes buffer alone opts out with pdf=False, since notes live in the .md and cannot change the PDF. An autosave is a data-safety feature, so an unknown path must cost a needless write and never a lost recovery. The snapshot is still written when the directory has no doc.pdf, because recovery reads it and notes must never be half a pair. Typing therefore now costs ~0 ms; drawing still pays ~500 ms once a minute. THREADS WERE MEASURED AND REJECTED, which was the user's own question -- autosave is not time-critical, so why not another core? Because the GIL is held: with a spinner thread standing in for the UI, document.save() left it 3% of its speed and the ink rewrite 47%, and the rewrite itself went from 420 to 975 ms under that contention -- the opposite of a multicore win. PyMuPDF is also not thread-safe, and the expensive phase MUTATES the document the render path reads. A forked process would genuinely parallelise (copy-on-write), but Python deprecates fork from a multi-threaded process and row 169 has just added a watchdog thread. Not worth it for a periodic 500 ms task. UPSTREAM BUG FOUND ALONG THE WAY: PyMuPDF 1.27.2.3's Annot.update() calls Annot.update_timing_test() unconditionally -- a leftover benchmark that counts to 30,000 in pure Python and whose return value the only caller discards. 0.68 ms per annotation, 144 ms of the 420. _defuse_pymupdf_timing_test() replaces it at import, guarded by hasattr so an upstream fix just makes it a no-op. Checked, not assumed: the written PDF is byte-identical apart from the trailer's random /ID, which differs between any two saves of the same document anyway -- worth re-verifying that way rather than trusting a hash. Should be reported upstream. NOT DONE: per-page ink rewriting, which is what would fix the DRAWING case (420 ms -> ~90 ms). It needs to know which pages' ink changed; a fingerprint derived at write time would avoid tracking it through every stroke/undo/lasso/merge path, but getting it wrong means strokes missing from a saved file, so it wants its own session rather than being tacked onto this one.

column2: The page strip selects like a text editor (Shift marks a region, Ctrl adds)
column5: Shift+click marks every page between the anchor and the clicked one; Ctrl+click adds or removes one; a plain click starts again from there. ONE anchor shared by both, which is what the convention actually promises — Ctrl to pick a starting page, then Shift to take the run from it — and Ctrl+Shift adds a second region without clearing the first. A Shift+click does NOT move the anchor, so widening and narrowing a range from one origin is a gesture repeated rather than a new range each time. TRAP: none of this can be left to GtkListBox's own MULTIPLE-mode selection. The thumbnail row carries a DragSource in the same CAPTURE phase, which swallows a stationary press — the reason Ctrl+click already needed its own handler (#65) — so Shift never reached the listbox's range code either, and the comment claiming Shift 'falls through to a native range op' was describing something that never ran. Handling both in one handler is also what lets them share an anchor. A Shift press is CLAIMED so the row is not ACTIVATED: marking a region is not a request to go to its last page. A plain press is deliberately NOT claimed — the listbox selects the row and the activation turns the page — but it still sets the anchor. The anchor is per session (DocumentSession.STATE) and dropped by _populate_thumbnails, because the rows it pointed into are gone and a stale index marks a region nobody chose. The web port already had this in _clickPage. Tests drive the handler with a stub gesture that records whether it claimed, and stand in for the listbox's own selection when it did not — which is what makes 'falls through' testable at all.

column2: Search paints the notes yellow, and the sheet actually goes there
column5: Two defects in one place, both reported from real use, both about the NOTES half of Ctrl+F -- the PDF half was already right and is what showed them up. (1) THE SHEET NEVER SCROLLED. _select_note_match ended with scroll_to_iter on the notes view, which on the text sheet does nothing at all: TextPageView wraps a non-scrollable child in a viewport, so the view holds no scroll of its own -- the documented reason TextPageView.scroll_to_offset exists (row 162 hit the same wall placing the caret). Ctrl+F in text mode therefore found every match, counted them, selected one, and left you looking at wherever you already were. It now takes the sheet's own path when the sheet is what is showing. The same call had a second bug behind it: on a PDF's full-notes sheet the buffer is the WHOLE sidecar while the hit offsets are into ONE page's stored notes, so they have to be rebased through note_offset_for_page(run_start(page)) -- row 162's translation, asked for the RUN because a linked page stores no body of its own. Without that the caret lands wherever that many characters from the top happens to be. (2) A NOTES HIT WAS SHOWN BY SELECTING IT, which meant the window's SELECTION colour -- grey, next to the page's own yellow/orange rects, i.e. the same search saying two different things -- and it marked only the CURRENT match, so the other occurrences on screen were invisible. Now the view owns two tags of its own (search-hit yellow, search-current orange, the page's palette) and the match is not selected at all: row 141 shows the SOURCE of every line a selection covers, so landing on a match un-rendered the very line you were sent to read. THE HIGHLIGHTS ARE FOUND BY SEARCHING THE BUFFER, not by mapping the model's offsets onto it: this is the one surface whose text RE-RENDERS underneath the highlight (\alpha is six columns of source and one glyph on screen), so a stored offset points at the wrong column the moment a line renders, while the text on screen is always right about itself. Three things hold it up: the tags are created OUTSIDE self._t, because _rehighlight clears every tag in that table on every pass while a highlight has to outlive a render (you search, then type) -- and created LAST, so they outrank code's background; _rehighlight re-applies them at the end of the pass, since a line it REWROTE dropped what it carried; and the current match is kept as a MARK PAIR rather than offsets, so it rides _buf_replace_line like the caret does. _carry_search_query hands the term over when the divider is crossed, or a search made on one side is invisible the moment you cross and the side you left keeps painting a term nobody is searching for.

column2: Task boxes, and Enter carries a list on
column5: `- [ ] milk` renders as a box you click to tick, and Enter in a list opens the next item. THE BOX IS A ONE-FOR-ONE SUBSTITUTION and that is the whole design: the state character between the brackets becomes the glyph (space -> box, x -> ticked box) and the `- [` and `]` around it are HIDDEN WITH TAGS -- so the construct is five columns of source and five on screen with three invisible, and the render's index map stays the IDENTITY across it. A box that changed the line's length would have to be mapped like a \command for no gain: nobody types a box, they type the brackets. It leaves `box milk` on screen exactly where a plain bullet leaves `- milk`. Opened from ANYWHERE on the line, like a heading marker (row 161) and for the same reason -- it is a property of the whole line, and revealing it only pushes the line sideways, nothing on it re-renders. TICKING IS AN ORDINARY BUFFER EDIT: toggle_task writes the state character over the glyph and lets the render pass splice it back onto the source through the index map, the same path as typing over a rendered alpha -- rewriting the source line by hand would be a second way of doing the one thing _line_source exists for, and it would drop every other symbol on the line to a literal. The click target is the box GLYPH and nothing else, one character wide: a checkbox you can tick is also a line you can type in, so the click that means 'put the caret here' must not be able to tick by accident. Not gated on a modifier -- a checkbox nobody can click is just a glyph. ENTER reads the marker from the line's SOURCE, never from the buffer, or it would write the box glyph itself into the .md; it repeats a bullet, counts a number on (1. -> 2., 9) -> 10)), and always opens an EMPTY task box, because you are writing the next task rather than copying the state of the one above. Enter on an item with nothing in it ENDS the list, which is how you stop -- without it the only escape is deleting a marker you did not ask for. Only at the END of the line: Enter anywhere else is a SPLIT, ordinary editing, and the caret's column there is a RENDERED column that would have to be mapped back to mean anything. NOT YET IN THE WEB PORT -- the browser editor is CodeMirror decorations, so the box wants a replace-widget with a click handler rather than this hide-and-substitute; a sidecar with boxes still reads as plain Markdown there, which is the honest fallback. FOLLOW-UP THE SAME DAY, from the user's own screenshot: the click did NOTHING and the box 'is not rendered like in obsidian as a real checkbox'. Both were real. (1) THE CLICK: _task_box_at compared get_iter_at_location's offset with the box's own column, and that API answers the question the CARET asks -- which boundary is NEAREST -- so past the middle of the glyph it returns the character after it and the right half of every box was dead. It is a COLUMN RANGE now, from the hidden bullet (zero width, so nothing can land in it) to the far edge of the glyph, stopping at the space behind it. A RECTANGLE is not available as a target here, which is the second measurement: get_iter_location returns the SAME x for two adjacent characters on a line carrying hidden runs (measured in the real app: glyph=(72,1,0,16) for the box and x=72 for the bracket before it). (2) DRAWING A REAL CONTROL WAS BUILT AND REVERTED, and neither reason will change: a GtkTextTag with foreground-rgba alpha 0 STILL PAINTS, so the glyph cannot be hidden under a drawing (the user's screenshot shows '[o]' beside the drawn box), and with no reliable per-character rect there is no cell to align a drawing to (the same screenshot shows it overlapping the word). What shipped instead is TEXT: the bullet and BOTH brackets hidden so the box stands alone against the left margin -- the user's own requirement, 'when deselecting a line the checkmark should go all to the left border' -- with the glyph at 1.3x, grey when empty and green when ticked. The colour is explicit because GtkSource paints a list marker RED and an empty box must not read as an error. Text aligns by construction; that is the whole argument. The only remaining route to a real widget is a GtkTextChildAnchor, which is a real character in a buffer that IS the .md -- offered to the user, not taken. THIRD ROUND, and the user's own question settled it: 'when clicking on the s in the already rendered [checkbox] sd it will click the checkbox because the line will extend because of the checkbox. but maybe we do not need derendering checkboxes at all?' Both halves are now in. (a) A BOX NO LONGER OPENS UNDER THE CARET, and it is the one construct that should not: row 161's heading marker reveals because you cannot read ## off what it renders, while a box renders its WHOLE state -- empty or ticked is all there is -- and the way to change it is to click it, not to type between the brackets. Opening it only cost: the line grew four columns the moment the caret landed, sliding the words out from under a pointer that had not moved. A SELECTION still shows the source (it is text about to be cut), which needs no special case: there the line is source again, so the branch does not run. (b) THE HIT IS RESOLVED ON THE PRESS and acted on at the release. That is the real fix and it outlives (a): by the time a release arrives the caret has landed and ANY reveal on that line has re-rendered around it, so the words have moved under a pointer that never left -- resolving there aims at whatever slid into that column. Only the layout as it was when the finger came down can say where the finger came down. The release only checks the press has not TRAVELLED (CLICK_SLOP_PX = 5, unrelated to HOLD_SLOP_PX's 16: that one forgives a hand holding a pen for half a second, this one only survives the twitch of a button being let go).

column2: --tmp: a scratch document that closes without a word
column5: Asked for by the user while trying the task boxes: 'add a --tmp commandline feature to create a new file but when closing, dont ask if the file should be saved. just for me to try out new features'. It is a MODIFIER on --new rather than a third kind of document -- on its own it means a blank page (there is nothing else it could mean) and it composes with --new-text for paper -- and a named path beats it exactly as it beats --new, because a file you named is a file you care about. THE FLAG IS ONE PREDICATE, not a special case per close path: _asks_to_save(s) is 'would closing this tab put the question up?', and the tab close, the window close and the autosave all read it. The autosave matters as much as the dialogs -- a throwaway that left a recovery snapshot would nag on the next launch about a page you deliberately threw away, which is the same question arriving by another door. _new_blank_document is the single place a launch flag makes a blank document: it calls the very ☰ menu actions (so the flag cannot drift from the menu item it mirrors) and marks the session they made afterwards, because the mark is a fact about the DOCUMENT and the menu never wants it. The title says 'Untitled (temporary)' so the window itself says the rule. Nothing else in the app ever sets _throwaway: it is a launch-time decision about a blank page, never something a real file can become.

column2: Smoother, free scrolling on the text sheet
column5:
From the user, 2026-08-17, WITH THE SCOPE ALREADY CUT BY THEM: 'maybe just do that for the trackpad. for mice scroll wheel this can be skipped. it should feel similar to scrolling in e.g. browsers.' So this is the TOUCHPAD path only -- Gdk.ScrollUnit.SURFACE, the `smooth` branch of TextPageView._on_sheet_scroll -- and a wheel notch keeps its present instant step (WHEEL_PAN_STEP), which is what a wheel does everywhere else. WHY IT IS OURS TO BUILD AT ALL: the sheet owns its plain scrolling instead of leaving it to the GtkScrolledWindow, because a drawing tool makes the ink overlay the event target and cuts the ScrolledWindow out of the propagation path (the reachability trap) -- so GTK's own kinetic scrolling never runs there, and _on_sheet_scroll sets the adjustment directly: no easing, no momentum, no overscroll. 'Free scrolling' was not pinned down and the reading to confirm with the user is scroll-past-the-end (so the last line can sit mid-screen), which is a separate change from the momentum. Watch the row 150 driver: a zoom already keeps its own float scroll and re-applies it per frame because a GtkAdjustment clamps against the extent of the layout it HAS -- an inertial scroll needs the same treatment or it will fight the clamp at the ends.

SHIPPED 2026-08-17, momentum only. GTK's own kinetic scrolling belongs to the GtkScrolledWindow, which a drawing tool cuts out of the event path -- so the coast is ours: the KINETIC flag on the sheet's own scroll controller, ::decelerate handing over a velocity in px/ms, and KineticGlide driving a tick callback from there (GLIDE_TAU_MS = 325, exponential like a browser, so one flick carries velocity x TAU). THE FLAG IS THE WHOLE OF THE 'TOUCHPAD ONLY' SCOPE the user asked for: GTK emits ::decelerate only after a CONTINUOUS scroll, which is the touchpad and never the wheel, so a notch keeps its instant WHEEL_PAN_STEP with no branch to maintain. Two things that are not obvious. (1) The per-frame step is the INTEGRAL of the decaying velocity across the frame, not v*dt with the decay applied after -- otherwise the same flick travels further at 30 fps than at 60, and a dropped frame under a relayout is exactly when it shows. (2) The end of the document is learnt from the ADJUSTMENT REFUSING TO MOVE, not from measuring the extent (_glide_scroll returns whether it moved): the sheet is a reflow, so its extent is whatever the last layout produced, and row 150 already had to stop trusting it during a zoom. Stops on anything that is a hand: a fresh scroll, a press, a pinch, a programmatic scroll_to_offset. PDF PAGES ARE DELIBERATELY NOT IN THIS, and it is not a parity gap to close quietly: a scroll on the canvas flips the page at a boundary (_handle_boundary_flip), so a momentum glide into one would fling you through slides -- that wants its own judgement in the hand. STILL OPEN, the user's call: scroll-past-the-end (so the last line can sit mid-screen) was the second reading of 'free scrolling' and is a separate change; browsers on Linux do not do it, so it was not built. The notes PANEL beside a PDF is untouched -- GTK scrolls it, since nothing cuts the ScrolledWindow out of the path there.

TOO FAST, FIRST TRY (the user, same day): 'the scrolling is waaay to fast. can't you just copy behaviour from firefox?' The references were then read rather than guessed at, and they say the opposite of what the complaint implies: GtkScrolledWindow decelerates at friction 4/s (tau = 250 ms) and multiplies the velocity GTK reports by 2.5 before it starts (MAGIC_SCROLL_FACTOR), and Firefox's APZ fling friction of 0.002/ms is tau ~ 500 ms -- so the shipped 325 ms was already gentler than every scrolled window on the machine and much gentler than Firefox. THE UNITS ARE NOT THE BUG EITHER: GTK's own documentation for ::decelerate says px/ms, which is what the code assumed. What that leaves is the thing no reference can supply -- a browser's curve is tuned for a page you SKIM, and this is a sheet of A4 you are writing on, where a flick that throws you a screen is a coast you have to chase. Cut to 150 ms, which is roughly half a screen for an ordinary flick. It is one number against one hand, so the fix is not to argue it: SIDEMARK_GLIDE_DEBUG=1 logs each flick's measured velocity and the travel it implies (at WARNING, so the session log survives a clean exit), which turns the next round into arithmetic instead of another guess. UNIT BUG, found 2026-08-18 from the user's report that the sheet was 'really really fast' while the sidebar beside it felt good. `GtkEventControllerScroll::decelerate` is DOCUMENTED as px/ms and is really px/SECOND: GTK computes it as (accumulated delta x 1000) / (last - first event time) over event times in ms, and its own consumer confirms it — GtkScrolledWindow hands the number straight to a kinetic solver whose clock is in seconds and whose friction is per second. Trusting the doc made every flick coast ~1000x too far, bounded only by the end of the document. `GLIDE_VEL_PER_MS` is the conversion and the note. Everything the curve was tuned by before this (325, then 150) was judged against that error and says nothing, so tau is now GtkScrolledWindow's own friction of 4/s = 250 ms: every other scrollable surface in the app IS a plain ScrolledWindow, and one app settles at one rate. What is deliberately NOT copied is the 2.5x `MAGIC_SCROLL_FACTOR` GTK applies to both its drag delta and its flick velocity — the sheet pans a surface delta one-for-one, so scaling the coast to match its own drag is what keeps a flick carrying on at the speed the fingers were moving the sheet. That proportionality, not the absolute number, is the invariant if it is ever retuned. LESSON: the two surfaces read the SAME signal, so when one scrolls unlike the other, suspect what is being READ before the curve. MADE IDENTICAL TO THE SIDEBAR (2026-08-18), on the user's question 'both are usable, how complicated is it to make both the same?'. It was one constant: `SURFACE_SCROLL_FACTOR = 2.5`, which is GtkScrolledWindow's `MAGIC_SCROLL_FACTOR` — a plain ScrolledWindow does NOT pan a touchpad delta one-for-one, it multiplies by 2.5, on the drag AND on the flick velocity. The sheet drives its own scrolling, so it now applies the same number in both places and is pixel-for-pixel the notes panel beside it. The PDF canvas deliberately does not take it: a scroll there flips the page past an edge and `TOUCHPAD_FLIP_THRESHOLD` is hand-tuned against raw 1-px deltas, so scaling them would silently retune how hard you push to turn a slide — a stated exception, not a parity gap. The pair is pinned by one test, since either number alone is only half the feel.

column2: Only what is RIGHT of the cursor falls back to source
column5: From the user, 2026-08-17: 'maybe everything on the right of the cursor should not be rendered, then its easier to mark things when editing but also everything gets rendered while typing.' CLARIFIED BY THEM: 'only right of the cursor in the selected line' and 'yes, prototype in the web first'. So: on the CURSOR LINE only, everything from the caret to the end of the line shows source, everything left of it stays rendered. THE REASON TO PROTOTYPE RATHER THAN BUILD: this inverts row 141's central rule (only what the caret TOUCHES falls back), and row 141 was itself the fix for something worse -- a whole line reverting under a click moved every symbol on it just as you aimed at one. The specific risk to feel is that the TAIL of the line you are editing now re-shapes on every keystroke as the caret advances (each character you type re-renders the expression you just left and un-renders the next), which is the same class of complaint. The upside the user is after is real and is the other half of the same coin: selecting to the end of a line, and seeing text render as you leave it behind. Prototype in web/ (CodeMirror decorations make this a change to one predicate in buildDecorations), judge it by typing a page of real notes, and only then port.

column2: Control-point shapes that stretch when text is inserted through them
column5: From the user, 2026-08-17: 'in text mode, structures with controll points (lines, polygons, circles etc) should be scaled when lines are added inbetween. e.g for a vertical line over several [lines]' -- and, asked how to proceed: 'different options could be prototyped first, so I can try them out. especially how the freehand would feel.' WHY IT IS NOT SMALL: a stroke has ONE anchor (a GtkTextMark plus per-point pixel offsets at a font size), so everything moves RIGIDLY, and that is deliberate -- row 162's line_map exists because ink moving non-rigidly TORE A DRAWING APART (measured: 29 real strokes, 23 changed paragraph, 161 px of spread). The four candidates to prototype, which is the actual ask: (A) today, one mark, rigid. (B) TWO-POINT -- first and last vertex get their own marks and the rest interpolate, so a vertical line spanning five text lines becomes six lines long. (C) PER-VERTEX -- every control point its own mark; follows the text exactly and can turn a rectangle into a trapezoid when text is inserted past only one corner. (D) BOX -- the bbox's top and bottom anchor and everything scales in y, which is the only one that touches FREEHAND. The user's own phrasing ('structures with control points') already excludes freehand from the default, and D is the one to feel.

column2: Draw while scrolling (the pen keeps its place in the document)
column5: From the user, 2026-08-17: 'I want to draw while scrolling. (mainly in text first mode). the drawing should be anchored to the position in the document when scrolled away. (so I could draw a line with just scrolling and holding the pen) similar behaviour to other tools when applicable, also for pdf mode' -- and, asked which gesture: 'i mean scroll while pen is down'. So it is the WHEEL/TOUCHPAD during a live stroke, not edge auto-scroll (that is a separate idea and was not asked for). THE TWO MODES ARE NOT THE SAME JOB. PDF is nearly free: current_stroke is already in PDF coords (_screen_to_pdf), so panning mid-stroke already keeps the ink where it was drawn -- what is missing is letting a scroll through while a drag holds the gesture. One thing to decide there: ink is PER PAGE, so a stroke cannot cross a page flip, and a scroll that would turn the page has to stop at the boundary while the pen is down. TEXT IS A REFACTOR: current_stroke is in OVERLAY coords and is only converted at commit (_anchor_stroke_at), so scrolling mid-stroke slides the whole stroke. The live stroke has to be kept in buffer coords with the painter converting back, which touches live smoothing and prediction (both read overlay coords) -- use _overlay_to_buffer_f, never the int-truncating helpers, or every point rounds.

column2: A snapped ellipse stays resizable while the pen is still down
column5:
From the user, 2026-08-17: 'when drawing a circle/oval and regognized and hoding, the circle should be resizable.' The pattern already exists for the other kinds: after the dwell fires, the pen keeps hold of the LAST control point of a line/path/polygon (index 0 for a closed ring) and every corner polyline on the page becomes a live magnet for it (row 127, _live_snap_shapes). An ellipse has no vertices -- it is a sampled curve, 24+ points, deliberately excluded from shape_vertices -- so the verb has to be its own: the drag sets the semi-axes and the shape is re-sampled each motion event from centre + axes. Both surfaces, one shared helper, like every other snap decision (recognize_shape / rect_bbox_of / SNAP_LABELS). A near-circle must still snap to a true circle while being resized, or the dwell's own answer changes under the hand.

SHIPPED 2026-08-17. The verb: the whole shape scales about the centre the dwell found, by how much further out the pen has travelled ALONG ITS RAY (ellipse_resize_state / resized_ellipse in sidemark.py, ported to web/src/shapes.js; both surfaces call it from the same _straight_mode branch that drags a held control point). Three decisions worth keeping. (1) UNIFORM, not per-axis: the dwell has already answered what shape this is, and pulling one axis would let a circle turn back into an oval while you were only making it bigger -- which also satisfies the row's own requirement that a near-circle stay a true circle for free, since the CIRCLE_TOLERANCE test is a ratio and so is scale-invariant. (2) The state records the PEN's own distance from the centre at the dwell, so the first motion event scales by exactly 1: a shape that re-settles under a hand which has not moved is the dwell changing its own answer, the same defect the row 160 anchor exists to prevent. (3) sample_ellipse now rounds the sample count up to a MULTIPLE OF FOUR. Nothing here stores geometry -- centre and axes are re-read off the ring, the rect_bbox_of pattern -- and off a multiple of four the ring misses the extremes, so the box is a hair small and its centre a hair off, which is exactly a jump on the first event (caught by the test, not by reading). The label anchor moved into snap_label_anchor() so a resized shape carries its glyph along. A rectangle and a grid divider stay frozen: only the ellipse gained a verb. NOT DONE: the web has the same maths under vector test (extras/export_shape_vectors.py exports the resize cases) and the same six lines of wiring, but no surface-level gesture test there.

STRETCH, NOT JUST RESIZE (the user, same day): 'the ellipse was supposed to be stretchable in both directions: y and x. so not just resize but changing the ratio.' The uniform scale was shipped on the argument that the dwell has already answered what shape this is and a per-axis pull would let a circle become an oval again -- the user's answer is that becoming an oval again is the POINT, and the verb they expected is the one every other selected shape already has: a box handle. So each axis now takes its own factor, from how much further out the pen has travelled ALONG THAT AXIS: sideways widens, down heightens, the corner does both. What survives of the old argument is circle_axes having the LAST WORD, applied to the result: inside its 12% tolerance a circle stays a circle under a shaking hand, and past it you get the oval you were plainly asking for. Ceiling: that tolerance is a dead zone around square, so the very flattest ovals are unreachable FROM a circle -- lift and draw one. THE ONE THING PER-AXIS NEEDS THAT UNIFORM DID NOT is a LEVER test (ELLIPSE_LEVER_MIN = 0.25 of that semi-axis): the factor is the pen's offset from the centre divided by what it was at the dwell, so an axis the pen was sitting ON divides by nearly zero and a pixel of hand tremor becomes a large factor -- a circle snapped at its equator would flatten the instant it moved. Such an axis FOLLOWS the other, which is exactly the uniform scale and the only honest reading of a pull with no arm to pull on; with the pen deep inside the shape and off both axes there is no ratio information at all, so it falls back to the radial pull. Recording the pen's OFFSET rather than its distance is what keeps the no-jump property on BOTH axes. Note the exported vectors needed new cases to be worth anything: every existing one rests on the x axis, where one axis can only follow the other, so the branch that matters was never run by the port's conformance suite.

column2: Nextcloud: open the .pdf/.md/-ink.json triple from a Nextcloud
column5: From the user, 2026-08-17: 'sidemark nextcloud integration? for the online version mainly' and then 'is there some kind of link sharing from within nextcloud to an external app? or maybe create a nextcloud extension/app to open files in the sidemark web version? what would be the simplest way? maybe first without writing. just read the pdf,md,json from nextcloud into sidemark?' ONE FACT DECIDES THE SHAPE OF THIS, and it is not a matter of taste: Nextcloud sends restrictive CORS headers, so a browser app on github.io cannot read WebDAV from a Nextcloud server AT ALL -- not read-only, not a public share link (nextcloud/server issue 3131). Two routes follow. (1) SHIP THE WEB BUILD AS A NEXTCLOUD APP: same origin so CORS vanishes, session auth for free (no OAuth, no secret, which also means no change to how the static site is deployed for everyone else), read AND write over WebDAV, and a registered file action puts 'Open in Sidemark' on a .pdf in Files. Costs a small PHP app skeleton and app-store packaging. (2) STAY ON GITHUB PAGES and require the existing WebAppPassword app (digital-blueprint/webapppassword), which exists for exactly this: it issues a temporary app password and sets the CORS headers with an origin allow-list. Near-zero work for us, but EVERY user must install and configure a server app first. Route 1 is the recommendation -- the server-side step is ours to do once instead of each user's to do for ever -- and read-only is the right first slice either way. STILL UNANSWERED and it decides between them: is this for the user's own instance, or for anyone with a Nextcloud?

column2: Why text mode keeps breaking: the GTK seam, not the model
column5:
AGREED WITH THE USER 2026-08-18, to be done as ONE session — the full plan is notes/text-mode-parity-plan.md and the diagnosis in it is not to be re-derived. The user asked why text-first mode keeps having hiccups (Ctrl+F dead, the thumb button, two-finger zoom, the scroll transition) and whether the fix is a translation layer to a unified model, or a new model for text mode. ANSWER, from the actual causes rather than the symptoms: not one of those was a model disagreement — every one was a seam with GTK (a widget in the hidden column; button 10 never reaching a GestureDrag; a GestureZoom starved by our own claim; the Viewport's scroll-to-focus; the TextView's built-in gchararray drop target; the ScrolledWindow that owns kinetic scrolling never seeing the event; and the 2026-08-14 abort, which was get_iter_at_location itself). So NO translation layer and NO new text model: the model is already unified where the decisions live (Bindings, the ink pipeline, the lasso geometry, the clipboard, the shape recogniser), and row 116 showed everything reusing them held parity. The difference is the SUBSTRATE — PDFCanvas is a canvas we author top to bottom and nothing else wants its events, while TextPageView is a GtkTextView inside a Viewport inside a ScrolledWindow, three widgets that already implement a text editor and compete for every press, scroll and focus change. Measured: ~3,300 lines re-doing over a foreign substrate what PDFCanvas does in ~4,900, both independently wiring the SAME eight controller types. The web port is not counter-evidence: it has no text-first mode at all, its sheet is the notes panel widened with no ink, so the hard case does not exist there — what IS worth stealing is one Surface class with docMode as a parameter, and the DOM having no claim race. THE THREE, in order, each a safety net for the next: (1) finish and STATE the adapter rule — the sheet never calls a raw GtkTextView geometry/iter API, each is wrapped once with its trap (iter_at_buffer_xy, _overlay_to_buffer_f, _buf_replace_line, _set_buffer_text, line_bounds are already members); (2) a parity matrix test, behaviours x {pdf, text}, driven at the WINDOW level because every bug above except the crash was a correct handler that could not be REACHED, with a one-sided entry failing rather than skipping; (3) one input front-end for the sheet — and the catch is that you cannot decide late, since GTK gives no way to hand a press TO another widget after looking at it, so merely unifying our own controllers still negotiates and leaves the seam. The version that matches PDF mode is to CLAIM EVERY PRESS and implement the caret as a tool like the pen: the TextView keeps laying out, drawing and taking keystrokes, and stops handling the pointer. Much of that is DELETION of code that exists to undo GTK's version (the triple-click idle denies the view's own selection drag, row 128's caret-jump fix, _reopen_context_menu). ~300-500 lines; risk in what cannot be tested headlessly (IME and dead keys, touch selection handles, accessibility), so it needs the panel in the user's hands. Rows 150 and 151 fall out of it for free, both being decisions AT the router. NOT fixed by any of this, and not to be unified away: the sheet is a reflowing editor, so ink anchors to marks and there is no page structure there.

DONE 2026-08-18, all three levers in one session as agreed. (1) THE ADAPTER RULE is stated in code above `iter_at_buffer_xy` and in CLAUDE.md: the sheet and the notes view never call a TRAPPED GtkTextView geometry/iter API raw, each trapped one is wrapped once with its trap in the docstring, and the sweep's NEGATIVE results are recorded beside it (get_iter_location, get_line_at_y, get_line_yrange, forward_display_line, get_iter_at_line) so nobody re-investigates them. The sweep found one live class of bug: five buf.get_text() calls read the buffer WITHOUT hidden characters while deriving their range from iters that count them, so a marker beside a rendered symbol came back short and quietly stopped matching — latent, because a SELECTED line shows source and that is when those paths run. (2) THE PARITY MATRIX (TestModeParityMatrix) drives eight behaviours in both modes at the window level, asserting PATHS and not pixels — is the widget in a visible ancestor chain, is the controller first, is the press routed, does the surface answer the key the window asks it. A behaviour absent from one mode must be declared with NotInMode(reason); today the only one is coasting on a PDF page. Two cells were verified by reintroducing the bug they exist for (the Ctrl+F container and the drop target) and both fired in both modes. The matrix found a trap on its first run that was in the ASSERTION, not the app: observe_controllers() lists controllers in REVERSE add order, so 'the touch latch is attached FIRST' tests the exact opposite of the invariant if you read the list as it comes — the latch's controller is now marked (_touch_latch) so the ordering can be asserted at all, which matters because it is an invariant that shipped dead twice and was previously only a docstring. (3) THE CARET IS A TOOL. The sheet's router now claims EVERY press — for a tool, for the caret, or for nothing when the chord is unbound — and never denies. caret_press/caret_motion/caret_release on MarkdownNotesView are the pointer half of a text editor written out: click places, drag selects, double takes the word, triple takes the LOGICAL line, Shift extends from the anchor, release ticks a task box or follows a Ctrl+link, and a selection drag autoscrolls. The reason it must be written out is that GTK offers no way to hand a press on after looking at it, so 'inspect the press then decide' and 'let the TextView do the caret' are mutually exclusive — deny-and-hope was the seam every text-mode input bug came through. Deliberately the SAME verbs GTK implements: a caret that behaves NEARLY like every other caret is worse than one that behaves unlike them. The click count is summed by hand because GTK4 dropped the DOUBLE/TRIPLE_BUTTON_PRESS event types and a second gesture would be cancelled by the router's claim; it reads the user's own gtk-double-click-time/-distance rather than a hardcoded pair. CONSEQUENCES, all deliberate: the paper-edge width drag became a BRANCH of the caret's tool because a second gesture on that widget can no longer see a press; the right-button context menu is opened by hand; an unbound chord no longer falls through to the editor to move the caret, which now matches a PDF page and what the toolbar's empty stripe has always promised. Row 150's leftover is closed BY CONSTRUCTION — the TextView never takes the first sequence, so its touch selection bubble cannot appear under a pinch. New ceiling in its place: our caret tool draws no touch selection handles, so a finger selecting text on the sheet has nothing to grab afterwards, and nobody has judged whether that is worse than the bubble it replaces. Row 151 (a survivor finger keeps panning) was NOT built — it is a decision, not arithmetic, and belongs to the user. NOT VERIFIED IN THE HAND and owed a session with the panel: every gesture above, IME and dead keys (keyboard-side, so expected untouched — verify, do not assume), touch selection, and accessibility. There is no key-injection tool on this machine.

column2: Phone as a remote drawing/input device (network ink transport)
column5: IDEA (2026-08-31, user-initiated): use a phone's touchscreen as a remote graphics tablet for Sidemark - draw on the phone, ink appears live on the desktop's PDF/text page, without needing to zoom in on a laptop trackpad. Distinct from handwriting RECOGNITION (row 183): this is pure stroke TRANSPORT and stands on its own even with no recognition ever built - 'draw from across the room / with a real touch surface when the desktop has none'. Chosen by the user as the FIRST of four ideas surfaced from an investigation into MyScript's SDK (myscript.com/sdk - text/math/diagram recognition demos, plus a 'superimposed characters' mode built for smartwatches/IoT where a keyboard doesn't fit), over the sequencing this session originally recommended (build recognition first against existing local pen input, since it needs no new transport to validate). ARCHITECTURE SKETCH: a lightweight local HTTP server embedded in Sidemark (stdlib http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer, no new dependency for the prototype) serves one page to the phone's browser - a full-viewport canvas using Pointer Events, batching points and POSTing them back. The desktop side must NEVER touch GTK from the server's request-handling thread (it is not the main loop) - every point is marshalled across with GLib.idle_add, the same discipline row 169's watchdog thread already uses for exactly this reason. Points arrive normalized (0..1 per axis) and are mapped onto the CURRENT VIEW (absolute tablet mapping - the whole phone screen corresponds to whatever is on screen right now, zoomed in or not), not onto the whole document, which is what makes it behave like a tablet rather than a second mouse. Reuses the real pipeline, never reimplements it: finish_ink_stroke/live_ink_stroke/draw_ink_stroke are the same functions a local stylus stroke goes through (rows 139/143) - a remote stroke is just a new SOURCE of points, not a new kind of ink. OPEN QUESTIONS, none decided yet: security (the prototype's only guard is an unguessable token in the URL path - fine for a home LAN, not vetted for anything public; a real pairing flow, e.g. a QR code with a short-lived token, is likely needed before this ships), latency feel over a real LAN (unmeasured - row 147's method applies: measure before tuning), whether pressure is even meaningful from a touchscreen finger (most phones report a flat ~0.5 for touch, so the taper/width profile may end up closer to the mouse's flat case than the stylus's), and how the connection is started/stopped in the real app (the prototype starts/stops manually; the real feature needs UI chrome and a lifecycle - start only on request, torn down with the window). PROTOTYPE (2026-08-31): extras/phone_remote_prototype.py - a standalone script (not wired into sidemark.py) that serves the page, receives points, and draws them into a minimal GTK/cairo window using the real sidemark.py ink functions, so the transport and the feel can be judged before anything touches the real app. See its docstring for how to run it. REVISED DESIGN (2026-09-01), after building the prototype and stepping back from the first framing: this ships as its OWN feature ('Draw from phone', a new menu entry), not unified into Share to phone as the first draft of this row proposed. Two reasons: Share to phone's mental model (a presenter showing OTHERS a live view, now including a public Tailscale Funnel link as of the 76fed5d commit) is wrong for what this actually is - one person drawing into their own document - and defaulting a feature that MUTATES the document to a public-internet-reachable link would be an unsafe default. Draw-from-phone therefore never offers a Funnel/public option, only LAN and Tailscale (private). No permission switch either - connecting to the URL IS the grant, since there is no audience to gate. No new 'connected' indicator widget - drawn ink appearing live is the feedback for a solo user, matching the minimal-UI-chrome lesson from Share's own '.success'-tinted button (no separate banner). THIS PASS ships the core loop only: phone shows the current page (the whole page for a PDF, the live visible viewport for a text sheet), one-finger drag draws with the desktop's CURRENT pen settings regardless of what tool the desktop's own left button is bound to, a plain Pen/Eraser toggle on the phone covers erasing, both PDF and text-first pages are supported (this app's 'both modes, always' rule - a text sheet has no reason to be excluded). DEFERRED, not abandoned - logged here so they are not lost: (1) an INDEPENDENT phone-side camera (two-finger pinch decouples the phone's own pan/zoom from the desktop's current view, so the phone's small screen can zoom in for precision without disturbing the desktop) plus a dashed indicator rectangle drawn on the desktop page showing where that camera currently is - designed in full (a {cx,cy,scale} camera in document units for PDFCanvas; a Gtk.TextMark-anchored buffer offset for TextPageView, since raw overlay pixels shift on scroll and cannot anchor a stable independent view on their own) but not yet built; (2) multiple phones drawing simultaneously - this pass targets one phone at a time even though a phone can still just VIEW via the separate Share feature with others; (3) a long-press tool picker (colors, width) on the phone beyond the plain Pen/Eraser toggle; (4) a 'typewriter' character-by-character input mode where the camera auto-advances after each glyph (ties to row 184's superimposed-character idea). REVISED AGAIN (2026-09-01, same session): the 'separate feature' design above shipped, then the user reversed it after seeing it in the header - 'no, now there is a draw button and a qr button, it should both live under the qr button... a toggle if sharing or writing should be active. both should automatically use the best mode of the three (public, tailscale, wifi only) so no separate infrastructure there.' This is a deliberate reversal of the safety argument two revisions up (never let a document-mutating feature default to a public link) - stated back to the user explicitly before building it, and accepted knowingly: viewing and drawing are now ONE _ShareServer/_Handler/dialog, and whichever address tier is picked (including the public Tailscale Funnel link) carries write access whenever the dialog's Sharing/Writing toggle is set to Writing. _DrawServer and its standalone menu entry/window/state are DELETED - _ShareServer gained drawing_allowed (default False, i.e. Sharing) plus a do_POST /ink route reusing _process_remote_touch and the map_point/ink_actions providers unchanged from the deleted class. _on_share_to_phone's guard was generalized off its old PDF-only canvas.document check to also cover a text-first page (row 182's 'both modes, always' requirement doesn't disappear just because the entry point merged), reusing TextPageView.render_snapshot_png for the phone mirror and _write_text_pdf for the Download button in that mode. The header's live indicator ALSO moved: it was a separate _draw_btn with its own pulsing dot+label, now merged onto _share_btn itself (_update_share_indicator does the content-swap that _set_draw_indicator used to) - one button, one indicator, matching the 'both live under the qr button' instruction literally. The ☰ menu keeps exactly one entry, 'Share to phone…', covering both. Everything else from the previous revision is unchanged: PDFCanvas/TextPageView's remote_stroke_*/remote_erase_*/remote_abort methods, _process_remote_touch's one-finger-draws/two-fingers-abort rule, and the deferred list (independent phone-side camera + indicator rectangle, multiple phones at once, long-press tool picker, character-by-character typewriter mode). TWO BUGS FOUND IN THE HAND (2026-09-01): (1) the phone's local preview stroke was cleared the instant a finger lifted (up()), on the assumption the real committed image would arrive almost instantly - it didn't (the poll loop only checks every 1500ms), so ink visibly vanished and only reappeared up to ~2s later. Fixed: the clear now happens in the img 'load' handler, once the real rendered stroke has actually arrived, and lifting a finger triggers an immediate re-poll (scheduleTick(150)) rather than waiting out the rest of the interval; a CANCELLED touch still clears immediately since nothing is coming to replace it. (2) touch-action:pinch-zoom was tried as a cheap stand-in for the deferred camera (letting one finger draw, two fingers use native browser pinch-zoom) and made things WORSE, not just zoom-less: in the hand, the browser did not cleanly split the two gestures - a single-finger drag was ALSO treated as pannable, scrolling the whole page (toolbar included) out of view, and a gesture the browser decides to pan is delivered as pointercancel rather than pointerup - which never commits ink at all (see (1)'s fix). REVERTED to touch-action:none + user-scalable=no (no zoom, but drawing works). Lesson: this is exactly the reconciliation problem that made the independent camera a deferred, deliberately-designed feature rather than a quick CSS property - don't try touch-action:pinch-zoom again without building real state (or a phone/emulator to test against; neither was available this session). DIALOG REWORKED (2026-09-01), on request, after the user flagged the dialog as 'too full': the instruction paragraph shrank from four lines to one ('Scan with your phone's camera.'); the Public/Tailscale/Wi-Fi choice moved from an always-visible 3-way Gtk.StackSwitcher (equal visual weight to the Sharing/Writing toggle, despite usually not being a decision at all - it already auto-picks the best reachable option) to a compact Gtk.DropDown that only expands when clicked; the QR grew from 160x160 to 220x220, since it is the one thing that cannot be smaller; and 'Stop sharing' lost its destructive-action (red) styling - nothing is lost by stopping, so treating it as equivalent to a delete overstated the action and fought the adjacent X for attention. The Sharing/Writing toggle keeps its prominence, being the one control that's a real decision most sessions. SHIPPED (2026-09-01), the phone now runs the REAL BROWSER PORT instead of a bespoke image-and-touch page, and the QR links straight to it. INVESTIGATION FIRST (notes/phone-web-port-sync-plan.md holds the numbers): the hosted GitHub Pages copy CANNOT reach a desktop privately, measured in Chromium 151 against a real stand-in server. Two INDEPENDENT walls, not one: mixed content (an https page may not open ws:// or http://), and Local Network Access (net::ERR_BLOCKED_BY_LOCAL_NETWORK_ACCESS_CHECKS), which treats the TAILNET 100.64/10 as local too. TLS does NOT lift the second - tested with a real cert and permissive CORS including Access-Control-Allow-Private-Network, still blocked, and a CDP permission grant did not help either. And a LAN address can never satisfy mixed content at all, because no CA issues a cert for 192.168.x.x. Only the public Funnel tier could work, which would have INVERTED the safety story (the one transport that works being the public one). So the answer is same-origin: the desktop SERVES the port. Nothing inverts - the phone stays a client and the desktop stays a server - which retires web/CLAUDE.md's 'a browser tab cannot listen on a socket' as the obstacle it was thought to be: the tab still does not listen. WHAT SHIPPED: _ShareServer serves web/ under its own token path (/<token>/app/, gzip + ETag, path-traversal guarded, HTTP/1.1 keep-alive because the port is 31 requests); /<token>/ 302-redirects to app/?live=1, so scanning the QR opens the editor with no landing page in between. _SHARE_VIEWER_HTML SURVIVES as the fallback for exactly two real cases - a TEXT-FIRST page (the port has no text mode) and an installed copy with no web/ - and web/ is now packaged by install.sh and both PKGBUILDs, which it never was. THE DOCUMENT: live.pdf is save_copy, NOT the 'pdf' provider behind the Download button - that one is the baked export with notes flattened onto the pages, which would reach the phone as a picture of ink that nothing can erase or undo; the port's readInk adopts real annotations into editable strokes. LAZY BY PAGE: page.pdf?n=N serves ONE page sliced from the same per-revision copy, and Doc.attachLazyPages fetches others as they are reached - measured on a 60-page deck, 535.8 KB -> 9.2 KB for a first paint, and visiting two pages fetched two pages and never the whole file. TRANSPORT: a hand-rolled stdlib WebSocket (_WSConn) at /<token>/ws - masked client frames, three payload-length encodings, continuation frames, all three silent if wrong. Each connection has its OWN sender thread with frame coalescing, because the desktop's live stroke is pushed from the motion handler on the GTK main thread and a socket write to a phone out of wifi would freeze the app under the hand that is drawing. BOTH DIRECTIONS ARE LIVE: the phone streams raw document-coordinate samples (the port knows the real page geometry, which is exactly what lets it draw under a zoom the desktop knows nothing about - map_point is identity here, and this is what dissolves the deferred camera problem rather than solving it), and the desktop mirrors its own in-progress stroke back, painted on the phone on top of the cached layer like its own live stroke. ON COMMIT the desktop pushes THAT PAGE'S STROKES AS JSON rather than the whole PDF - re-serialising cost ~500 ms plus a re-parse on the phone for every single stroke. The delta REPLACES rather than merges and needs no reconciliation, because the desktop's list is the whole truth for a page (ink the phone drew is in it, having been committed there); a structural change is the exception the phone detects from the page count and answers with a full reload. Pushes SKIP the connection that caused them (ink_origin, parked on the server for the duration of one main-thread apply), or drawing would reload the document under the hand that drew. THE BUG WORTH REMEMBERING: phone->laptop ink died PERMANENTLY and stayed dead until reload. The port nulls `active` in several places OUTSIDE _onUp (converting a circle to a lasso, a second finger starting a pinch), so the stream's close never fired, the pointer id stayed in _process_remote_touch's `active` for ever, and its two-finger rule latched `blocked` on the next stroke. Fixed on BOTH sides on purpose: the client closes from a catch-all in _onUp, and the server treats a new gesture id as implicitly ending the old one - a transport must not be one client bug away from wedging itself. ALSO: the phone reports its viewport and the desktop draws it as a dashed rectangle (deferred item 1's indicator, now free because the phone has a real camera), and the mobile layout is a body class - binding stripes hidden (one finger, one answer), sidebar and notes collapsed, presenter and Download in the hamburger, open/save hidden in a shared session on ANY device, and in landscape the toolbar becomes a rail down the left so the page keeps the height (--header-h is overridden there, which is what everything floating under the header measures from). STILL DEFERRED: multiple phones at once, a long-press tool picker, and the typewriter mode (row 184). EXTENDED (2026-09-01, same session). A PHONE-VIEW TOOL: draw a region (ctrl+shift+left, PDF only) and the connected phone goes there; grab the dashed rectangle showing where it is looking and drag it and the phone follows LIVE, not on release. The design is the user's own correction of two options offered: there is ONE box — the indicator that already says where the phone is — so the tool writes to the same state the phone does and neither owns it. After a move the box is where the phone is because that is where it went, and the phone stays free to pinch away, at which point its own reports drive the box again. No separate lifetime, no lock, no second rectangle. A CLICK sends it back to the whole page (the escape zoom-to-region already has), and the whole-page box paints nothing, since a rectangle around everything says nothing. The button is in the bar only while a share is live (_sync_phone_tool_chrome; and hidden at CONSTRUCTION too, because a GTK widget is visible by default and _update_header_for_mode does not necessarily run before the window is shown), and the chord is INERT without a share — the binding stays in the table, because a chord that vanished when you stopped sharing would be exactly the second mapping row 132 forbids. The phone's own reports are ignored while the box is being dragged here: they are a round trip behind, so accepting one mid-drag makes the rectangle stutter between the hand and the phone. WRITE-AND-ADVANCE tuning (row 187) and the mobile layout are described there and above. THE DIALOG'S TOGGLE now defaults to WRITING (the user's call): the phone is overwhelmingly a tablet for your own document, so starting read-only meant flipping the same switch every session. 'Sharing' is renamed 'Read only', 'Public' is 'Public link', the two lines that said the same thing are one, and a ? explains when each address works — including that guest wifi and eduroam block device-to-device traffic in a way that looks exactly like a bad QR code. REFINED IN THE HAND (2026-09-01, a long session on a real Pixel). ONE PHONE DRAWS AT A TIME: the canvas has a single current_stroke, so two phones drawing interleaved into one corrupted line (A's begin, B's begin resetting it, A's next point landing on B's stroke, one commit for both — reproduced in a log). A connection now holds the pen for a gesture and a second phone's ink is dropped; a phone that vanishes mid-stroke releases it, or it would lock everyone out for good. A VIEWPORT BOX PER PHONE: one shared slot meant two phones overwrote each other and the rectangle flickered between them, describing neither. Dragging one box moves THAT phone (pointing one person at something must not drag everyone else off what they were reading); drawing a region points them all. THE GRAB AND THE PAINTER READ ONE LIST (visible_remote_rects): a phone looking at the whole page has a box covering it, deliberately not drawn — and while the grab had its own hit test that invisible box swallowed every press, so a region could not be drawn at all until every phone happened to be zoomed in. Same painter/hit-test drift the lasso frame documents, new place. MODIFIER KEYS CAN REACH THE PHONE (opt-in, remembered): hold a modifier on the laptop and the phone's finger follows the same binding table, resolved on the DESKTOP because a copy of that table on the phone is what row 132 forbids. Only pen/highlighter/eraser have remote verbs, so a modifier bound to lasso or pan is ignored rather than half honoured — which also makes the default case right, since `finger` is bound to pan and the phone simply keeps drawing. MOBILE: 100dvh (html height 100% resolves against the LARGE viewport, so the bottom strip of the page sat below the visible area and could not be reached), a fullscreen button beside the hamburger in landscape plus the menu entry (Android only — Safari implements requestFullscreen for video and nothing else; Add to Home Screen is the iOS route and the meta tags for it are in), and lazily fetched pages are EVICTED to a window of 8: each is a whole pdf.js document whose memory lives in the WORKER, so the leak was invisible in performance.memory and would end as a killed tab. A BROWSER THAT DIES LEAVES A RECORD NOW: the server logs every request with its user agent (independent of the phone's JS, which is the point — a browser that dies before running a line of ours still made requests), and the phone posts breadcrumbs to /diag with a keepalive fetch rather than sendBeacon, which Brave neutralises by returning TRUE and discarding. Routine breadcrumbs are INFO; only errors warn, after 242 heartbeat lines buried the two that mattered. BUG, reported and fixed 2026-09-08: with 'Link the phone's tool to this computer' ON, NO stroke drawn on the phone ever arrived on a PDF. _apply_remote_ink_actions resolved the held modifiers as `canvas.get_held_mods()` — but get_held_mods is a TextPageView callback (set on `tp` when the sheet is built) and a PDFCanvas has never had one, so the guard `if canvas.get_held_mods` was itself the AttributeError, raised before a single verb was dispatched. The transport was fine throughout; the ink died one call short of the canvas. Now the window's own _finger_tool_now() is used, which is where the held modifiers are actually tracked (_held_mods) AND is the same function _push_share_tool sends to the phone — so the tool the phone displays and the tool the desktop applies are one answer rather than two computations that can disagree, which is the same rule that keeps the binding table off the phone. WHY THE SUITE MISSED IT, which is the more useful half: TestShareModifiers tested apply_modifier_tool and Bindings.tool_for in ISOLATION and they were always correct — the bug was in the wiring that calls them, exactly the proxy-assertion trap. TestApplyRemoteInkActions passed self=None, so getattr(self, '_share_modifiers', False) was False and the branch never ran; and a mock.Mock() canvas would not have caught it either, since a Mock grows whatever attribute you ask it for. The regression tests use a REAL PDFCanvas and a duck-typed window with the link ON, and all three fail on the old code. SECOND BUG, same session: opening the QR on a phone showed a BLANK page until you pinched, and page turns stalled for a beat. Root cause was Surface.fit() against a container that has no size yet — `(0 - 48) / 595` is a perfectly good NEGATIVE number, so the zoom went negative, _renderScale asked pdf.js for a negative viewport, doc.render clamped it to a 1px canvas rather than throwing, and draw() refuses to blit a bitmap that narrow — white page. Worse, the dud was CACHED under _pageKey, so nothing re-rendered until a gesture happened to change the scale, which is precisely the reported 'blank until I zoom in a bit'. Three fixes, each of which stands alone: (1) fit() refuses a box under 1px and leaves _fitPending set instead of inventing a view, clamps the margin to the box (a narrow column is a small page, not an inverted one) and floors the zoom at MIN_ZOOM; (2) draw()'s owed re-fit moved OUT of the canvas-resize branch — it was only paid when the canvas happened to change size, so a fit owed while the canvas was already right was never paid at all; (3) _renderPage renders into a PRIVATE canvas per pass and swaps it in only if that pass still wins, and never caches a degenerate result — one shared buffer meant a slower earlier render could finish last and overwrite the bitmap the key claims is on screen. SMOOTHNESS, asked for in the same message: a page with nothing on screen now renders a small PREVIEW_SIDE bitmap first and replaces it with the full-scale one when that lands, so a page sharpens instead of appearing — skipped when the page is already showing, where the bitmap in hand is the better placeholder and dropping to a soft one would be a visible step backwards, and skipped when the full render is already small enough that the preview would be the same work twice. And Doc.prefetchPage warms the neighbours on every page turn, which is what actually fixes the stall: in live mode a turn costs a round trip to the desktop before a pixel can be rasterised, and reading is overwhelmingly sequential. It restores _lastPage synchronously, because that is what _evictLazyPages treats as 'here' and a prefetch that moved it would evict the neighbours of a page nobody is looking at; a no-op when the whole document is already local. web/test/render.mjs covers all of it — 9 of its 38 checks fail on the old code.

column2: Stroke-based handwriting recognition (ink to text)
column5: IDEA (2026-08-31): recognize a finished ink stroke sequence as text and feed it into the Markdown notes / a text layer, instead of leaving handwriting as an opaque pixel blob. Surfaced alongside rows 182/184/185 from an investigation into MyScript's SDK; NOT MyScript itself (commercial, doesn't fit a project distributed as free software with optional deps, like ocrmypdf is today - row 4). The recommendation from that investigation, still unimplemented: prefer an ONLINE recognizer (one that reads the stroke SEQUENCE - order, direction, speed, timing - the same data finish_ink_stroke already has) over an OFFLINE/image-based one (Tesseract, TrOCR) that only sees a rendered picture and has to re-derive what the pen already told us for free; online beats image-based on both accuracy and cost here, not just one. Leading candidate: Google's Digital Ink Recognition models (small per-language .tflite files, free, offline, fast on CPU) loaded through a generic TFLite runtime OUTSIDE the official Android/iOS SDK - NOT YET VERIFIED that this is legally and practically usable standalone; that check is the very next step before committing to it. Tesseract (already an optdepend via ocrmypdf) was ruled out for handwriting specifically - fine for neat block printing, weak on cursive. TrOCR-class transformer models were ruled out as the default path: real accuracy gain on messy cursive, but pull in torch/transformers (hundreds of MB, seconds/line on CPU) for a project with zero ML dependencies today, and they throw away the stroke data Sidemark already has. Follows the OCR pattern (row 4): an OPTIONAL external tool/dependency, gated behind its presence, never bundled. Use cases that justify it (see row 185 for a related but separate idea): (1) SEARCH reaches ink - today Ctrl+F only searches the Markdown notes, and anything drawn by hand is invisible to it; (2) CONVERT TO TEXT - lasso-select ink, get real editable Markdown text out of it, so it can participate in linking/task boxes/math like typed text does; (3) an exported PDF's handwritten annotations gain a text layer, mirroring what OCR already does for scanned printed pages; (4) MATH specifically ties into the existing live-Markdown math grammar (\alpha, scripts) - draw an equation, recognize it into the same command/script syntax the notes panel already renders live. Deliberately NOT: training a model from the user's own handwriting from scratch (discussed and set aside - collecting enough labelled data yourself is a lot of work for uncertain payoff; fine-tuning a pretrained model afterward is the more realistic path if a pretrained baseline disappoints). SEQUENCING NOTE: this needs NO new transport to validate - it can and should be built/tested against the app's existing local pen/mouse input before row 182's phone transport is involved at all; the two are additive, not sequential dependencies of each other. GATE ANSWERED, 2026-09-02, and the answer is NO on BOTH halves -- do not design around ML Kit. LEGALLY: the digital-ink models are not published anywhere as files (not on Kaggle Models/TF Hub, which is where Google's open models live), have no standalone licence and no redistribution grant; they are fetched at runtime by ML Kit's own RemoteModelManager and governed by the ML Kit Terms of Service, which say 'you may not reverse engineer or attempt to extract the source code or any related software'. Extracting them is exactly the prohibited act, so this cannot be the optional-dependency pattern row 4 uses -- Tesseract is Apache-2.0 and distro-packaged, these are proprietary blobs a free-software project would be shipping instructions to obtain in breach of their terms. PRACTICALLY it fails independently, so a licence change alone would not rescue it: the SDK is Android/iOS only, there is no Linux or Python distribution channel at all, and a model is ~20 MB PER LANGUAGE. It is also not one .tflite you can hand to an interpreter -- the only reverse-engineering precedent (michaellee8/google-ml-kit-reverse-engineering, and it covers TEXT recognition, not digital ink, which nobody has done) shows a BUNDLE: protobuf .bincfg configs, a flatbuffer schema, separate .conv_model/.lstm_model binaries and class lists, i.e. a pipeline to reimplement rather than a model to load. And the runtime half is worse than assumed: tflite-runtime is not in Arch's official repos, while python-onnxruntime-cpu IS (extra). WHAT SURVIVES: the ARCHITECTURE is open even though the weights are not -- 'Fast Multi-language LSTM-based Online Handwriting Recognition' (arXiv 1902.10525) is the published Gboard/ML Kit system, Bezier-curve input encoding into a BLSTM/QRNN stack trained with CTC, which independently CONFIRMS this row's online-over-image call rather than merely asserting it. Open stroke-based models exist with published weights (chunkyjasper/IAMhwr, 6.2% CER on IAM-OnDB; recent work such as Col-OLHTR reaches 1.61%) but none ships a ready-to-drop ONNX/tflite artefact.
