THE FORK, and it is the user's call, not a technical one: (a) train/convert ONE small BLSTM+CTC model to ONNX and optdepend on python-onnxruntime-cpu -- realistic packaging, much lighter than torch, but somebody has to do the training run and the payoff is uncertain; (b) drop general recognition and do the writer-dependent, character-level thing instead, which needs no ML dependency at all -- CellWriter (GPL, Linux, grid-entry, learns YOUR hand, Unicode) is the existing art and is worth reading even though it is GTK2-era and unpackaged on Arch; this is also row 184's territory, and it revives the 'train on the user's own handwriting' option this row had set aside; (c) park it until a permissively licensed off-the-shelf stroke model appears. REJECTED here and now: Google Input Tools' undocumented endpoint (inputtools.google.com/request?ime=handwriting, what the deprecated handwriting.js used, still live) -- it is a network round trip for an OFFLINE notes app, undocumented and revocable at any time, and it would send every stroke of the user's private notes to Google.

column2: Superimposed single-character quick-entry mode
column5: IDEA (2026-08-31), from MyScript's smartwatch demo specifically: their trick for tiny surfaces is not 'small-screen recognition', it is SUPERIMPOSED CHARACTERS - you write one glyph at a time, on top of the previous one, so the surface only ever needs to hold a single character (the SDK page's own framing: 'small-surface devices like smart watches or IoT, where a virtual keyboard is difficult to use'). A phone screen has no such size problem, but the INTERACTION is what's worth borrowing: a small dedicated box (on the phone, over row 182's transport, or even on the desktop itself) where writing one character appends one recognized glyph as real text - effectively a handwritten keyboard replacement, and specifically a way to get text INTO Sidemark on a desktop with no touchscreen at all, using the phone as the surface. Depends on BOTH row 182 (getting strokes off a device) and row 183 (recognizing them) existing first; simpler than row 183's general case because there is no word/line segmentation to get right - input is already one character at a time. Not started; revisit once 182 and 183 both have something working to build on. ANALYSED, not built (2026-09-01, user asked while testing row 182's phone editor): the hard part is SEGMENTATION, not recognition. Knowing WHERE one character ends is what superimposed entry needs; knowing WHICH letter it was is only needed to turn ink into text. A pen lift plus a pause - the user's own suggested heuristic - segments single-stroke letters correctly and mis-segments every multi-stroke one: i, j, t, x, f and most capitals. A timeout long enough to hold them together is long enough to feel laggy on every other letter, which is why MyScript uses recognition for exactly this and not for the transport. So this stays its own feature with its own prototype. What DID ship from the same conversation is the part that needs neither: write-and-advance (row 187), where the question is only 'have you run out of room?', which a stroke's own end position answers exactly.

column2: Ink beautification / snap-to-glyph once a character is recognized
column5: IDEA (2026-08-31), the user's own suggestion: once recognition (row 183) knows what character a stroke IS, could the drawn ink itself be cleaned up/corrected to look like a nicer version of that letter - the same MOVE as recognize_shape's dwell-triggered snap (row 121), which already replaces a wobbly rectangle/circle/line with a clean geometric version, generalized from five geometric primitives to an alphabet of letterform templates. The disanalogy that makes this genuinely harder, not just bigger: a rectangle has ONE clean form to snap to, so the primitive's own geometry defines success; a letter has enormous variation between people and even between two attempts by the same person, so 'the clean version' is not obviously well-defined the way a rectangle's four right angles are - get it wrong and it either looks uncannily uniform (loses what makes it THEIR handwriting) or barely changes anything (not worth the complexity). Also: if row 183's recognition is working, the user may not want 'nicer ink' at all so much as the option to just render the recognized result as real TEXT, which is the whole point of building recognition in the first place - beautification is really only interesting for someone who wants to KEEP the ink/handwriting look while making it tidier (the reMarkable/Samsung Notes-style 'neaten as you write' feature), a different value proposition from search/convert-to-text. Deliberately parked rather than sequenced: worth returning to only once rows 182/183 exist and it's clear there's still an appetite for 'better-looking ink' as distinct from 'ink converted to text'.

column2: Public link sharing via Tailscale Funnel (Share-to-phone extension)
column5: PROTOTYPE, extended from Share-to-phone (#62) at the user's request (2026-08-31): the existing LAN/Tailscale share dialog gets a third option, a public link via TAILSCALE FUNNEL (`tailscale funnel --bg --yes <port>`) — the phone needs no Tailscale app, no shared network at all, just the link/QR, reachable from anywhere. Attempted only when _tailscale_ip() already shows the machine connected; the CLI's own stdout carries the public hostname on success, and its own error text is surfaced as the dialog's hint on failure (never a bespoke message guessing why). Two real bugs found and fixed while driving it in the hand, both worth remembering: (1) `tailscale funnel` shows a ONE-TIME interactive confirmation on first use per node, which a non-interactive subprocess.run just hangs against — fixed with `--yes` (skip the prompt) and `stdin=DEVNULL` (fail fast if some other prompt ever shows), timeout raised 10s->25s for first-run ACME cert issuance. (2) Funnel fronts the node's ROOT, not our server's `/token/` path — the CLI's own printed URL was used directly as the QR link, which rendered fine and led nowhere; fixed by having _tailscale_funnel_start return just the HOSTNAME and building the actual link through `server.url_for(host, scheme="https", port=None)`, the same helper every other entry already uses. UX, reworked twice more with the user live: entries come back from _share_prepare in PRIORITY order (public link, tailnet, LAN — was 3 side-by-side columns, now a Gtk.StackSwitcher defaulting to the first entry that actually has a url, so the best reachable option is what you see first). AND sharing now OUTLIVES its own window: closing the QR window (the X, or just walking away) no longer tears the server down — only "Stop sharing" (in the reopened window), a 10-minute safety-net timeout, or the app quitting does (_stop_sharing, wired into _destroy_all). Reopening a live share (_reopen_share_window) rebuilds just the chrome around the cached (server, entries) — no re-running tailscale/funnel/QR work. A generation counter (_share_gen) guards the one real race this created: closing the window WHILE STILL LOADING (before anything went live) abandons the in-flight worker instead of letting it resurrect a share nobody is looking at anymore. Discoverability without extra chrome: no separate "currently sharing" banner (tried, the user asked for something lighter) — the existing Share button IS the live indicator, tinted with Adwaita's own `.success` CSS class while active (_update_share_indicator); its click behaviour never changes (always opens/reopens the panel), only the look does, which is what keeps a plain click unambiguous — a real toggle here would leave "does clicking an active toggle stop it or view it?" unanswered. NOT YET VERIFIED IN THE HAND after this latest round (indicator tint, smaller window/QR, switcher default) — needs a pass with the panel like every gesture-shaped feature in this file. Tests: TestShareToPhone (funnel start/stop CLI wrapping, entry priority order, url_for's scheme/port override) and TestShareStopUX (the close-vs-stop state machine, duck-typed against the window so no real GTK/weston is needed for the logic half). TWO REAL DEFECTS FOUND AND FIXED (2026-09-01), both from the user asking why the QR dialog was slow. (1) It was slow for two reasons and the BIGGER one was not the Funnel: `HTTPServer.server_bind` calls `socket.getfqdn()` to fill in `server_name`, which on our 0.0.0.0 bind is a reverse lookup with nowhere to go — MEASURED at 5004 ms, every single time the dialog was opened, for a value this server never emits (it is only ever read for CGI variables). A three-line server_bind override removes it. The Funnel was the other half: seconds, with a 25 s ceiling, computed inline, so the LAN QR that was ready in 0 ms waited on a public link most sessions never open. It is now provisioned on a second worker and slotted in (_share_finish_funnel) with the QR already scannable. _share_prepare went 5059 ms -> 24 ms. The arriving link deliberately does NOT take the dropdown: it would become 'the best entry with a url' and swap the QR under you mid-scan, which — now that Writing is the default — quietly widens who can draw on the document. So a re-render keeps the address on screen and the public link is something you PICK. (2) CTRL+C LEAKED A LIVE PUBLIC FUNNEL. `_on_sigint` called `win.destroy()`, which deliberately skips close-request so it never blocks on a save prompt — but close-request was the ONLY path reaching `_stop_sharing`, so a public hostname stayed mapped to a dead port with nothing left running that knew to remove it (the mapping lives in tailscaled, not in us). Found by reading `tailscale funnel status` on the user's own machine and seeing a stale mapping. Now `_on_sigint` goes through `_destroy_all`, SIGTERM is wired to the same handler (a logout leaked identically), and `_live_funnels` + atexit drop anything this process mapped as a last resort. Nothing can cover SIGKILL. THREE MORE DEFECTS, all found by using it (2026-09-01). (1) A LATE TEARDOWN KILLED A LIVE FUNNEL. The stop is NODE-WIDE (`--https=443 off` is the only spelling the current CLI accepts) and the port is now stable, so an abandoned share's teardown turned off the funnel a NEWER share had just brought up — and both were :8756, so nothing distinguished them. It now only tears down when nothing has taken its place. (2) The success line was logged where the funnel was PROVISIONED, not where it was KEPT, so the log said 'public link live' about a link that had just been turned off again. Moved, and every teardown now logs its caller with a stack — a public link that dies for no visible reason is the hardest failure this feature has. (3) STILL BROKEN, and NOT OURS: with the funnel confirmed on, the node advertising IngressEnabled, the funnel attr granted, HTTPS certs enabled, AllowFunnel true on :443 proxying to a listening port, Tailscale's PUBLIC ingress accepts the TCP connection and closes during the TLS handshake before the ServerHello — and tailscaled logs nothing, so the connection never reaches the machine. Verified repeatedly against all three ingress IPs with fresh DNS. The tailnet path works throughout. `funnel reset` and restarting tailscaled changed nothing. This is a Tailscale-side problem and the reproduction is above; do not go looking for it in this code. SEPARATELY, and independent of it: Cloudflare's resolver returns NXDOMAIN for the .ts.net name even while the funnel is up, while Google and Quad9 both resolve it — so a device on Cloudflare DNS (Brave's own Secure DNS commonly defaults to it) cannot reach the link at all, whatever the ingress does. TWO CAUSES, one symptom; the second is the one a user can actually act on.

column2: Write and advance (the page moves along as you write on a phone)
column5: SHIPPED (2026-09-01), asked for by the user while testing row 182's phone editor: writing on a phone runs out of room in about four words, and the page has to move. The only moment it can move WITHOUT interrupting you is after you have finished a stroke near the edge and not started another — so the trigger is a stroke ending in the right-hand band plus a pause, and a new press cancels it. Off by default, in the phone's hamburger menu: a view that moves on its own is the last thing you want when you are not writing prose. TUNED IN THE HAND, twice: the move was increased (the writing's right edge now lands at 15% rather than 28% of the viewport), and the trigger reads the RIGHTMOST POINT WRITTEN ACROSS THE RUN rather than the last stroke's — the stroke that finishes a word is often a short backward one (an i-dot, a t-bar), so judging by it alone meant the page refused to move at exactly the moment you had run out of room. At the page edge it wraps to the next line, back to the page's own left margin (not the run's leftmost point, which by then is wherever the last move left it) and down by the size of what you have actually been writing — so it self-calibrates to your handwriting and needs no configured line height. PURELY A CAMERA MOVE: the phone already holds its own view and ink commits in document coordinates, so this cannot displace a stroke or desync a shared session; the worst it can do is scroll at a moment you did not want. DELIBERATELY NO CHARACTER SEGMENTATION — 'have you run out of room?' is answered exactly by where a stroke ended, while 'was that a letter?' is not answered by a pen lift at all (row 184).

column2: `sidemark --version` (which copy am I actually running?)
column5: SHIPPED (2026-09-01), from a real confusion the user hit: edits appeared not to land after install.sh, while running the script directly was up to date. install.sh was working the whole time — there were TWO installs (an AUR `sidemark-git` at /usr/share, dated three weeks earlier, and install.sh's at ~/.local/share) and /usr/bin precedes ~/.local/bin in PATH, so typing `sidemark` ran the old one. So --version answers 'WHICH copy is this?' as much as 'which version': the running FILE's path, its date, the commit, HOW MANY FILES have changed since that commit, and — when there is more than one sidemark on PATH — all of them, with an arrow at the one that wins. An installed copy has no .git, so install.sh and both PKGBUILDs stamp a `build.json` at install time; that is also the only moment the source tree's dirtiness is still knowable. A PRE-GTK FAST PATH, like --help and --list-recent, because the question is at its most useful when the app will not start. TRAP MET WHILE WRITING IT: `${x:+..}${x:-..}` is NOT an if/else — when x is set BOTH halves expand, which wrote `"abc123"abc123` into build.json and made it unparseable.

column2: The share address is stable, nameable, and public links get their own
column5: SHIPPED (2026-09-01), from a real confusion: the share URL 404'd on the phone because BOTH halves of it changed every session — a random high port and a fresh token. The port was unfirewallable by construction (ufw with DEFAULT_INPUT_POLICY=DROP allowed 53317/53/25565 and nothing else, so the phone's connection was simply dropped and the page never loaded — Chrome showed nothing, and no code of ours ever ran), and the token made every bookmark and home-screen shortcut die overnight. NOW: a preferred port (8756, falling back to a random one if taken) so a single `ufw allow` holds for good, and the Same Wi-Fi entry DETECTS a running firewall and prints the exact command — this failure is otherwise silent from inside the app, because the connection never arrives. The token PERSISTS in settings.json, can be RENAMED to anything URL-safe of 4+ characters (it IS the path, so a space would arrive percent-encoded elsewhere and a slash would split it in two), and can be rolled, which revokes every saved copy at once. A stale link no longer 404s bare: it says the address changed and to scan the new QR — for a NAVIGATION only, since a stray HTML body in place of a script is worse than an honest error. TWO SECRETS, NOT ONE, and this is the part that matters: a permanent secret is what makes the address bookmarkable and exactly what must not travel over the PUBLIC tier, where it leaks in ways a per-session one cannot (browser history, a photo of the QR, a screen share) and stays valid until somebody thinks to rotate it. So the private tiers keep the address your own devices know and the public link carries its own, fresh every session and never saved. The flaw was introduced and caught within the same session: permanent link + public tier + Writing-by-default is a standing, writable, public URL, and each of the three was individually reasonable. A ONE-TIME toggle covers handing a link to somebody else deliberately. ALSO: stopping a share froze the UI for up to half a second (socketserver's shutdown waits for an accept loop that polls at 0.5 s) — row 169's watchdog caught it and named the frame; the teardown runs off the main thread now, 0.3 ms.

column2: Sidemark as an installed app on the phone (PWA, scan-to-link, an installable share address)
column5: SHIPPED (2026-09-08), asked for by the user: install Sidemark on an Android phone, scan a share QR to link a computer to it, and have the integration feel native rather than like a bookmark. THE CENTRAL CONSTRAINT, and the reason the shipped shape differs from the one asked for: an installed page has the SAME ORIGIN and the same network rules as a tab — installing is not a permission grant, and both checks happen per REQUEST. So the hosted copy on GitHub Pages cannot speak the share protocol to a desktop however it is packaged: a LAN address fails MIXED CONTENT (no CA issues a certificate for 192.168.x.x, so there is no https version to ask for) and a tailnet address over real TLS is refused by Chrome's LOCAL NETWORK ACCESS, which counts the tailnet as local — both already measured on row 182, and 'serve structured JSON instead of a page' does not reopen either, because the block is on the request, not the payload. WHAT SHIPPED INSTEAD, in three parts. (1) The Pages copy is a real PWA: manifest.webmanifest + sw.js, an own icon, a standalone window, and a 43-entry precached shell (4.3 MB, vendor/ is most of it) so it opens with no network. Plus the two things that actually make it feel installed and which nobody asked for: SHARE_TARGET, so Android's share sheet gains 'Sidemark' and a PDF sent to it opens here — the service worker takes the multipart POST, parks the files in a Cache (never IndexedDB: db.js owns the one database and its one version, and a worker opening it on its own schedule is exactly the mismatch that file exists to prevent) and 303s to ./?shared=1, which the app collects and empties; and FILE_HANDLERS, so 'open with Sidemark' arrives carrying HANDLES and therefore saves back in place with no second gesture. (2) 'My desktops' in the ☰: an IndexedDB list of ADDRESSES filled by a QR scanner (BarcodeDetector, native on Android Chrome, one capability check and a paste box everywhere else — a vendored decoder would be 40 kB carried by every visitor for a button most never press). Tapping one NAVIGATES; there is no probe first, because 'is it sharing?' is the cross-origin request this page may not make, so the answer comes from arriving. In a standalone window that leaves for a browser tab, which is the visible seam of the whole design and is stated rather than hidden. The scanner earns its place on the PUBLIC tier specifically: that token is fresh every session and never saved (row 189), so it is the one address that cannot be a bookmark. (3) A fourth share tier, 'Install on phone': `tailscale serve --bg --https=8443`, a real Let's Encrypt certificate on the node's own name with nothing published — the only PRIVATE https address this machine has, and therefore the only one a phone can install the desktop's own copy from. PORT 8443 AND NOT 443 is load-bearing: 443 is Funnel's front, and _tailscale_funnel_stop is node-wide (`--https=443 off` is the only spelling the CLI takes), so sharing the port would make a share ending silently drop the other mapping with nothing to tell them apart. Provisioned in the BACKGROUND and starting `pending`, like the funnel and for the same reason (row 186): a certificate takes seconds and a late tier must never take the tab under a scan. It carries the PERMANENT token, deliberately unlike the public link — an installed icon whose start_url expired at the end of the session is an icon that opens a 404, and this address never leaves the tailnet. The desktop GENERATES its manifest (app_manifest) rather than serving the port's file: start_url is ./?live=1 (without the flag the icon opens the app in its ordinary mode on the desktop's origin — a blank page that reads as a broken share), the name carries the hostname so two computers are two distinguishable icons, `id` carries the token so the second install does not replace the first, and share_target/file_handlers are dropped for the same reason Open and Save are hidden in a live session. Everything else comes from web/manifest.webmanifest so the two cannot drift. THE WORKER HAS TWO FLAVOURS, one file, flagged in the script URL: hosted is precache + cache-first (instant, offline, a deploy one launch later); live is network-first with no precache, because the desktop serves web/ off a checkout somebody may be editing and a cache-first worker there would hand the phone yesterday's app. Neither can touch the session's data — ../state, ../live.pdf, ../page.pdf and ../ws sit one level ABOVE the app directory the worker is scoped to, unreachable by construction rather than by a rule. REGISTRATION GATES ON isSecureContext, not on a protocol test: a hand-rolled hostname check quietly left the loopback addresses out, which is how the first browser run showed no worker at all. STILL OPEN, and the one thing that would collapse this design into the one the user originally described: Chrome has been moving LNA toward a user PERMISSION PROMPT. Row 182's measurement records that a tailnet https fetch from a public origin was blocked, but not whether a prompt was offered and refused or never appeared — different findings, only one durable. web/lna-probe.html settles it from the phone in ten minutes (no-cors on purpose, so a refusal is the network refusing and not CORS, with the plain-http address tested alongside as the contrast that can never change). If a prompt appears and can be granted, the hosted app can talk to the desktop directly and 'My desktops' stops being a launcher and becomes a client. Tests: web/test/pwa.mjs (124 checks — the precache list against the directory both ways, the manifest, the sw/pwa handoff constants agreeing, registration refusing sandbox and plain http, and what a scanned code is allowed to be) plus the desktop half in TestShareToPhone; the whole share-target path was additionally driven through a real service worker in headless Chromium. FIXED SAME DAY, from the user's first run: 'Install on phone' produced no QR and the dialog showed the CLI's own words — 'Another client is changing the serve config; please try again. / Preconditions failed: etag mismatch'. Cause was this row's own doing: _share_finish_serve and _share_finish_funnel each started their own thread, and `tailscale serve` and `tailscale funnel` write the SAME etag-guarded serve config in tailscaled — run at once, one is rejected outright and its QR never appears. Fixed by SEQUENCING them onto one thread (_share_finish_addresses), serve first because the funnel can sit for its full 25 s ceiling on a tailnet with Funnel off and somebody waiting to install should not queue behind a link they may never open; each _share_finish_* now RETURNS its worker rather than starting one. _TAILSCALE_CONFIG_LOCK plus a bounded retry in _tailscale_config_run covers writers this process does not own (a second Sidemark, a terminal, the admin console) and now carries every serve/funnel start AND stop, since a teardown races a provisioning thread just as readily. Second half, asked for explicitly: the CLI's text is TRANSLATED (_tailscale_hint) into a sentence with a cause and a next step — busy config, not signed in, no HTTPS certificate, Funnel not enabled, timed out — and the raw text is kept behind a 'What Tailscale said' expander rather than thrown away, because it is what a bug report needs and not what a reader needs. Tests cover the sequencing, one tier failing not stranding the other, the retry giving up rather than spinning, and that no translated sentence contains the words 'etag' or 'precondition'.

column2: Exported notes keep their maths (an embedded Unicode font)
column5: SHIPPED (2026-09-11). A LIVE BUG, and phase 0 of row 168's plan (notes/text-objects-plan.md), which is where it was found and where it is standalone by design. The PDF export wrote every glyph with base-14 `helv`, which is LATIN-1: all 64 symbols the notes grammar can produce and all six combining accents (`\alpha`->a, `\sum`->S, `\R`->R, `\to`->arrow, `\hat{x}`) reached the file as `?`. Measured, not estimated: 60 of the 64 were lost (the four survivors are Latin-1's own +- . x /). It was silent and it was terminal -- the maths went missing at the one moment the notes leave the app, and you find out after handing the file to somebody. It hit TWO surfaces, not one: `_draw_page_marks` is shared with the phone-share render, so a callout's maths was drawn as `?` into the PNG a phone sees live. THE FONT: DejaVu Sans, chosen by probing every font installed on this machine against `_MD_SYMBOLS`+`_MD_ACCENTS` rather than by eye -- AdwaitaMono also covers 100% but is monospace and would have changed how every export looks; no PROPORTIONAL font installed here covers the set (best was Noto Sans CJK, missing 10; AdwaitaSans misses 16, incl. every blackboard-bold letter). That confirms the plan's 2026-08-14 finding, which is why a dependency was the answer and not a lucky `fc-match`. `ttf-dejavu` is now a hard dep (fonts-dejavu-core / dejavu-sans-fonts elsewhere): an export that silently drops the maths is worse than a 750 KB package. Resolution tries the four distro paths, then TeX Live's copy (same font, deliberately outside fontconfig), then `fc-match` -- whose answer is CHECKED against the family asked for, because fc-match ALWAYS replies and here it offers Liberation Sans, which has neither R nor the combining marks. An unverified reply is exactly how a 'Unicode font' silently becomes Latin-1 again. Missing it falls back to base-14 rather than failing the export. THE TRAP WORTH KEEPING: measure with the font you draw with. Four places size a box from the text that goes in it (_NotesWriter._wrap, the callout and text-box height probes, the anchor label's centring), and `insert_textbox` renders NOTHING when the text does not fit, so a height measured in another font is an EMPTY box, not a clipped one. `_export_font()` hands out name and file together and `_fit_export_box()` is now one helper both boxes call, so the pair cannot drift. Fonts are subset before save (1.49 MB -> 67 KB measured). Tests generate their cases FROM the two symbol tables, so a new command is covered without anyone remembering to; they were confirmed to fail without the fix (60 symbols, 6 accents, the callout reading 'energy ?and ?'). REGRESSION CAUGHT IN USE, SAME DAY: subsetting was unconditional at first and froze the window for ~27 s on a 428-page, 82-font book -- reported by row 169's watchdog during an ordinary export. TWO things made it invisible in testing. `subset_fonts()` HOLDS THE GIL for its whole run (measured: 469 ms of work, 469 ms of main loop starved), so running the export on a worker thread -- which it already does -- buys nothing; and the cost is the SOURCE's fonts, not ours, so it never showed on the small documents the tests build. Measured in the export path: 17 fonts/23 ms, 22/76, 28/244, 38/763, 47/3072, while the saving stays FLAT at ~800-930 KB because it is only ever our own font being shrunk (a book's fonts arrived subset, and re-subsetting them is not ours to do). So it is gated on the finished document's font count against STALL_WARN_MS, the app's own 250 ms 'hitch a hand notices': small exports subset and stay ~60 KB, big ones keep the full font and export in 1.4 s instead of 28.9 s, +0.75 MB on 7 MB. The test asserts the glyphs survive EITHER WAY, so the limit can be retuned without re-checking the text. ceiling: a large export carries the full font; if that size ever matters more than the wait, subset the notes pages in a scratch document and insert_pdf them so the cost follows our pages. NOT ours and still open: the export's final save() holds the GIL ~950 ms on a 7 MB document -- measured identical before this change.
